22487-journal-of-a-young-lady-of-virgini:
Journal of a Young Lady of Virginia, 1782, preserves a girl's diary of revolutionary years. Lucy, the young writer, records reading, visits, and walks in a clear hand. One morning's entry shows her daily pleasures plainly.

She spent the morning in reading, much to her satisfaction. Old Mrs. Gordon came to spend the day at the house. Lucy Gordon and she returned from walking out together with delight. They walked to a narrow river they only call a river. Its banks are beautiful, covered with moss and wild flowers. All that a romantic mind could form, she writes. Such entries give social history a young woman's fresh, exact voice.
an-account-of-some-experiments-on-mercur: An Account of Some Experiments on Mercury, Silver and Gold, 1782. The Guildford experiments. This book preserves that account. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
arxiv-2512-00082:
Judging how visually complex a web page looks is a task people do at a glance. Divendar Murtadak and Yoon Kim test whether multimodal language models can do it reliably, in a 2025 case study. Their test pages are Amazon search results pages, rated against judgments from human experts.

The authors compare diagnostic prompting with standard prompting based on gestalt principles. Diagnostic prompting improved how well the model matched human complexity judgments in their tests. The study matters for design and retail research, where automated page assessment could speed up work that now needs human raters. Design teams routinely face this judgment when they compare page layouts.
arxiv-2512-00182:
Jayce Getz and co-authors develop a new function space for harmonic analysis on reductive groups in 2025. The space is named in the title after a representation of the group's Langlands dual. Suitable assumptions on that representation shape the whole construction.

Spaces of test functions control which integrals and transforms are well behaved in the Langlands program. That program is a vast web of conjectures linking number theory and representation theory. A well-chosen Schwartz space can make trace formulas and period integrals work more smoothly. The work is deep pure mathematics for specialists in automorphic forms. The assumptions on the representation decide which groups and fields the theory covers.
arxiv-2512-00482:
Speech enhancement models are usually judged only by how clean their output sounds. Yair Amar, Amir Ivry, and Israel Cohen instead probe the internal representations of an enhancement model in 2025. They use MUSE, a transformer-convolutional model trained on the VoiceBank DEMAND corpus.

Activations are analyzed across the encoder, latent space, decoder, and refinement blocks while input noise levels sweep widely. Watching representations change with noise reveals whether the model organizes sounds sensibly or relies on brittle shortcuts. Such probing helps engineers build hearing and communication tools that degrade gracefully in real-world noise. VoiceBank DEMAND is a standard noisy-speech corpus, which makes the probing comparable to other work.
arxiv-2512-00782:
Aviv Aroch, Shimshon Kallush, and Ronnie Kosloff work on controlling noisy quantum gates in a 2025 paper. Quantum systems pick up noise from their surroundings and from imperfect control fields. That noise lowers the fidelity of gates, the basic operations of a quantum computer.

The team uses optimal control, which shapes control pulses carefully to hit a target despite the noise. Their setting is a multilevel system, where each unit holds more than the usual two states, and the noise is thermal. Better pulses for noisy multilevel systems could make quantum hardware more reliable without new materials.
arxiv-2512-00982:
Christoph Pütz classifies certain power series in a 2025 math paper. A Laurent series is like a power series that also allows negative powers. Pütz studies those that converge on the unit circle over a non-Archimedean local field, a number system measured by a prime-like valuation rather than size.

He fully classifies the series that send infinitely many roots of unity to roots of unity. Roots of unity are the special points that multiply back to one after fixed steps. For series over fields of positive characteristic, he proves effective bounds on how many such roots can occur. Classification results pin down rare, rigid behavior.
arxiv-2512-01082:
Praphull Kumar, Dean Townsley, and Hunter Anz study vibrating white dwarf stars in a 2025 astronomy paper. White dwarfs are the final fate of most stars in our galaxy, so they trace stellar history well. Some white dwarfs pull matter from a companion star in cataclysmic variable systems.

A subset of those systems undergo dwarf novae outbursts, episodes of rapid mass transfer and brightening. The authors relate major physical parameters of these accreting white dwarfs to their normal mode frequencies. Those frequencies are the tones at which the star naturally oscillates, set by parameters like mass and temperature. Those frequencies, if observed, could reveal the star's hidden properties.
arxiv-2512-01182:
Yuri Shimane, Karl Berntorp, Stefano Di Cairano, and Avishai Weiss build a navigation pipeline for lunar orbits in a 2025 paper. Near-rectilinear halo orbits are large, elongated loops around the Moon, planned as parking orbits for lunar stations. Staying on one takes careful navigation and station-keeping in a high-fidelity model of real gravitational dynamics.

Their pipeline generates synthetic camera images and feeds them to a horizon-based optical navigation algorithm. An extended Kalman filter turns those sightings into a state estimate, and a controller keeps the spacecraft near its reference orbit. Self-reliant navigation reduces dependence on Earth tracking.
arxiv-2512-01282:
Jiahao Yuan and co-authors work on chat tools that give kind, helpful replies. Good support needs more than soft words. A tool should know who the user is and what that user feels over time. Many past tools lose track of the user and give vague replies.

The team built Kardia-R1 to fix that gap. It trains a language model to think step by step about a user's state. A judge based on clear rules scores each reply for care and fit. Strong scores guide the model to learn. The goal is support that feels both warm and well aimed.
arxiv-2512-01582:
Junran Peng and co-authors release RoleMotion, a large set of human motion data. It holds role-play and task motions fit to set scenes. Past text-motion sets were built from scattered parts. Their clips were isolated and not tied to real social acts.

RoleMotion ties motions to scenes and roles in fine detail. Each clip is labeled for its role and goal. Models trained on it can make motion that fits a scene, not just a prompt. That helps animation, games, and robot training where acts must suit the place.
arxiv-2512-01682: Guilherme Seidyo Imai Aldeia completed a thesis in Santo Andre in November 2025 on current challenges in symbolic regression. Fabricio Olivetti de Franca supervised the work. Symbolic regression searches for short math formulas that fit a data set. It does not fit a fixed model form. The thesis covers four open problems in that search. They are how to optimize candidate formulas, how to select among them, how to simplify them, and how to benchmark methods fairly.
arxiv-2512-01782:
Chenhao Sun, Yuhao Mao, and Martin Vechev improve randomized smoothing beyond one global noise level. Smoothing certifies that a network resists small attacks. Noise size sets a trade-off. Small noise certifies small radii well, large noise certifies large radii well. One variance cannot do both.

Their dual method uses two noise scales at once. That split aims for high accuracy at both small and large radii. Certified defenses matter for vision systems in safety roles. Dual smoothing could widen the certified range without a matching loss in clean accuracy. Dual scales compose at inference, so one deployed net carries both certificates without doubling its size or its serving cost.
arxiv-2512-01882:
Self-driving cars must fuse camera images, laser scans, and heading data into split-second decisions, and the computing budget on board is tight. A 2025 paper by Aref Ghoreishee and four co-authors proposes a new spiking architecture for this multi-modal decision-making, built around reinforcement learning from end to end.

Their perception module uses cross-attention transformers to merge the different sensor streams. Transformers are powerful but costly, which limits their use on small edge hardware in vehicles. Spiking networks, which compute with brief pulses like real neurons, promise a cheaper route. The work tests whether that promise can meet the demands of driving decisions.
arxiv-2512-02182:
Checking cheap measures against true ones costs money. So studies check a small subset of patients with the costly test. Sarah Lotspeich and Cole Manschot build a 2025 plan for this two-phase check. It works across several models at once and stays easy to grasp, with help from principal components.

In phase one, cheap facts are gathered for all in the study. In phase two, a subset gets the costly, more exact checks. The hard part is to pick and weigh that subset so the fix serves many models, not just one. Good design saves funds in large health data banks, where no one can test all with care.
arxiv-2512-02282:
Chat systems now talk with folks in deep distress. A careless reply in a crisis chat can do real harm. Han Luo and Guy Laban built DialogGuard in 2025. The tool grades the safety of model replies in such raw, touchy talks.

It grades five grave risks. They are leaks of private facts, biased or unfair acts, sly steering of the user, harm to the mind, and insults. A team of agents shares the grading, since one pass can miss much. Checks of this sort must come first, before chat tools are let near crisis help lines.
arxiv-2512-02482:
Vishwesh Nath and colleagues at NVIDIA and Northwell Health build tools for seeing inside the body during surgery. Small scope surgery needs fast, accurate 3D views of soft tissue that bends and shifts. Recent Gaussian splatting methods render such scenes in real time, which suits live use in an operating room.

Many of those methods rest on code that firms cannot use in products, which blocks real deployment. The team's G-SHARP pipeline is built to be commercially usable from the start. Fast, lawful, and accurate tissue views could help surgeons work with more confidence during delicate procedures. In time, such views could cut risk when a cut must be placed with great care.
arxiv-2512-02682:
P. Bisconti and four co-authors warn that AI safety tools built for one model fail when models talk to each other. Current practice guards single agents with prompts, fine tuning, and moderation layers. Those layers constrain one model's behavior but leave group dynamics ungoverned.

The 2025 study builds a taxonomy of risks that arise in model to model interaction. New failure modes can emerge from feedback loops, imitation, and shared blind spots between agents. A shared risk map gives regulators and builders a starting point for governing multi agent systems before they scale further. Two safe bots can still make an unsafe pair, and that is the gap this map tries to name first.
arxiv-2512-02782:
Hu Cang and Yuan Wang ask whether quantum spacetime itself would blur gravitational waves as they cross the universe. Microscopic curvature fluctuations, if real, should leave a mark on long traveling waves. The authors build a gauge invariant framework, free of coordinate artifacts, for that cumulative effect.

Working from the Riemann tensor's two point function, they use the extreme slowness of cosmic expansion versus wave frequency. Phase diffusion emerges as the unique leading imprint, not fading or mode mixing. A clear, falsifiable target helps future detectors test quantum gravity ideas with real data. A phase drift is a faint mark, but faint marks are what the next wave of gear is built to catch in flight.
arxiv-2512-02882:
Youkang Wang and five co-authors spend a language model's test time budget where it counts most. Test time policy optimization lets a model adapt to shifted tasks using feedback from its own trial answers. Common methods estimate rewards by majority vote over a fixed number of rollouts, wasting compute.

OptPO allocates rollouts adaptively, giving more trials where the reward is still uncertain. That principled budgeting trims substantial redundancy, the authors argue. Smarter allocation could make self improving inference cheaper, helping deployed models adapt without retraining or human labels. Trials cost time and coin, so a plan that spends them where doubt is thick is a plan that pays for its own keep.
arxiv-2512-02982:
Xiang Xu and six co-authors model moving 3D worlds from LiDAR sequences while tracking where the model is unsure. Dynamic scene modeling underpins 4D worlds for autonomous driving and embodied AI. Existing generative frameworks treat every region alike, ignoring how uncertainty varies across a real scene.

Uniform generation leaves artifacts in complex or ambiguous regions, hurting realism and temporal stability. U4D makes generation uncertainty aware, spending care where the scene is hardest. Worlds that know their own weak spots are safer to train and test driving systems inside. Marks of doubt on the map warn the car where to slow. A plain map with no doubt marks can not serve that use at all in fog or glare.
arxiv-2512-03082:
Large language models can favor their own past choices. Nan Zhuang and five co-authors study that flaw, called choice-supportive bias, in this 2025 work. When a model judges options, it may back the one it picked before, which can skew fair decisions.

Most past fixes target bias about social groups, not this kind of thinking bias. The authors build a method based on how reasons depend on each other. Their aim is to make model judgments more even and fair. Fair judging matters as these models help with hiring, grading, and other key choices. For model evaluators, the work shows that bias can hide in choices, not just in data about people.
arxiv-2512-03482:
Special wave functions on exotic surfaces hide number patterns. Jiaqi Hou studies Kakeya-Nikodym norms of Maass forms in this 2025 work. The setting is a compact arithmetic complex hyperbolic surface, with a Hecke-Maass form of large spectral parameter.

Hou applies the amplification method to bound the norm. The result gains a power saving over the trivial bound. Such bounds show how evenly wave functions spread. They connect analysis, geometry, and number theory in the study of quantum chaos on arithmetic spaces. Amplification boosts a chosen form's signal, a standard trick with delicate tuning.
arxiv-2512-03582:
Propaganda works through stories, not just slogans. This 2025 study proposes fine-grained narrative classification in biased news articles. Narratives organize persuasive techniques into coherent stories that assign blame and build identification with a camp.

The authors also explore article-bias classification as a precursor task. Sorting narratives at a fine grain could help analysts track how biased outlets frame events. Such tools may support media literacy and research on polarization. They must be used with care to avoid labeling disputes. Bias classification first helps sort articles before the harder narrative labels are applied, giving the pipeline a staged path to fine detail.
arxiv-2512-03782: Marco Adamo Seveso develops an explicit p-adic integration theory in this short 2025 number theory note. The setting is the Igusa towers built over Siegel modular varieties, families of spaces that organise modular forms of higher genus. P-adic integration assigns sizes to sets in the p-adic world, where distance is measured by divisibility by a prime. Seveso states that the theory he builds has applications to explicit reciprocity laws, a central theme in modern number theory.
arxiv-2601-06782:
Sungtaek Son, Eardi Lila, and Kwun Chuen Gary Chan wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on care plans built for each patient. Such plans are called individualized treatment regimes, or ITRs. A plan gives a treatment based on facts about that patient. The paper works with data from studies that watch patients, not trials that assign care.

Past methods can fail when each patient record holds a great many facts. Too many facts can hurt how well a plan works and how clear it is. The authors cut the list of facts down to a small set. That small set still holds the gap in results between one treatment and the next. In this way the plan can stay sharp while it stays simple to read and use.
arxiv-2601-07082:
Valentin Nkana Ngan and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with efficient hyper-reduced-order model for segregated solvers for geometrical parametrization problems. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The authors propose an efficient hyper-reduced order model (HROM) designed for segregated finite-volume solvers in geometrically parametrized problems. The method follows a discretize-then-project strategy: the full-order operators are first assembled using.

Finite volume or finite element discretizations and then projected onto low-dimensional spaces using. A small set of spatial sampling points. Selected through hyper-reduction techniques such as DEIM. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07182:
Ruiyi Ding and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers PRPO. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Policy optimization for large language models often suffers from sparse reward signals in multi-step reasoning tasks. Critic-free methods like GRPO assign a single normalized outcome reward to all tokens, providing limited guidance for intermediate reasoning .

While Process Reward Models (PRMs) offer dense feedback, they risk premature collapse when used alone. As early low-reward tokens can drive policies toward truncated outputs. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07382:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by J-B. Roux and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers superspace worldline formalism approach to quantum gravity. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Using the ADM formalism, we show that the Hamiltonian formulation of Quantum Gravity is exactly.

In the form of a worldline (WL) formalism in the superspace. We then show that the Keldysh partition function reduces to the partition function of Euclidean 3D gravity. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07582:
Huhai Zou and colleagues present ES-Mem, a memory design for dialogue agents that must remember over long conversations. Memory lets an agent stay coherent across many sessions and adapt over time. Without it, long-term interaction breaks into disconnected chats. Their 2026 preprint builds memory around event segmentation.

Event segmentation splits a stream of experience into meaningful episodes. ES-Mem uses that idea to organize what a dialogue agent stores and recalls. Well-placed boundaries can make retrieval cleaner than storing one long transcript. The design targets long-term dialogue, where relevant facts may sit far in the past. Readers building assistants and companion agents get a memory approach modeled on how events naturally divide.
arxiv-2601-07682:
Emiliya Poghosyan and coauthors align an electron beam with sub-pixel accuracy to study advanced detectors. Hybrid pixel detectors are radiation hard, fast, and have high dynamic range. They now serve diffraction work and even imaging work with electrons. Their pixels, though, are about ten times larger than those of direct detectors made for imaging. Spread from hits inside them is also stronger in them.

Machine learning study of them needs a beam spot known with great care. Sub-pixel alignment squeezes position knowledge finer than the pixel grid. That precision helps separate detector effects from real sample signals. The work supports using these robust detectors in electron microscopy. Staff who build and run such tools are the natural readers. The work is hands on, and it deals with beams, grids, and faint signals.
arxiv-2601-07982:
Howard C. Gifford derives a likelihood ratio for a binary classifier that works under a noise-exclusion model. The statistical ideal observer here performs holistic visual search, or gist processing. It places thresholds on the minimum extractable image features. In this model, the ideal observer reduces the number of free parameters. The system it describes becomes smaller and more tractable. Gifford's 2026 preprint develops the theory.

Likelihood ratios are the core of optimal classification decisions. An ideal observer sets the ceiling for any real or model observer. Noise exclusion captures the idea that some variability should simply be ignored. Gist processing matches how humans grasp a scene before detailed search. The paper serves imaging scientists who model detection and search. It tightens the theory behind thresholded observer models used in image quality work.
arxiv-2601-08382: Zoe Falomir presents a qualitative model for reasoning about object rotations. The 2026 arXiv paper applies the model, called QOR, to the Cube Comparison Test. That test asks whether two drawn cubes could be the same object in different orientations. Qualitative reasoning uses relations and landmarks rather than exact angles or coordinates. A model that solves cube comparisons this way mimics some human spatial strategies. Such models serve research in cognitive systems, education testing, and spatial AI that must explain its answers.
arxiv-2601-08782:
Tangyou Huang, Lei Du, and Lingzhen Guo work on codes that shield quantum data from flaws. Such codes store one unit of data in the wavy state of light or of a trapped atom cloud. Past ways to build them used slow ramps over many drive rounds. That slow pace makes them hard to use in real work.

The team gives a way to build a code in just one drive round. Their math is exact, not a rough guess, and it can make a wide class of target moves. One round means less time for flaws to creep in. A reader in quantum work gets a fast build path. It may bring shielded quantum memory close to real use.
arxiv-2601-08882:
Thomas Snyder and three co-authors shrink large image models for use on small field gear. The models read earth images from space and air. They do well, but they hold vast counts of set values. Field gear in a farm or a storm zone can not run them at full size. Shrinks tend to cost score.

The team uses a math frame called DLRT to shrink the models while they learn a new task. The frame keeps the shrink on a curved set of low rank forms. That keeps key traits safe as size falls. A reader who maps the earth gets a path to small, strong models. They may run on site, with no need for a far host.
arxiv-2601-09082:
Christopher Blake and three co-authors make the proof that Bitcoin is safe both strict and more broad. Bitcoin lets a crowd keep a shared log with no boss. Its safe proof must hold when a foe can slow blocks as they spread. Past proofs had gaps or loose steps that a strict read could not pass.

The team works in a model where a foe can hold a block for a set time span. They let blocks hold more than one score type, not just one hash count. The proof holds in that broad case too. A reader in crypto work gets a proof with less hand wave. It shows what the safe claim rests on, in plain terms.
arxiv-2601-09182:
JungMin Yun and three co-authors argue that chat models should coach peer reviewers, not write reviews for them. Peer review is short of skilled hands as AI paper counts soar. Past tools just draft a review by prompt. That path may add weak reviews and cut the skill growth of new reviewers. The team calls the gap the Reviewer Gap.

They give a frame where a model acts as a mentor. It gives feed back on a draft review, asks for grounds, and shows what a strong review checks. The human still owns the call. A reader in science work gets a use of AI that lifts the pool of reviewers, not one that thins it.
arxiv-2601-09582:
Sung-Yi Liao, Thang Pham, and Chun-Yen Shen work on a problem in geometric measure theory. Their 2026 arXiv paper gives L2 estimates for quadratic images of product Frostman measures. A Frostman measure spreads mass in a controlled way, like a dust with a fixed dimension.

The authors push three copies of such a measure through a fixed non-degenerate quadratic polynomial. They study the resulting measure on the real line. Estimates of this kind test how polynomial maps stretch fractal sets. They connect to wider questions about distance sets and patterns inside thin sets.
arxiv-2601-09682:
Christopher J. R. Clark, Roberto J. Avila, Alyssa Guzman, and Norman A. Grogin explain the shifting glow behind Hubble images. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses 23 years of data from the ACS/SBC camera aboard the Hubble Space Telescope. Background levels vary a lot between observations, by more than a factor of ten in most filters.

For the shortest wavelengths, airglow from Earth's own atmosphere dominates the background. For other filters, the drivers of change are poorly pinned down. The authors aim to explain and predict the variations. Better background forecasts help astronomers plan exposures and clean faint signals from the noise.
arxiv-2601-09782:
Kazi Ranjibul Islam, Samuel Awelewa, Andrey V. Chubukov, and Maxim Dzero compute the sound-like modes of an unconventional superconductor. Their 2026 arXiv paper analyzes collective modes in superconductors with d-wave order. Long-range Coulomb forces shape how these modes spread.

The team uses diagram tools and a near-classical theory to do the math. They read off how the modes spread, both along and across the flow, from pair response functions. Collective modes reveal how the condensate responds as a whole, beyond single electrons. How they behave is a test that lab work can check in d-wave materials of many kinds.
arxiv-2601-10282:
Jose Marie Antonio Miñoza curbs the over fit of physics led nets. Such nets learn to solve field laws. They train on a set span of space and time. Past that span, they oft fail. They fit the train span too well and lose the law.

Miñoza adds a sparse Koopman term to the loss. Koopman terms track how states move in time. A sparse form keeps just the key modes. That term guides the net to learn the true move rules. The tool is named SPIKE. It aims for nets that hold up past their train span.
arxiv-2601-10482:
William Dorrell, Peter Latham, and James Whittington ask why nerve cells code facts as they do. One past claim says cells code to waste as low as they can. That claim is named efficient coding. It casts cell acts as the best solve of a cost task. But its math can be hard to work with.

The team give a convex form of the claim. Convex tasks have one best point and fast solves. Their form keeps the core of the old claim. It makes the claim fit for tests on real cell data. It also shows which code forms the claim rules out.
arxiv-2601-10582:
Mridankan Mandal and Smit Sanjay Shende look at AI agents that run on small edge devices. These devices have weak hardware, so code must use each thread well. Python code needs many threads to hide slow input and output. But Python's Global Interpreter Lock forces threads to take turns, which blocks real parallel work.

The authors show that simply adding more threads can backfire. Past a point, speed drops by at least a fifth, a drop they call a saturation cliff. The drop shows up at very high thread counts on edge-like setups. Their tests warn builders of edge AI systems to tune thread counts with care, not just raise them.
arxiv-2601-10682:
Pin-Hsun Lin, Hadi Aghaee, Christian Deppe, Eduard A. Jorswieck, and Holger Boche build an oblivious transfer protocol from polar codes. Oblivious transfer is a core tool in secure computation. One party picks one of two items, and the sender never learns which. Here the transfer runs over a noisy binary-input Gaussian channel.

Polar codes give the scheme its structure. The design uses two decoder views linked by symmetries of the polar transform. The encoder is drawn at random in public from that symmetry group. The work shows how coding theory built for error correction can also carry privacy duties on real noisy links.
arxiv-2601-10782:
Asher Berlin, Dawid Brzeminski, and Erwin H. Tanin survey sources of high-frequency gravitational waves. Waves above 100 kilohertz would be a major find. Any signal that strong in that band must come from new physics in the late universe. Many detector ideas exist for this band, yet the list of promising sources stays very sparse.

The authors narrow down which sources could realistically shine at such high frequencies. A clear source map tells instrument builders where to aim. It also tells theorists which models are worth the math. The paper serves the small but growing field that wants to open a fresh window on the cosmos, far above the band of current observatories.
arxiv-2601-11082:
Anshu Gautam, Tanisha, Satyajit Puhan, Arvind Kumar, and Harleen Dahiya study the rho meson inside symmetric nuclear matter. The rho is a light vector meson, a bound quark-antiquark state. Matter at nuclear density can shift its mass and decay constant. The authors compute those traits in the light-front quark model, first in vacuum.

They also compute the meson's leading-twist distribution amplitudes, which describe how momentum is shared inside it. Then they track all these quantities at different baryonic densities. Heavy-ion collisions create such matter for instants. Knowing how the rho changes inside it helps decode what collision detectors record.
arxiv-2601-11182:
Martin Spisak, Ladislav Peska, Petr Skoda, Vojtech Vancura, and Rodrigo Alves link two hot tools. Their 2026 preprint joins sparse autoencoders with recommender systems. Sparse autoencoders first grew in work on large language models. There they help expose clear features hid in dense code.

Those features can be read at more than one scale of detail. They can also be switched on to steer what a model writes. The team now brings that trick to joint filtering for picks and ranks. The aim is a recommender whose taste can be tuned by hand. Users could turn clear knobs, not just take what the black box gives.
arxiv-2601-11282:
Junjie Wang, Gaole He, Alisa Rieger, and Ujwal Gadiraju study how media shape views. Their 2026 preprint sets search pages next to AI-made podcasts. Search result pages are the old gate to facts on the web. AI podcasts are new and ask for less work from the listener.

A podcast tells a smooth story in a warm, natural voice. The two forms now meet in daily habits of seeking facts. The team asks how their mix moves user attitudes. The test topics are hot ones, full of values and debate. Such topics are where framing can sway views the most. The work maps a risk that grows as AI audio spreads.
arxiv-2601-11682:
Ayrton Draux and five coauthors watch a thin sheet wrinkle on liquid. Their 2026 preprint studies universal wrinkling dynamics in that setup. The sheet is elastic and floats on a viscous liquid. It is indented or compressed while it floats there.

Deformation speed controls the dynamics in their results. Fast compression picks a much smaller wrinkle wavelength. That wavelength beats the one from quasistatic compression. Once active compression stops, the wrinkles coarsen again. Their wavelength relaxes toward the equilibrium value in time. A universal pattern across speeds is the paper's claim. Such sheets model skins, films, and floating structures.
arxiv-2601-12482:
Minhua Ding, Prathapasinghe Dharmawansa, Italo Atzeni, and Antti Tolli, at the University of Oulu, study channel estimation in wireless systems. Their setting uses MIMO antennas and receivers that keep only one bit per sample. One bit systems are cheap and save power, but they throw away a lot of signal detail. The question is how well the channel can still be estimated.

Past work often assumed that noise at distinct antennas is independent. In practice, noise can be correlated in space, due to jamming, clutter, or other disturbances. The team analyze how that correlation affects the best mean square estimator. They note this effect had not been explored in the one bit setting before. The results matter for low cost 6G hardware design.
arxiv-2601-12582:
Work with no author named in the record tackles a stubborn problem in materials science: reproducibility. Results from simulations often cannot be rerun by others with confidence. Workflows and parameters get reported only in loose text and tables. Literature data hold value for validation and reuse, but they resist machine reading.

Without machine readable workflow descriptions, large scale curation is blocked. Systematic comparison across studies suffers as well. Text mining tools so far cannot extract complete workflows with all their parameters. The work proposes ontology aligned structuring of multimodal materials data and workflows. An ontology gives shared terms that machines can check and reuse. The aim is automatic reproduction of published results at scale.
arxiv-2601-12882:
Sudip Chakrabarty analyzes YOLO26, a framework for real time object detection without a classic post step. The YOLO family has long been the benchmark for fast detection. Versions from YOLOv1 through YOLO11 still rely on non maximum suppression. That post processing step adds latency and brings sensitive hyperparameters.

YOLO26 eliminates that suppression step in favor of native end to end learning. The model itself must then avoid duplicate detections without outside cleanup. Chakrabarty gives a comprehensive analysis of this redefined paradigm. End to end detection could simplify deployment on cameras and edge devices. The analysis weighs what is gained and what is risked in the change.
arxiv-2601-12982:
Alexandros Papadopoulos and seven co authors build codebooks for smart radio surfaces. Next gen networks need links that are fast and steady in tough indoor spaces. Sound like echoes bounce off walls and blur the signal. Smart surfaces that can be set by software offer a fix, since they can steer those waves.

A codebook is the set of saved settings for such a surface. The team build theirs with the physics of the waves kept in the loop. Their case is near field beam focusing, where two real effects spoil naive plans. One is coupling between the cells of the surface, and the other is mirror like bounce. Codebooks that face both should work far better in real rooms.
arxiv-2601-13782:
Shir Tapiro Moshe, Yariv Aizenbud, and Barak Sober bridge two fields that study the same estimation task in 2026. Local polynomial regression grew in statistics, while moving least squares grew in approximation theory. Both fit local trends to scattered data points. Stats work fights sampling noise with probability tools.

Moving least squares theory tracks smoothness and convergence via fill-distance, a resolution measure. The team takes a stochastic approach that drops a strict quasi-uniformity need. Quasi-uniform data has points spread in a regular way. Dropping that need fits real data, which is often messy and uneven.
arxiv-2601-13982:
R. Dragland and co-authors map two traits of ferroelectric crystals at once in 2026. Ferroelectric materials hold electric polarization that can flip with a field. In polycrystals, many small grains each hold domains of like polarization. Knowing grain orientation and domain structure together is key to how the material acts.

They use interferometric vector piezoresponse force microscopy for the joint map. That method is a recent extension of piezoresponse force microscopy. It maps local crystallographic orientations and domain structure of grains at once. Correlated maps can reveal why some grains switch well and others lag.
arxiv-2601-14482:
Daniela Egas Santander, Matteo Santoro, and Jason P. Smith count orderings in this 2026 math paper. Counting linear extensions is a fundamental problem in poset theory. A linear extension is a full ordering of a partially ordered set that respects all its rules. The count is known to be #P-complete, so exact formulas exist only in special cases.

The team develops new recursive formulas for that count. They apply to posets whose modular partitions have particular structure. The paper also counts directed cliques via the same partition idea. Readers get fresh exact tools for a counting problem that is hard in general but tractable for structured orders.
arxiv-2601-14782:
O. Pavlas and seven co-authors present detector hardware in this 2026 paper. Timepix2 Lite is a miniaturized readout interface for the Timepix2 hybrid pixel detector. It is designed to provide high spatial and temporal resolution in a wide range of radiation detection applications. The interface enables simultaneous energy and precise timing measurements on the nanosecond scale.

It also supports advanced real-time data acquisition and visualization through the TrackLab software framework. The title names the target use: enabling nanosecond-scale half-life measurement. Short-lived nuclei decay in such spans, and only fast detectors can time them. The box is small. That is the point: fast, fine timing that can go where the work is. Readers get a compact readout that brings lab-grade timing to a small box.
arxiv-2601-15182:
Naghmeh Farzi, Laura Dietz, and Dave D. Lewis help lawyers check AI summaries of legal depositions. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a risky new habit. Large language models now sum up long legal documents, but in law a wrong fact can do real harm.

A deposition summary must stay true to the sworn record. The authors build support for humans who evaluate these summaries. Their route rests on nuggets, small key facts pulled from the text. Nugget-based checks have proven helpful for scoring summaries, and the work adapts them to legal needs.
arxiv-2601-15382:
Salmoli Ghosh, Preeti Kharb, and co-authors map the magnetic skeleton of a radio outflow in a nearby galaxy. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with NGC 4151, a Seyfert galaxy with an active core. The nature of radio outflows in such radio-quiet galaxies is poorly understood.

The team took polarization observations on kiloparsec scales with the Very Large Array. They observed at 3 and 10 gigahertz. Polarization reveals the magnetic field's structure in the outflow. Their title reports a stratification: the field's layers are arranged in an ordered, layered pattern across the outflow's many scales.
arxiv-2601-15682:
Wei Dong and Li Ge set tight bounds for a private statistics task in a 2026 arXiv paper. The task is estimating the mean of a Gaussian distribution. The privacy rule is personalized differential privacy. Under it, each record carries its own privacy budget. Not everyone needs the same level of protection. The authors study two common variants of the setup.

In bounded PDP, budgets are public, and neighboring datasets differ by replacing one record. In unbounded PDP, the rules differ in how records enter or leave. Tight bounds mark the best accuracy any method can reach. They also show that a matching method exists, or that none can do better. For data holders, such bounds tell them the true price of personalized privacy.
arxiv-2601-15782:
An unsigned 2026 arXiv paper surveys mesoscopic fluctuations in statistical systems. A fluctuation counts as mesoscopic when its size sits in a middle range. It is much larger than the spacing between nearest neighbors. It is still much smaller than the whole system. At that scale, fluctuations behave unlike the matter around them. They can be read as patches of one phase forming inside another host phase.

The abstract frames the topic in general terms, without naming authors or a specific system. Readers should expect a broad theoretical treatment. Mesoscopic effects matter in small devices and materials, where the middle scale is the working scale.
arxiv-2601-16082:
Marcos Silva studies where a star would tear apart near a black bounce. His 2026 preprint works with the Simpson and Visser space form. That form bends the black hole view into a bounce. Tidal pull from a black hole can rip a dense star as it nears. The rip point is known as the Roche limit.

Silva works out the tidal pull in this bounce space. He asks how the bounce shifts the rip point from the known case. Shifts would show where this space form parts from the old view. Such maths helps teams test new gravity forms with star acts. The work stays at the level of pure theory and proof.
arxiv-2601-16182:
Arshia Ataee Naeini and three coauthors solve live text search with wild card marks. Their 2026 preprint deals with search where marks can stand for any sign. Up to a set count of wild marks may sit in the search term. Both the text and the term can change live. Changes span add, drop and swap of signs.

The team gives steps that keep search fast through all such changes. Fast live search serves code bases and data sets that shift oft. Wild marks add reach but also add cost to each check. Steps that hold cost down have wide use. The work is in the theory of text code steps.
arxiv-2601-16282:
Peter Jansen and three coauthors build science views from huge text sets at scale. Their 2026 preprint deals with the build of theories, not just tests. Past AI work in science has stressed tools that run tests. Tools that build views from past work are far less built. A theory here joins rules of both kind and count type.

The team frames how to draw such rules from big text hoards. They then test the frame on sets drawn from past work. Drawn rules that hold true would speed new science thought. The work aims at the high level step of theory craft. It treats past texts as the raw ore for views.
arxiv-2601-16482:
A study of the Langmuir film task weighs if its maths is well set. The 2026 preprint deals with thin films on a fluid base. The film is of the Langmuir type, one grain thick on top. It pairs to a Stokes flow in the fluid just past it. Past bulk terms can be cut to leave a film lone flow.

That cut leaves a flow ruled by a Dirichlet to Neumann map. Well set means small data shifts give small act shifts. Proof of that trait lets codes trust the film maths. It also firms the base for wave and flow sums. The work is a maths check of the film model.
arxiv-2601-16582:
Yuqian Zheng and Mariana Georgescu build a composed video search tool in plain form. Their 2026 preprint, named X-Aligner, deals with search by pic plus words. A user gives a clip cue and a word cue as one ask. Past tools fuse the two cues in one step at once. That one step fusion gave just small gains past base tools.

A staged align of cues aims for more large gains. Each stage lines cues up in a more fine way. Plain form with strong scores would ease real use. Search by cues serves clip hoards in film and news work. The work strips spare parts from the tool build.
arxiv-2601-17282:
Nathan Shettell and Alexia Auffèves measure how well Bayesian inference uses each new clue. Inference is how an agent updates belief as data comes in. It sits under science, machine learning, and daily choice. Each measure cuts doubt about a hidden state. The authors define an inferential efficiency as a ratio tied to that cut.

They call the frame entropic efficiency. It asks how much of the gain a protocol could get, it does get. A clear yardstick lets users compare protocols on fair terms. It may also show where data is wasted. For sensor and lab design, waste means cost. A sharp measure helps teams spend measures where they count most.
arxiv-2601-17682:
David M. T. Kuo tests if topological interface states in graphene nanoribbons survive their environment. He studies sandwich structures with armchair graphene heterostructures. Boron nitride ribbons flank the graphene core. One stack keeps the same topology on both sides. The other reverses it. Interface states live at the joins between zones.

Environmental breakdown would limit real devices built on these states. Stability checks must come before device claims. Kuo asks the question in the title with care: is breakdown true? The paired stacks give a controlled comparison. Graphene nanoribbons are a test bed for topological electronics. Results here guide whether that promise holds in air and heat.
arxiv-2601-18282:
Lei Wei, Jinpeng Ou, Xiao Peng, and Bin Wang make language models think inside the act of calling a function. Their 2026 preprint deals with function calling for autonomous agents. Models are good at it, yet they lack clear reasoning while they fill in parameters. That gap bites for complex functions whose parameters depend on each other. Chain-of-thought prompting works at the agent level, above the call itself. It cannot give fine-grained reasoning at the point where a value is chosen.

The authors embed the reasoning inside the call. Think-augmented calling aims for more accurate parameters. Agent tools are only as safe as the values they pass. Small parameter errors can book, buy, or delete the wrong thing.
arxiv-2601-18382:
Kees Wapenaar, Johannes Aichele, and Dirk-Jan van Manen study two sound tricks and how they link. One trick plays a sound field back in time to focus it at its source. The next trick pulls a key response curve out of noise, with no need for a real source at all. For still stuff that does not change with time, the link between the tricks is well known.

Fresh work has pushed both tricks to stuff whose traits shift as time goes by. The team asks how the two tricks link in that new case. They also ask how that link maps to the old case. Sound tools of this kind serve scans of the earth, tests of parts, and care of health. A clear link helps staff pick the right trick for each job.
arxiv-2601-18582:
Yuan Cao and six colleagues recast a trait-guess task as a rank task to get more from language models. The task reads a person's posts and guesses their type on a famed four-scale quiz of traits. Past tools had models pull key text from posts and then train a sorter to pick one type. That pick is coarse: a near miss counts the same as a wild one.

A rank list is finer. It can put the true type high even when the top pick is off. The team train and grade models to rank types, not just to name one. A finer grade should show small gains that a plain pick would hide. It may also give users a range of fits, not a flat tag. Trait tools are used in hires and ads, so fine grades count.
arxiv-2601-19082:
Trung-Kiet Huynh and a large team test how stakes and language steer model agents in cooperation traps. As language models act more on their own among other agents, their strategic choices matter for safety and for shared systems. The team places agents in classic dilemmas where greed and trust pull apart.

They vary two things: how big the payoffs are, and which language the game is played in. Both knobs, it turns out, are worth watching as shapers of agent conduct. Knowing what bends an agent toward or away from cooperation helps design multi agent systems that do not spiral into mutual harm.
arxiv-2601-19182:
Roberto Rubboli and Marco Tomamichel pin down a hard limit on pulling clean randomness from weak sources when a quantum foe watches. Randomness extraction turns messy random data into near perfect random bits. A strong converse exponent grades how fast the chance of failure grows when you push past the limit.

The pair find a tight value for that exponent under a composable error rule. That rule stays safe when the bits are used inside larger protocols. Tight limits tell builders of quantum safe systems exactly how much clean randomness a source can yield.
arxiv-2601-19382:
David Jones and a large team find a carbon rich dwarf star hiding inside a nebula that looks carbon poor. The Necklace nebula is a two lobed planetary nebula left after a shared envelope phase between two stars. Its central star has been shown to be a dwarf carbon star, rich in carbon by type.

Yet the nebula around it reads as poor in carbon, a flat contradiction at first glance. The team appraises how both facts can hold at once. Cases like this test the story of how paired stars trade material and shed their outer layers.
arxiv-2601-20282:
Viet Hung Dinh, Ming Ding, Youyang Qu, and Kanchana Thilakarathna study how transformer models retrieve what they have memorized. Interest in explaining these models is rising, partly due to rules that demand transparency and accountability. Machine unlearning, which removes chosen data from a trained model, also needs this understanding to protect privacy.

The authors use the encoding specificity principle, an idea from memory research, to read how attention layers store and fetch information. That lens may show where a memory sits inside the model. Such insight would help builders delete data on request and prove that it is gone.
arxiv-2601-20782:
Massimo Solinas and three co-authors ask how little numerical precision quantum simulations can get away with. Their 2026 paper studies neural quantum states computed in mixed precision. Scientific computing has long relied on double precision, with sixty-four bits per number. That standard guarantees accuracy in simulations of real phenomena. But it is slow and hungry next to newer hardware.

Graphics processors now make low-precision formats attractive. They run faster, use less memory, and save energy. The question is whether neural quantum states stay accurate when parts of the math use fewer bits. Mixed precision blends formats, using care only where it counts. The paper tests that trade-off for a method that represents quantum wave functions with neural networks. Its lessons guide simulations that need both speed and trust.
arxiv-2601-20882:
Yuheng Tang and a large team test AI agents on the full life of software. Their 2026 paper presents DevOps-Gym, a benchmark for agents in the DevOps cycle. AI agents shine at writing code and fixing issues. Their skill at building, shipping, and running real software is still unknown. DevOps work demands more than code. It needs project-scale analysis and choices made in sequence.

An agent in this cycle has to work through large projects. It must grasp how programs behave as they run. It must use trade tools with care. And it must plan many steps in order. DevOps-Gym measures agents on that whole cycle. The test exposes gaps that pure coding tests hide. It gives labs a harder target for agent research.
arxiv-2601-20982:
Samantha Adams and a large team of co-authors catalog polarized radio sources in a deep sky field. Their 2026 paper studies the Wide Chandra Deep Field South. The field covers ten square degrees. Observations span the S-band, from two to four gigahertz. The image reaches an angular resolution of fifteen arcseconds. Its noise level is about fifty microjanskys per beam in total intensity.

The team measures linear polarization for the sources in this field. Polarization reveals magnetic order in distant galaxies and jets. A wide, uniform catalog lets astronomers compare source classes fairly. It also feeds studies of how cosmic magnetism evolves. The paper is a survey report, rich in measured properties. It gives radio astronomers a reference sample for follow-up work.
arxiv-2601-21182:
Xin Peng and Ang Gao revisit how generative models are refined after sampling. Their 2026 paper rethinks refinement for diffusion and flow-based models. Such models often exhibit systematic biases that degrade sample quality. The problem grows in high-dimensional settings. Refinement methods exist to correct those biases. The standard view ties correction to resampling with fresh noise. The authors show that view is too narrow.

Effective bias correction, they demonstrate, can be a post-hoc procedure. It needs no noise injection and no multi-step resampling of the sampling process. A finished sample can be adjusted directly. That makes refinement cheaper and simpler to bolt onto existing models. Better samples matter in imaging, design, and scientific generation. The paper simplifies a step many pipelines rely on. It reframes refinement as cleanup, not regeneration.
arxiv-2601-21282:
Rishi Upadhyay and nine co-authors build a test for whether AI world models truly grasp physics. These generative models are pitched for hard jobs like robot planning and training self-driving systems. For such work, a model must mimic real dynamics with high fidelity, not just look plausible.

Their benchmark, WorldBench, is designed to separate look-alike cases that obey different physical rules. A model that confuses them will fail when the hidden rule matters. The tests work as a diagnostic, showing which parts of physics a model has learned. That helps builders fix weak spots before trusting a model with real tasks.
arxiv-2601-21382:
Madona Mekhael, Timo Stolt, and five co-authors build a surface that shapes light differently at each color. Patterned surfaces can steer light and change its frequency in compact devices. Older designs based on geometric phase give a fixed response with no color selectivity.

Their thin film of lithium niobate uses tuned resonances to shape doubled-frequency light. Because the response is tied to resonance, it can pick out chosen wavelengths. That selectivity opens finer control for tiny optical devices. The work points to chips that route and convert light with color-level precision.
arxiv-2601-21582:
Jonas Knupp, Jan Hendrik Metzen, Jeremias Bohn, Georg Groh, and Kristian Kersting give latent reasoning in language models the attention it lacks. Depth recurrence lets a model think by looping through shared layers. Past work, though, compared unfair baselines and left much of the depth unused.

A fixed hidden size also chokes long chains of hidden thought. The authors mix attention across depths to loosen that choke point. Their checks match rivals on compute, size, and memory for fairness. Stronger hidden reasoning could let small models punch above their weight on hard problems without writing long visible chains.
arxiv-2601-22082:
Yi Fei Cheng and co-authors give conversational agents a voice that seems to come from somewhere. Embodiment, having a perceptible body, raises how present an agent feels. That presence is usually built visually, through avatars. But visual channels are not always available, as with headphones or glasses without displays.

The team explores auditory embodiment instead: spatialized sound and situated audio cues that place the agent in the listener's space. Their 2026 preprint tests how those cues affect the sense of presence. Voice-only interfaces are everywhere, from earbuds to car assistants, so knowing how sound alone can ground an agent has direct design value.
arxiv-2601-22282:
Huyen Nguyen, Haim Bar, Zhiyi Chi, and Vladimir Pozdnyakov model how stem cells renew a tissue over time. Stem cells can copy themselves or turn into cells with a set job. Their 2026 preprint uses a branching process whose rates shift as time passes.

In such a model, each cell may split, change type, or die. Tracking the counts shows how a tissue grows, holds steady, or heals. It can also show how a fault tips growth toward disease. The math gives labs a frame for real cell counts. It links cell fate rules to whole-tissue trends.
arxiv-2601-22382:
Natalie Maus and a large team let AI agents, with no task training, search for new biological designs. Their 2026 preprint frames drug finds, germ-fighting peptides, and protein design as black-box searches over vast spaces. Past tools lean on raw shape data and skip the rich text of past science.

Their agents read that text and use it to guide the search. The method needs no gradient or model of the space itself. It aims to find good designs in far fewer costly tests. The work suits any lab task where each test is dear. It turns reading into a search skill.
arxiv-2601-22582:
Youngeun Kim strengthens a group-based training method for the case of few tries per prompt. Group-relative methods grade a batch of model replies against their shared mean. Their 2026 preprint, MC-GRPO, notes that with small batches that mean is noisy.

Noise can flip the sign of the learning signal, teaching the wrong lesson. Centering on the median, not the mean, steadies the baseline. Steadier signals matter most where compute is tight. The fix is small but pointed. It aims to keep cheap training honest. Small budgets are where most teams live.
arxiv-2601-22682:
Yaoshuai Ma, Xiao Wang, Wei Yao, and Jin Zhang work on bilevel optimization spread across many machines. In bilevel problems, one task sits inside another, like tuning settings while a model trains. Their framework, SUN-DSBO, handles cases where the inner task is not convex, a shape older methods mostly avoided.

Nonconvex inner tasks are common in deep learning, meta-learning, and tuning work. A shared framework that does not need a central server lets groups train together while keeping data local. The authors aim to close the gap between theory and real, messy models.
arxiv-2601-22782:
Qishuo Yin and Dylan S. Small look at how the design of an observational study shapes its trust. In such studies, a treatment was not assigned by chance, so hidden traits may bias the results. The authors ask how a study should split its sample to test that bias well.

A split sample lets one part build the study plan and the other part test it. How the split is done changes how much hidden bias the study can stand before its findings fall apart. Good splitting rules give health and social research a fairer test of cause and effect.
arxiv-2603-01482:
Fake speech made by AI can fool voice checks and spread false claims, yet tests for spotting it lag behind. A 2026 benchmark study takes up that gap with a test suite called Spoof-SUPERB. Speech models that learn from raw audio now do well on many tasks, but fake speech had sat outside fair shared tests.

The suite scores twenty such models, spanning three broad design types, on data from both known and new sources. Large models that learn to tell voices apart did best, helped by training in many languages and by sheer size. When sound quality dropped, one design type fell fast, while the voice-aware models held up well. The suite gives labs a shared baseline for safer speech tools.
arxiv-2603-02382:
Lua Airoldi, Gustavo Alves, Pedro Machado, and Peter Vander Griend study neutrino decoherence from a light scalar field in this 2026 paper. Neutrinos change flavor as they travel, in a pattern called oscillation. An ultralight scalar field coupled to neutrinos would shift their masses over time and place. Each experiment samples many field states, which blurs the oscillation pattern.

That blurring is decoherence, and the team models it as an open quantum system. They map a full model onto the simpler phenomenological formulas used before. One key scaling differs from common assumptions: the damping grows with distance squared over energy squared. Past studies usually assumed a milder distance over energy growth. The correction matters for how experiments should fit decoherence searches.
arxiv-2603-02682:
Yaohua Hu, Hao Wang, and Xiaoqi Yang study a math tool that recovers simple answers from messy data. Their 2026 paper concerns a penalty method that favors sparse solutions, meaning solutions where most values are zero. The method is widely used, but its theory and best algorithms still had gaps.

On the theory side, they define a new eigenvalue condition tied to the penalty and prove accuracy bounds for the best possible solution. On the computing side, they propose two thresholding algorithms that use trimming and gradual easing tricks. Under a standard condition, both methods provably reach the true sparse answer within the noise level. Early tests beat popular rival methods at recovering sparse signals.
arxiv-2603-03082:
Mohamed Serry, Maxwell Fitzsimmons, and Jun Liu map the safe starting region for unstable-looking control systems, and teach a network to certify it. Many nonlinear systems settle into a robust attracting set, but only from the right starting states. Estimating that domain of attraction under uncertainty and state limits is notoriously hard.

The authors define new value functions over sets of states and derive the equations they must satisfy, of Bellman and Zubov type. A physics-informed neural network then learns those functions with the equations baked into training. A verification step, using formal tools, turns the learned estimate into a certified region. Four numerical examples with constrained, uncertain dynamics show the method working where earlier approaches struggle.
arxiv-2603-03182:
Jaszmine Defranco and Andrew Nemec build entanglement-assisted error-correcting codes from almost any quantum code. Such codes let a sender and receiver who pre-share entanglement communicate over a noisy quantum channel more reliably. Most known constructions live inside the stabilizer framework, which limits their shape.

The key move links erasure channels to entanglement assistance: if a code can recover a lost subset of qubits, that subset can serve as the receiver's pre-shared share. For degenerate codes, that share can sometimes be compressed, trading away some robustness when the shared entanglement itself is noisy. The paper gives the first permutation-invariant and XP-stabilizer examples of such codes, stepping outside both the stabilizer and codeword-stabilized traditions.
