cia-0000049282: Moves toward cooperation in El Salvador are the subject of a CIA paper from 1983, preserved in the Truth Commission file series. Cooperation, in that war, could mean talks, shared commands, or parties agreeing to anything at all. The paper catches a moment when some door, somewhere in the system, was opening.
cia-0000049382: Suspected kidnappers released in El Salvador is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049382, dated March 1, 1989. The item carries a Truth Commission note and records the release of suspects. Readers find a brief declassified notice whose title states the outcome plainly, kept among the agency's many short records on crime and justice in El Salvador.
cia-0000096582: The Arab Boycott, subtitled A Study in Gamesmanship, is declassified CIA document 0000096582, dated July 2, 1967. The playful subtitle sets this study apart from plainer agency headings. Readers find a short declassified study of the boycott as a contest of moves, its title promising analysis of tactics rather than a simple news report.
cia-0000098282: Memorandum of conversation with Dr. Kissinger, Mr. Karamessines, and Gen. Haig at the White House, in shortened heading form, is declassified CIA document 0000098282, dated September 4, 1970. Three men are named in the title. The brief file records a White House conversation, preserved as a memorandum rather than a report. Its catalog entry preserves the original heading word for word.
cia-0000107982: Weekly Surveyor Article re Pakistan-china: Nuclear Cooperation is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000107982, dated May 1, 1977. The title describes an article on nuclear cooperation between Pakistan and China. Two countries and one field, nuclear work, fill the short heading. The brief record is a weekly article item from the spring of 1977 in the files.
cia-0000108482: Untitled Cable re Guatenalan Human Rights Issues is the heading, with Guatemalan misspelled, on declassified CIA document 0000108482, dated July 6, 1981. The catalog marks the file an untitled cable, then names its subject: human rights issues. No case or victim is named in the heading itself. The brief record preserves the misspelling exactly as released in the files.
cia-0000126882: Dated August 1968, this CIA report tracks the status of Warsaw Pact forces inside Czechoslovakia after the invasion. The open question was whether the troops would leave or stay. The paper follows the occupation's footprint as it first formed that month. The forces in question stayed for more than twenty years in the end, a fact that gives this first footprint survey the character of an opening chapter.
cia-0000126982: An October 1975 CIA report notes that Soviet press coverage of Angola continues heavy. Moscow's papers were working hard on the colony's war that autumn. Heavy coverage signaled heavy commitment, and the paper tracks the drumbeat as a sign of Kremlin intent. Press volume was treated as a dial of commitment: the louder Moscow's papers argued Angola's cause, the deeper analysts judged the Kremlin's stake in the outcome.
cia-0000132282: Situation Report 591 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series, dated January 4, 1991, is a special spot commentary describing Saddam Hussein as defiant and determined. The headline itself is cut short in the record. Defiance was Saddam's public strategy through the Kuwait crisis, and analysts tracked how long he could hold that posture. The entry gives the agency's quick take on his stance at that moment.
cia-0000132382:
Cuba fills a CIA briefing package dated June 3, 1960, with further briefing material attached to it. By the middle of 1960 the file on Castro's government had grown thick. Washington was already weighing plans to bring that government down.

The package preserves the briefing as it was assembled for its readers, layers and attachments together. Its bulk alone tells a story about the place Cuba had taken in American planning. For readers today, it shows a file swelling month by month. Relations with Havana were sliding toward open hostility and a final break, and the paperwork grew with every step down that road.
cia-0000132482: New Cuban attacks on the United States fill part three of a CIA item dated April 6, 1960. The section is headed the West. Havana's war of words against Washington was growing sharper that spring. The attacks were verbal for the time being, while the armed clash was still a year away. The short item catalogs the latest statements as the agency recorded them.
cia-0000132582: Fidel Castro commenting on current Cuban policies fills item 10 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated September 4, 1960. Every major Castro speech was read closely in Washington for signs of his next move. His own words counted as prime intelligence for analysts. The short item reports what he said about his government's course that season.
cia-0000132782: Coverage of Cuba stayed intense into the fall, and this third CIA entry dated September 4, 1960 completes another same-day set in the Cuban Developments series. Cuba was a campaign issue that year, with the American election two months away, and the series ran at full tempo. The declassified text is preserved through the CIA Reading Room mirror at the Internet Archive.
cia-0000136282: Filed on 2 May 1954, this CIA cable concerns the urgency of delivering planes on time, late aircraft meaning a grounded air campaign. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136982: Distorted press coverage distresses the writer of this May 1954 message. Guatemalan developments are misreported in American and foreign papers, he says. An Agence France Presse cable missed the boat completely. It was picked up widely in Europe, chiefly Scandinavia. One paper did an excellent but almost unique job. The writer has done some checking himself. He cites his former experience and unofficial access to facts. He asks that a message go to Fernand Moulier at AFP. It must carry no personal or official attribution.
cia-0000138982: Japanese arms passed to China's Communists are listed in this April 1946 report. The transfer took place in the Antung area. The Russians made the handover. It included 13,000 Model 38 rifles from a Japanese garrison unit. It included 6,000 Model 99 rifles from other Japanese units. It included 2,400 rifles from Manchukuo garrison troops at Fengcheng. A Washington note corrects a unit code number from an earlier report. The supplement records the Soviet handover of captured Japanese arms in Manchuria.
cia-0000139482: Among the last SUN STREAK records in this set, document 0000139482 dates to 1988 and belongs to the remote viewing program run for American intelligence in that decade. The work asked viewers to picture hidden targets and describe them in words and drawings, which staff then checked against the real sites. No special subject marks this file in the record. Released with the program archive in the 1990s, it shares the fate of the whole effort: much kept paper, no proven results.
cia-06190282: MODIFICATION ONE DATED 31 DECEMBER 2012, a CIA document. The year-end modification. This file preserves that declassified paper. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
cia-06777582: AGENCY/SERVICE REQUEST TO CREATE FACEBOOK CHANNEL, a CIA document. The social media request. The library retains it. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
cowper-john-gilpin-1782:
William Cowper first shared his comic ballad John Gilpin among friends, and it was printed in 1782. Gilpin, a London draper and train-band captain of good standing, plans a wedding anniversary trip to Ware with his wife. He borrows a horse for the ride, and the plan falls apart at once.

The horse bolts, and Gilpin clings on through town and country while crowds laugh and stare. Cowper tells the chase in brisk, rhyming stanzas that beg to be read aloud. Light and endlessly quoted, the poem became one of the most loved funny verses of the 1700s and stayed in print in illustrated editions.
crevecoeur-letters-1782:
Hector St. John de Crevecoeur, a French settler turned farmer, issued his Letters in London in 1782. Warren Blake's introduction recalls Hazlitt ranking the unknown author high among colonial writers. Hazlitt praised his feel for a new country, from a battle of snakes to the flutter of a hummingbird.

Twelve letters describe frontier farms and the whalers of Nantucket at close range. One letter asks what the American is, this new man, in words still quoted today. As the Revolution ended, the book gave Europe its most vivid picture of the new republic and the people forming it.
donnelly-atlantis-the-antediluvian-world:
Ignatius Donnelly, an American writer and former congressman, published Atlantis: The Antediluvian World in 1882. Donnelly argued that Atlantis, the lost island in Plato's dialogues, was a real place and a real early state. He claimed its people spread farming, myth, and building across the world before a flood destroyed them.

Donnelly compared myths, alphabets, plants, and ruins from Egypt, Europe, and the Americas to build his case. He treated similar flood stories and sun worship as traces of one lost source. Scholars rejected most of his proof, but the book launched the modern Atlantis craze and still defines how lost-continent claims are argued.
dope-pg1182: Sax Rohmer's 1919 thriller about London's opium underworld, where the detective chases a drug ring through Limehouse dens. Lurid, racist by modern standards, and undeniably pacy, it is a prime specimen of the pulp thriller at its most sensational.
europmc-pmc10096782:
Yusuf and colleagues review nanoparticles as drug delivery systems in a 2023 paper. Nanoparticles are carriers far smaller than a cell, built to ferry drugs to the right place in the body. Their size, shape, and surface chemistry shape how the body handles them, for better or worse.

The review explains how those physical traits affect drug loading, travel, and release. It weighs benefits such as targeted delivery against risks such as toxicity. The authors close with the steps needed for safe clinic use. The paper is a broad guide to tiny carriers in medicine.
europmc-pmc10482982:
Doman and colleagues used virus-driven evolution in 2023 to shrink and sharpen prime editors. A prime editor is a gene tool that rewrites DNA letters with great care. It can fix many kinds of small errors in living cells. The standard editor is big, which makes it hard to ship into cells.

The team let bacteria viruses breed faster versions of one editor part. Gains ran up to 22-fold in editing speed for the compact parts. New editors came out 516 to 810 DNA letters smaller than the standard one. Doman found that distinct parts suit distinct edit types. In mouse brains, one pair of virus carriers placed a marker gene at 40% success, a 24-fold gain.
europmc-pmc1054882:
McGuinness and co-authors found in 2005 a guard that keeps chromosome glue in place at the right spot. The glue, cohesin, holds twin chromosomes together until cells divide. Most glue leaves the arms early in division, but glue at the centromere, the chromosome hub, must stay. It lasts until a cut frees the twins at the right moment.

A protein family called shugoshin fills the guard role. When the team drained the guard from human cells, the hub glue fell off too soon. McGuinness reports that twins then lost their bond and drifted from line, and the cells froze in division. A tag-proof form of a glue part saved the bond. The guard seems to shield the glue from tag-adding kinases.
europmc-pmc10584682:
Li and co-authors showed in 2023 that blocking fat burning can let adult mouse hearts regrow. After birth, heart muscle cells switch fuel from sugar to fats. They also leave the cell cycle, which bars repair in adult hearts. The team shut off fat burning in these cells by cutting a gene, Cpt1b.

Mutant cells resisted low oxygen and began to divide again. After a blood flow injury, their hearts healed in ways normal hearts cannot. Li found a build-up of a chemical, alpha-ketoglutarate, in the mutant cells. It woke an enzyme, KDM5, that strips gene marks for mature states. Cells slid back to a younger state that can split. The work ties fuel choice to heart repair.
europmc-pmc10767982:
Cannon and co-authors rebuilt the Drug-Gene Interaction Database in 2024 as DGIdb 5.0. The bank pools records of which drugs act on which genes. Doctors and labs use it to form ideas for care and for drug hunts. This release splits the service into twin apps, one for data and one for display.

A new query tongue, GraphQL, lets users shape their own searches, Cannon reports. The web face was rebuilt in ReactJS with live charts. Six new sources joined, from FDA drug lists to cancer drug sets. Grouping rules for drugs and genes were honed as stand-alone steps. The changes lift how well the data meet FAIR rules for shared science data.
europmc-pmc10776382:
Baek and colleagues address a stubborn gap in computer modelling in this 2024 paper. Tools can now predict the shape of a lone protein quite well. They still struggle when a protein binds to DNA or RNA, which is a paired shape called a complex. The team set out to extend a proven protein tool to cover these paired forms.

Their new network, RoseTTAFoldNA, takes sequence data and builds a 3D model of the pair. It also gives a score for how much each model can be trusted. Models the tool rated as sure proved far more exact than older methods. The authors say labs can use it to study natural pairs and to design proteins that bind a chosen stretch of DNA or RNA.
europmc-pmc1079782:
Sullivan and co-authors read the full gene sets of three ocean viruses in this 2005 paper. The viruses infect Prochlorococcus, a tiny sea microbe that makes food from sunlight and is a major food maker in the oceans. Such viruses, called phages, can kill host cells and shape how host groups grow and change over time. The team asked what these virus genomes hold and how they compare with known phages.

Each genome matched a known phage family in shape and core genes, the authors found. Each also carried genes that look borrowed from sea microbes. All three held genes for making food from sunlight, which may keep the host active while the virus copies itself. One virus also held a gene that hints it can slip its DNA into the host, a first for its group if proven.
europmc-pmc10804282:
Ashton and a large team tested a blood test for Alzheimer disease in this 2024 study. Alzheimer disease is a brain illness that slowly destroys memory and thinking. A protein form called phosphorylated tau 217 builds up in the brain as the disease takes hold. The question was whether a shop-bought blood test for this protein could spot that brain change well.

The team pooled data from three patient groups, each tracked at a single research centre. They checked the blood test, a standard lab assay for this protein, against known signs of Alzheimer disease in the brain. The paper notes this protein shifts more sharply than two related tau markers. One of the groups, with 268 people, spanned healthy adults through to dementia cases. A blood test with strong accuracy could sort Alzheimer disease from other causes of memory loss without scans or spinal fluid tests.
europmc-pmc10805282:
Gattrell and colleagues created the first checklist for reporting expert agreement studies in this 2024 paper. In biomedicine, experts often must agree on guidance when proof is thin, mixed, or missing. Such consensus work shapes care rules and policy, yet it is often reported poorly. Readers then cannot tell how the agreement was reached or how much to trust it.

The team followed steps set by the EQUATOR Network, a group that promotes clear research reporting. They reviewed past studies, then ran a Delphi process, a method where experts rate items over rounds until views converge. A panel of 72 experts from six continents took part. The final ACCORD checklist has 35 items, and 21 of them cover how methods are reported. Five cover results, three cover the opening, and the rest cover debate and extra details. The counts show where past reports most often fell short.
europmc-pmc11223882:
Madeira and colleagues describe updates to a European framework that runs sequence analysis tools in this 2024 paper. The EMBL-EBI Job Dispatcher lets scientists run popular bioinformatics applications without installing them. Free access comes through web pages and through program interfaces for automated use. The tools are woven into major resources such as UniProt, InterPro, and Ensembl Genomes.

Recent improvements include a brand new website and documentation, the authors report. Visualisations of results were enhanced, and job management was improved. Use of the service is rising notably from low- and middle-income regions, a trend the paper highlights. The framework covers a diverse range of sequence analyses, from similarity searches to protein feature scans. The authors present the update as keeping a heavily used community service current and reachable.
europmc-pmc1131882:
Kapitonov and Jurka trace the origin of the immune system's gene-shuffling machinery to jumping genes in this 2005 paper. Jawed vertebrates reshuffle antibody genes by a reaction called V(D)J recombination. Two proteins, RAG1 and RAG2, run it, and they were thought to descend from transposons, DNA segments that copy themselves around the genome. No matching transposon enzyme had been found.

The core of RAG1, about 600 amino acids, closely matches the enzyme of Transib transposons, they show. Those transposons occur in flies, mosquitoes, sea urchins, silkworms, hydra, and other species. The signal sequences that guide the shuffling derive from the transposon's end repeats. Both enzymes share the same three-part catalytic motif, called DDE. The authors read this as strong evidence of common descent.
europmc-pmc11532982:
Burt and colleagues present an image processing pipeline for electron cryo-tomography inside a major software suite in this 2024 paper. Cryo-tomography images frozen, hydrated samples in 3D, revealing molecular complexes in their native surroundings. Averaging many copies of a complex can yield structures sharp enough for atomic modelling. Many tools exist, but lack of standardisation blocks newcomers.

Their pipeline, in RELION-5, spans the import of unprocessed movies to automated building of atomic models in final maps. Metadata items describing each step are explicitly defined. That definition is designed for interoperability with other software, so pipelines can be mixed and audited. The authors frame the work as a framework for further standardisation of the field. It lowers the entry barrier for labs adopting the technique.
europmc-pmc12016282:
Lu, Breitwieser, Thielen, and Salzberg presented a counting method called Bracken in 2017. DNA sampling can reveal which microbes live in a sample. Knowing the species list is only half the task. Their shares in the mix matter just as much.

Bracken builds on Kraken, a fast tool that labels DNA reads. It then re-sorts those labels with genome details. The result is abundance estimates at species level or above. Tests showed fast and accurate counts from raw reads. Lu gives labs a practical way to weigh community members. It appeared in PeerJ Computer Science in 2017.
europmc-pmc12310982:
Mao, Zhao, and Sun reviewed a master gene switch in 2025. The switch is called NF-kappaB, a protein family that turns genes on. It shapes immune response, swelling, growth, and cell survival. When its control slips, disease follows.

Overactive signaling drives long-term swelling and metabolic disorders. It can also disturb immune guard cells and aid autoimmunity. In cancer it helps tumors grow, spread, and resist therapy. Mao sums up new findings on these paths. Drugs aimed at the switch may treat both inflammation and cancer. It appeared in Cellular and Molecular Immunology.
europmc-pmc1240282:
Miedema and Oudshoorn modeled how traffic noise annoys people in 2001. Noise from planes, roads, and rails disturbs daily life. Two standard measures sum noise across day and night. Planners need clear links between those measures and annoyance.

The model describes the full spread of annoyance at each noise level. It was fitted to survey data for each transport type. Simple formulas give shares of people annoyed at set cutoffs. Cutoffs mark slightly annoyed, annoyed, and highly annoyed groups. Miedema supplies tools for fair noise policy and planning. Formulas are given in forms planners can compute directly.
europmc-pmc1241582:
Mazdai and co-authors measured flame retardants in mother and fetal blood in 2003. PBDEs are used in plastics, electronics, textiles, and building goods. Rodent studies hint they may harm brain development. Lower thyroid hormone in blood is one suspected route.

Twelve paired mother and cord blood samples were collected in Indianapolis. Six PBDE types were measured in each sample. Total levels ranged from 15 to 580 nanograms per gram of fat in mothers. Fetal samples ranged from 14 to 460 on the same scale. Fetal levels closely matched the paired maternal levels. Samples came from women in labor at two hospitals in Indianapolis, Indiana.
europmc-pmc1327682:
Patil, Rocha, Förster, and Nielsen used evolution-style computing to redesign microbe metabolism in 2005. Genetic engineering can tune microbes for useful traits. Metabolic networks are too tangled to predict edits by hand. Genome-scale models capture that structure for computer search.

Finding the best gene deletion set grows fast hard. Their evolution-style search method searches that space far faster. It breeds and selects deletion strategies against a target trait. Patil demonstrates the method on model objectives in silico. Faster search makes computer-guided strain design practical. The method was shown on model cases in the paper.
europmc-pmc1440782:
What a mother eats in pregnancy can mark her young for life. Dolinoy and co-authors showed that in 2006 with yellow agouti mice, whose coat color tracks gene activity. They fed pregnant mice genistein, the main plant estrogen in soy, at levels like a high-soy human diet.

Pups of fed mothers shifted from yellow toward a mottled brown coat. A DNA tag, methylation, rose at six spots near the Agouti gene and stayed high in adult life. The gene spoke less, and the pups were shielded from obesity. Dolinoy offers the first proof that food in the womb can reset the gene control layer, called the epigenome.
europmc-pmc1557782:
An island people offered a rare chance to weigh genes against upbringing. Pilia and co-authors measured 6,148 Sardinians in 2006, spanning ages 14 to 102 and 34,469 relative pairs. They gauged heritability, the share of trait spread due to genes, for 98 traits of heart health and personality.

Every trait showed a significant genetic share. Genes explained about 40 percent of spread in blood tests, 51 percent in body measures, and 19 percent in personality traits. Four traits showed signs of X-chromosome influence. Shared genes linked many traits, including personality facets and metabolic syndrome features. Genetic spread ran larger in women and the young.
europmc-pmc1634882:
A molecular gatekeeper reads a tag on proteins to install them in the cell's outer wall. Robert and co-authors studied that gatekeeper, Omp85, in 2006. Barrel-shaped proteins must be assembled into the outer membranes of Gram-negative bacteria.

Refolded Omp85 formed channels in lab membranes. Adding unfolded membrane proteins or their tail-end signature peptides changed the channel behavior. The recognition was species-specific: a Neisseria protein failed in E. coli until its tail signature was adapted to the host's dialect. Robert shows the tail tag, not the whole protein, is the passport Omp85 checks.
europmc-pmc1661682:
A probiotic guest changes what a resident gut bacterium eats. Sonnenburg, Chen, and Gordon proved that in 2006 with germ-free mice. They colonized the mice with Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron, a major human gut resident, plus Bifidobacterium longum, a common probiotic.

With the guest present, the resident widened its menu of sugars, adding mannose- and xylose-bearing ones. The mouse gut also switched on innate immunity genes. The resident's sugar expansion held across two mouse strains and appeared with a dairy Lactobacillus strain too. Sonnenburg offers the setup as a controlled lens on probiotic effects.
europmc-pmc1779282:
Topolski and colleagues set out in 2006 to build a short way to judge how active older adults are. Their tool, called RAPA, was meant for adults over age 50. It had to be quick to give and easy for clinic staff to score.

The team reviewed past work, surveyed doctors who treat older patients, and ran focus groups and interviews. They built a nine-item form that asks about strength, stretching, and how hard and how often a person moves. In 115 adults with a mean age near 73 years, RAPA matched a longer proven survey better than two rival short forms did. RAPA found 81 percent of truly active people, and its strength and stretching items also scored well.
europmc-pmc1808482:
Civitarese, Ravussin and the CALERIE Pennington Team tested in 2007 whether eating less changes the power plants of human muscle. Mitochondria are the cell parts that burn fuel for energy, and calorie restriction extends lifespan in many species. The trial asked if restriction grows new mitochondria in healthy people.

Thirty-six young, overweight adults were assigned for six months to normal eating, 25 percent calorie restriction, or restriction plus exercise. Daily energy use fell in both restriction groups even after weight loss was accounted for, and it was unchanged in controls. Genes for mitochondrial work, including PPARGC1A, TFAM, and SIRT1, switched on more strongly. Muscle mitochondrial DNA rose by 35 percent with restriction alone, and by 21 percent in the combined group.
europmc-pmc1832182:
Schilling, Aseltine and Gore followed teenagers into young adulthood in 2007 to test the lasting mental health effects of bad childhood experiences. Prior work tied such experiences to mental health trouble, but early adult outcomes and group differences drew little study. Many earlier samples also failed to represent the wider population.

The team drew a random sample of 1,093 high school seniors from varied communities, interviewed in 1998 and again two years later. They related lifetime exposure to a range of adverse experiences to depression symptoms, drug abuse, and antisocial behavior. Most single experiences tied strongly to all three outcomes. Piling up several experiences raised risk further, by a similar amount for each outcome. Gender differences appeared for most experience types, with sexual abuse and assault the exception.
europmc-pmc1885282:
Lin, Liu and co-authors mapped in 2007 every place the estrogen receptor alpha protein binds DNA in breast cancer cells. The receptor switches genes on when estrogen docks into it, driving growth in hormone-sensitive tumors. Its true binding map across the genome was largely unknown.

Using a pull-down and paired-end sequencing method in MCF-7 breast cancer cells, they found 1,234 high-confidence binding clusters. About 94 percent were judged genuine receptor sites. Only five percent sat near gene starts, in the classic promoter zone. The vast majority lay inside genes or far away, implying control over long distances. Most sites held a full or half estrogen response element, the DNA motif the receptor grips. Nearby genes were enriched for estrogen response and split patient tumors by receptor status.
europmc-pmc1904382:
Tarca, Drăghici and colleagues introduced machine learning to biologists in 2007 as a primer on algorithms that learn patterns from data. Machine learning builds classifiers and predictors from existing examples, with both the building and the running meant to be mechanized. Limited human input in construction reduces the chance that human bias steers the result.

The article lays out core ideas: pattern recognition, classification, and prediction grounded in concrete, observable data. It stresses that a learned classifier must run feasibly on real hardware, not just in theory. Applications in biology include sorting genes, proteins, and patients by measured features. The authors trace the history of ties between the two fields and survey where these methods fit biological research. It serves as an entry point rather than a report of new experiments.
europmc-pmc1913582:
Bell, Samet and co-authors mapped in 2007 what fine particle air pollution is actually made of across the United States. Such particles, called PM2.5, are linked to many health harms, but which ingredients do the damage was unknown. Health studies need to know which components are worth tracking.

The team built a database of 52 particle components in 187 counties for the years 2000 to 2005. Composition varied strongly by season and region. Only seven components made up at least one percent of total particle mass on yearly or seasonal averages. The biggest were ammonium, organic carbon matter, sulfate, and nitrate, plus elemental carbon, silicon, and sodium. Total mass tracked ammonium most closely over a year, and organic carbon and nitrate in winter.
europmc-pmc1950082:
Fraser set out in 2007 to make epidemic tracking numbers that can be computed live, from thin data, while an outbreak unfolds. A reproduction number counts how many people one typical case infects. It tells officials whether spread is growing or dying out.

The paper gives a new way to estimate the individual reproduction number that reads the epidemic's state at a moment in time. It then builds a household version, the number of households each infected household infects, from a model of spread within and between homes. Simulations of influenza and measles built from historical data validated the method. Estimates follow for what emerging flu and measles epidemics would look like. The household number helps judge household-targeted isolation, vaccination, and school or workplace closures.
europmc-pmc2124782: A medical paper on experimental epidemic poliomyelitis in monkeys. The polio model. This article preserves that virology research. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. The paper lasts as a quiet witness to its time.
europmc-pmc2125082: A medical paper on studies of circulation in man, blood flow in the feet. The foot's blood. This article preserves that physiology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2125182: A medical paper with experimental operations on the sigmoid valves of the pulmonary artery. The valves, operated. This article preserves that surgery. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. Those who study the era will use it in their work.
europmc-pmc2131182: A medical paper on the fundamental properties of the fibroblast and the macrophage. The cells' nature. This article preserves that cell biology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2140382: Given time, living things can learn to take the heat, as this paper showed. The study followed how heat-toughness passed down. The hothouse change, traced. The article keeps that life-change study. Kept for study.
europmc-pmc2206382:
Le Maitre, Hoyland and Freemont compared two inflammatory signals in human spinal discs in 2007. Disc degeneration and disc herniation are leading causes of low back pain, but their biology is poorly understood. The signals IL-1beta and TNFalpha were prime suspects, yet no study had measured both at once in degenerate or herniated discs. The team used gene counting and tissue staining on non-degenerate, degenerate and herniated discs.

IL-1beta gene activity appeared in 79 percent of discs, against 59 percent for TNFalpha. Degenerate discs carried about 1,300 copies of IL-1beta message against 250 for TNFalpha, per standard sample. Their IL-1 receptor levels ran ten-fold higher than in healthy discs. About 80 percent of their cells showed the receptor. TNF receptor levels did not rise. IL-1 looks the dominant signal and the better drug target.
europmc-pmc2258182:
Barrick and Breaker surveyed metabolite-binding riboswitches in 2007, RNA elements that sense small molecules and control genes. A riboswitch folds into a precise receptor, called an aptamer, for its target molecule, then reshapes nearby RNA to switch a gene off or on. More than a dozen classes respond to ligands from amino acids to coenzymes. The team compiled a comparative genomics data set for ten classes through systematic database searches.

Their phylogenetic analyses mapped where each riboswitch class occurs across microbial groups. Most examples sit in bacteria, with others in archaea, fungi and plants. Structural analysis updated the aptamer models for each class. Different bacterial groups preferred different control mechanisms, such as stopping transcription early or blocking ribosome binding. Newly found variants sharpened understanding of how these RNA switches work without any protein help.
europmc-pmc2291482:
Fernando and co-authors reviewed and pooled thirty years of research in 2008 on the human MHC region and autoimmunity. This chromosome 6 region holds about 250 genes and shapes how the immune system presents invaders. Its variants link to many autoimmune diseases, but strong correlations between neighbouring genes make causal ones hard to pin down. The team consolidated evidence for six diseases: multiple sclerosis, type 1 diabetes, lupus, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease and rheumatoid arthritis.

Their synthesis confirmed established MHC associations for each disease. It also surfaced predisposing variants that earlier small studies had missed. Comparing across diseases revealed shared patterns and sharp differences. Some mechanisms look general to autoimmunity, while others are specific to one condition. The work shows most past studies sampled only about twenty of the region's genes, usually in Europeans. Broader, better-designed studies are needed to find the truly causal variants.
europmc-pmc2376782:
Clifford and colleagues pooled worldwide data on HPV types in cervical cancer in 2003. HPV, human papillomavirus, causes nearly all cervical cancers, but about 40 types infect the genital tract. Knowing which types dominate, region by region, matters for designing vaccines.

They combined 85 studies covering 10,058 cases. HPV16 led everywhere in the main cancer form, squamous cell carcinoma, making up 46% to 63% of cases depending on region. HPV18 came next there, but it led in the glandular form, adenocarcinoma, at 37% to 41% of cases in every region. That rarer form also showed lower overall virus detection, 76.4% versus 87.3% for the squamous form. Types 58 and 52 stood out in Asia. About a quarter of all cases traced to 16 further types beyond 16 and 18.
europmc-pmc2556082:
Moussion, Ortega, and Girard mapped where a signalling protein called IL-33 sits in the healthy human body in this 2008 study. IL-33 belongs to the interleukin-1 family and activates immune cells through a partner receptor. The team had first found it in the nucleus of cells lining certain blood vessels, raising the question of where else it occurs.

Using antibody staining across tissue collections, they found IL-33 permanently present in the nuclei of endothelial cells, the vessel lining. It ran throughout vessels large and small, in tumours and in most normal tissues. It also sat in skin cells and in the lining of the stomach, tonsils, and salivary glands, surfaces exposed to the outside world. The authors propose IL-33 acts as an alarmin, a danger signal released when such barrier cells are damaged.
europmc-pmc2567082:
Michelakis, Webster, and Mackey reviewed in 2008 the case for an old generic drug, dichloroacetate, as a metabolic treatment for cancer. Most solid tumours run an odd metabolism called the Warburg effect, burning sugar by glycolysis even when oxygen is plentiful. That switch is tied to tumours resisting apoptosis, the programmed cell death that normally culls faulty cells.

Dichloroacetate blocks an enzyme called pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase, pushing sugar fuel into the mitochondria, the cell's power stations, for full oxidation instead. In laboratory and animal studies this revived mitochondrial death signalling and suppressed tumour growth. The drug is taken by mouth and long used for other conditions. The authors lay out the scientific and clinical rationale for moving it quickly into early cancer trials.
europmc-pmc2579282:
Nafees, Stafford, Gavriel, Bhalla, and Watkins measured in 2008 how the British public values health states in advanced lung cancer. Cost-effectiveness studies need utility scores. These numbers capture quality of life for each stage of disease and each severe treatment side effect. The team adapted descriptions from breast cancer states. They refined them with oncologists and specialist nurses. They built 17 states covering disease response and toxicities like fatigue, rash, and low blood counts.

One hundred members of the public rated the states in standard gamble interviews, choosing between certain impaired health and risky gambles. Stable disease with no toxicity scored 0.653 on the utility scale, where 1 is full health. Responding disease with no toxicity scored highest, at 0.673 on that scale. Progressive disease fell to 0.473 in this analysis. Every disease state and toxicity significantly lowered the score.
europmc-pmc2617782:
Touchon and colleagues compared the genomes of 20 Escherichia coli strains in 2009 to map how this species organises its remarkable genetic diversity. E. coli spans harmless gut residents and serious pathogens, all churning through rapid genetic change. The team re-annotated every genome uniformly, sequenced seven of them fully, and grouped roughly 18,000 gene families.

Only about 2,000 gene families were shared by all strains. Recombination proved far more frequent than mutation, yet the family tree stayed readable, with the B2 group near its base. Gene gain and loss clustered at a few conserved hotspots in the chromosome, and acquired genes then spread between strains through recombination in flanking core genes. Few genes specific to gut-external virulence appeared, complicating vaccine hopes. Metabolism diversification drove adaptation in B2 and Shigella strains.
europmc-pmc261882:
Carmena and colleagues demonstrated in 2003 that monkeys can learn to reach and grasp with a robot arm controlled purely by brain activity. Their brain-machine interface read signals from large ensembles of neurons in frontal and parietal cortex. Mathematical models extracted hand position, velocity, gripping force, and muscle signals from that activity in real time.

Accuracy demanded recordings from many neurons at once, since single neurons each encode several movement features. With practice, both the models' predictions and the monkeys' performance improved significantly. Using only visual feedback, the monkeys produced robot reaching and grasping movements while their own arms stayed still. Learning came with reorganisation across cortical areas. It was as if the brain had absorbed the robot arm into its own body maps.
europmc-pmc2626282:
Smith and colleagues reported in 2009 the first American evidence that pigs and pig workers carry the livestock-associated MRSA strain ST398. MRSA is a drug-resistant staphylococcus, and Dutch and Canadian studies had found this strain widespread in swine herds. The team swabbed the noses of 299 pigs and 20 workers at two production systems in Iowa and Illinois covering about 87,000 animals.

Overall, 49 percent of pigs and 45 percent of workers carried MRSA. One system was saturated. Prevalence there ranged from 36 percent in adult pigs to 100 percent in pigs aged 9 and 12 weeks. And 64 percent of its workers were colonised. The other system was entirely clean. All typed isolates were the single clone ST398, unrelated to common American human strains. The authors warn farm animals could become an important reservoir.
europmc-pmc2631682:
Engberg, Aarestrup, Taylor, Gerner-Smidt, and Nachamkin reviewed in 2001 how Campylobacter bacteria are becoming resistant to the two antibiotic families used against them. Human infections with Campylobacter jejuni and C. coli had risen markedly over the previous decade, and resistant strains were rising with them. The authors tracked resistance trends in human isolates and related them to antibiotic use in food animals.

Quinolone resistance had grown enough that the review warns fluoroquinolones may now be of limited use for empiric treatment, treating before test results, in many regions. Macrolide resistance remained less common, so erythromycin and related macrolides should stay the drugs of choice in most areas. The authors call for systematic surveillance and control measures to be maintained. They link veterinary drug use to the human treatment problem.
europmc-pmc2631782:
Hutin and colleagues investigated in 2001 a large outbreak of human monkeypox in the Democratic Republic of Congo during 1996 and 1997. Monkeypox is a smallpox-like zoonotic disease from rainforest animals, mainly squirrels, whose spread between people was thought too weak to sustain itself. Reports from the Katako-Kombe Health Zone suggested unusually long transmission chains, so the team surveyed twelve villages.

They found 88 cases of febrile pustular rash over twelve months, an attack rate of 22 per 1,000 people and a case-fatality rate of 3.7 percent in this outbreak. Seven active cases were confirmed by virus isolation. Antibodies appeared in 54 percent of patients tested and in 25 percent of wild-caught animals. Smallpox vaccination, which protects against monkeypox, had ended by 1983, steadily enlarging the susceptible population.
europmc-pmc2642882:
Mukrasch and co-authors used magnetic resonance methods in 2009 to map the tau protein piece by piece. Tau helps hold up the cell's inner scaffolding in brain cells. In Alzheimer disease it clumps into tangles, a hallmark of the illness. At 441 building blocks, this longest form of tau is large and floppy, which had blocked detailed study.

The team split the protein into smaller segments, read each one, then matched the readings to rebuild the whole picture. Tau proved highly flexible, moving almost like a loose chain, yet with distinct regions. Distant parts of the chain touched each other briefly in a web of fleeting contacts. Those contacts may be the very ones that start clumping. The work also showed how tau grips the cell scaffolding it normally supports.
europmc-pmc2647682:
Zamboni and colleagues reported in 2009 a vein problem they tied to multiple sclerosis, a disease in which the immune system damages the brain and spinal cord. They asked whether the veins draining the brain and spine work normally in these patients. No one had checked those outflow routes closely before.

Using ultrasound scans, the team studied 65 patients and 235 comparison subjects, including healthy people and patients with other nerve diseases. Signs of blocked or narrowed outflow appeared far more often in the sclerosis patients. Follow-up dye tests showed multiple severe narrowings in the main neck and chest veins of patients, but not of controls. The authors name this pattern chronic cerebrospinal venous insufficiency. Different disease courses matched different narrowing patterns, and pressure across the narrow spots ran slightly higher in patients.
europmc-pmc2650282:
Pillai and colleagues, with the ICGN Investigators, hunted in 2009 for genes that make some smokers develop chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a slow lung illness that blocks airflow. Most smokers never get it, so genes likely shape the risk. The only clear gene known then caused a rare lack of a protective lung protein.

The team scanned the genomes of 823 Norwegian patients and 810 smokers who stayed healthy. Two spots near a nicotine receptor gene, CHRNA3/5, stood out. The same spots held up in family studies and in two more groups from the United States. One variant alone accounted for about 12 percent of cases in the wider population. A second locus, near a gene called HHIP, also showed a link. Both loci tied to measured lung function as well.
europmc-pmc2703782:
Zhang and co-authors studied how insulin, a hormone that controls blood sugar, helps fat cells form through a chain of signals. At the center is mTORC1, a protein complex that drives cell growth, and TSC2, a protein that holds mTORC1 back. A key fat gene called PPAR gamma must switch on for new fat cells to mature.

In mouse cells and a standard fat cell line that lacked TSC2, fat formation was stronger than normal, even with weak insulin signals. That boost needed high mTORC1 activity, which raised PPAR gamma levels. Blocking all the insulin-linked sites on TSC2 stopped the signal and blocked fat formation, which pins TSC2 as a main gate in the process.
europmc-pmc2837382:
Parnell, Inger, Bearhop, and Jackson presented a new statistics package in 2010 for reading animal diets from stable isotopes, the natural chemical fingerprints stored in tissue. Ecologists estimate what fraction of an animal's diet each food source supplies by solving mixing models. Older models either ignored natural variation or listed every feasible answer without saying which were likely.

Their package, SIAR, uses Bayesian methods, which turn uncertainty in sources and tissue values into honest probability estimates for each source's share. It copes when there are more sources than isotopes to separate them, a common dead end before. Released as open source in the R language, it is built to grow into a single suite for isotope work.
europmc-pmc2852382:
Kirchhoff, Clavien, and Hahnloser reviewed in 2010 what goes wrong during and after colorectal surgery, and how surgical teams can prevent it. Searching three decades of literature, they catalog complications across operations ranging from cancer resections to repairs for inflammatory bowel disease and obstruction. Problems split into those arising mid-operation, such as bleeding, bowel injury, and ureter or bladder damage, and later ones.

Postoperative dangers center on wound infection, leaks where bowel ends are rejoined, bowel shutdown, and bleeding. The review credits the spread of keyhole surgery, better surgeon training, higher hospital volumes, and standardized care pathways for falling complication rates. Its practical message: knowing which risk factors can be changed before surgery is the surest route to fewer complications.
europmc-pmc2876182:
Lacy reviewed in 2006 how neutrophils, the most common white blood cells, release their stored chemical weapons, a process called degranulation. Neutrophils rush from the blood into inflamed tissue and fire enzymes and toxins from packed granules. That firepower also damages the body's own tissue and drives severe asthma attacks and other lung diseases.

Release turns out to be selective rather than an all-or-nothing dump. Inside the cell, several signal chains control which granules fuse with the surface, including scaffolding proteins, a molecular motor switch, and membrane fusion tags shared with other secreting cells. Different granule types answer to different chains, which means drugs might block the harmful releases while sparing useful ones. The review assembles what each control piece does.
europmc-pmc2908682:
Todesco, Rubio-Somoza, Paz-Ares, and Weigel released in 2010 a toolkit that blocks nearly every microRNA family in the plant Arabidopsis, one family at a time. MicroRNAs are small regulators that fine-tune development, but their genes come in families with many near-identical copies, so deleting one copy shows little. The team used artificial target mimics, decoy molecules that soak up a whole family's microRNAs inside the plant.

About a fifth of the families produced visible defects in leaves and stems when blocked, and all of those are ancient families shared across land plants. Younger, lineage-specific microRNAs rarely changed appearance, suggesting they polish traits rather than run core development. Several mimic plants matched the look of plants carrying a single resistant target gene, hinting that one main target carries most of each family's effect.
europmc-pmc3022582:
Brenet and colleagues asked in this 2011 study where a chemical mark on DNA actually switches genes off. The mark is methylation, the adding of small tags to DNA letters. Earlier work had focused mostly on the stretch just before a gene starts. The team compared marks and gene activity across the whole genome in human cells.

Marks crowded around the start of a gene were tied to silence, but marks farther inside the gene body were not tied to how strongly the gene ran. The tightest link sat in the first exon, the first coding block after the start. Marks there tracked shutdown more closely than marks in the upstream control region. Once copying had begun, marks downstream did not slow it much. The findings suggest the first exon helps block a gene from starting.
europmc-pmc3072482:
Antonaci and coauthors reviewed in 2011 the well documented pairing of migraine with psychiatric illness. Migraine is very common, strikes in attacks, and often travels with other conditions. The review weighs population surveys and clinic studies in adults and children, focusing on mood and anxiety disorders measured under standard psychiatric categories.

Across general population studies, people with migraine carry a clearly higher risk of depression and anxiety disorders than people without it. A link with bipolar disorder looks plausible, while a link with substance dependence does not. The migraine with aura subtype shows the strongest psychiatric overlap. Patients whose headaches become daily fare worse psychiatrically than those with plain migraine. How the pairing arises is still poorly understood. The authors stress that it changes treatment choices and long term outcomes, so it deserves priority in research.
europmc-pmc3084482:
Talhout and coauthors built in 2011 a modern list of the hazardous chemicals in tobacco smoke, replacing a famous older list that covered only cancer agents from nineteen nineties data. Smoke holds more than five thousand chemicals. The team assembled a database of over two thousand known smoke components, found emission levels for several hundred, and identified those with established human inhalation risk values.

Ninety eight components made the hazardous list, spanning cancer, heart, and lung harms, the three great causes of smoking deaths. For chemicals not on the list, the authors derived cautious exposure thresholds from the listed values, so regulators can still judge them. They recommend the new list for regulatory use, including product testing and disclosure rules. The work gives health agencies a defensible, up to date inventory of what makes smoke dangerous.
europmc-pmc3085482:
Schwessinger and colleagues showed in 2011 that one plant helper protein runs three defense and growth programs through different chemical settings. The helper, called BAK1 in short, partners with several surface sensors in the small plant Arabidopsis. Some sensors detect steroid hormones for growth, while others detect bacterial parts and raise the alarm. A new mutant version of the helper split those jobs apart.

Plants carrying the variant lost alarm signaling through two bacterial sensors almost completely. Yet their hormone responses and their control of cell death stayed normal. The sensors themselves are weak enzymes, and simply joining with the helper needed no enzyme activity from either side. The variant's enzyme activity was, however, required for the alarm defect. The authors conclude the helper uses phosphorylation, a chemical tagging step, to tune each pathway separately.
europmc-pmc3095282:
Xin and colleagues cataloged in 2010 the tiny regulatory RNAs that respond when wheat is attacked by powdery mildew fungus or stressed by heat. These microRNAs fine tune gene activity after genes are read, and they steer both development and stress responses in plants. The team sequenced small RNAs from wheat leaves under each stress and sorted them into families.

They found over one hundred fifty microRNAs in total, spanning known families and many never reported before. Two dozen responded to the fungus and a dozen to heat, with predicted targets among stress and development genes. Wheat feeds much of the world, and both stresses cut harvests heavily. Knowing which regulators move first gives breeders and engineers precise handles for building hardier varieties. The authors present the catalog as a starting map for that work.
europmc-pmc3096582:
Michie, van Stralen, and West introduced in 2011 the behaviour change wheel, a tool for designing programs that change what people do, from quitting smoking to prescribing wisely. Many frameworks for such programs existed, but the authors found none covered the full range of options or tied interventions cleanly to a model of behavior. They evaluated nineteen frameworks against coverage, coherence, and that missing link.

At the wheel's hub sits a simple system: behavior happens when people have the capability, the opportunity, and the motivation together. Around it sit nine intervention functions, from education to coercion, and around those, seven kinds of policy that deliver them. Reviewers applied the wheel reliably to a national tobacco strategy and to obesity guidance. The authors offer it as a shared design language, so programs can be built from a full menu rather than habit.
europmc-pmc3117882:
Katherine Hunt and colleagues charted bacteria living in human milk in a 2011 study in PLoS ONE. Milk was long assumed sterile, but recent work kept finding microbes in it. The team used gene sequencing on samples from sixteen women, taken three times over four weeks, to map the full mix and its stability.

Milk communities proved richer than earlier reports suggested, with several bacterial groups each making up a notable share. A woman's milk mix often stayed fairly steady across the month, though not always. The authors ask what these microbes do for the baby's gut, which milk bacteria may help seed, and for breast health itself. Their map sets a baseline for studying milk as a living fluid.
europmc-pmc3120982:
Peter Austin settled a practical question for health researchers in a 2011 paper in Pharmaceutical Statistics. When treatments are not assigned by chance, researchers pair treated and untreated people with similar predicted chances of treatment, so groups compare fairly. How close those paired scores must be, the matching width, had little guidance behind it.

Austin ran wide-ranging computer simulations for both whole-number and yes-or-no outcomes. A width set at one fifth of the spread of the transformed score worked best or near best in most settings. It removed nearly all of the starting bias and gave error ranges with the right coverage. When all pairing factors were yes-or-no traits, the exact width mattered far less. His rule gives analysts a firm default.
europmc-pmc3178582:
Yibing Wang and colleagues achieved the first genetic transformation of a major sexually transmitted pathogen in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. The bacterium lives only inside human cells and had resisted all attempts to insert foreign DNA, blocking study of its genes. The team exploited an antibiotic quirk: treated infected cells stall the bacterium in a state that inserted resistance genes could rescue.

Their shuttle carrier, built from the bacterium's own plasmid plus a standard bacterial origin, entered the pathogen and displaced its native plasmid. Foreign promoters worked, reporter enzymes were made, and glowing transformants were isolated. Adding the plasmid back to a plasmid-free strain restored its ability to store sugar, proving the system can test gene function. The breakthrough opens the pathogen's genome to direct study.
europmc-pmc3277482:
Fauzia Imtiaz and colleagues tested a simple blood ratio as a marker of body-wide inflammation in a Karachi population sample, in this 2012 paper in the International Archives of Medicine. The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio comes free with a routine blood count, and inflammation is implicated in chronic diseases from heart disease to cancer. Most earlier prognostic work had ignored other illnesses that might raise inflammation, so the team related the ratio to prevalent conditions directly.

Just over a thousand apparently healthy adults gave blood and answered health questions. Hypertension was more common in the middle and highest thirds of the ratio than in the lowest. People with hypertension or diabetes were also substantially more likely to sit in the upper thirds. The authors conclude the ratio tracks systemic inflammation associated with common chronic conditions, while calling for follow-up studies to establish which comes first.
europmc-pmc3310682:
Nordmann, Naas, and Poirel reviewed the worldwide spread of gut bacteria that resist last resort antibiotics, in a 2011 article. The bacteria, common residents of the human intestine, cause many hospital and community infections. Carbapenem antibiotics are often the final option against them, but some bacteria now make enzymes, called carbapenemases, that destroy even these drugs.

The review sorts these enzymes into three chemical classes and traces how each has traveled. One family, first spotted in the United States in the nineteen nineties, has since caused outbreaks across Europe, Asia, and South America. Because the resistance genes ride on mobile DNA that jumps between bacteria, the authors frame the spread as a global public health threat needing coordinated tracking.
europmc-pmc3334582:
Scheinfeldt and colleagues looked for genetic adaptations to thin air among Ethiopians living at high altitude, reporting in 2012. Mountain peoples in the Andes and Tibet carry gene variants that help them cope with low oxygen, several tied to hemoglobin, the oxygen carrying protein. Ethiopia's highlanders, among the world's oldest high altitude populations, had not been studied this way.

Scanning the genomes of highland and lowland Ethiopians, the team found clearly different hemoglobin levels between the groups. Signals of natural selection pointed to a fresh set of candidate genes. Most had not appeared in Tibetan or Andean studies, though two sit in the same oxygen sensing pathway, suggesting the same system was tuned independently. The authors conclude that Ethiopian highlanders adapted through their own evolutionary path, a case of similar problems solved more than once.
europmc-pmc3394782:
Deckers and colleagues reviewed in 2012 how atopic eczema, a chronic itchy skin condition, changed worldwide between 1990 and 2010. Good trend data guide health planning and hint at causes. The team searched seven databases for studies that measured the disease at least twice with comparable methods.

Sixty-nine reports qualified, but differing measures and shifting diagnostic labels clouded the picture. Even so, the share of people with eczema appeared to be rising in Africa, eastern Asia, western Europe, and Britain. Other regions showed no clear trend, and repeated studies of new cases were scarce. The authors call for cleaner definitions and reporting so future trends can be trusted.
europmc-pmc3400082:
Greene-Schloesser and co-authors reviewed radiation injury to the brain in 2012, a late cost of treating brain tumors. About one hundred thousand American tumor patients a year now live long enough to face it. Old teaching held the brain highly resistant, but subtler harm, fading memory, attention, and planning, can wreck quality of life.

Animal studies long blamed lost nerve-cell birth in the memory hub, the hippocampus, and suggested shielding it. Studies in older rodents complicate that story: their thinking slipped without lost new neurons or white-matter death. The authors argue the injury spans many brain regions and subtler changes. New imaging tools, they say, can hunt markers and drug targets across the whole brain.
europmc-pmc3414782:
Medrek, Pontén, Jirström, and Leandersson asked in 2012 whether macrophages inside breast tumors predict how patients fare, and whether where the cells sit matters. These tumor-associated macrophages usually take the repair-minded form that helps cancers invade and grow blood vessels. The team stained tumors from well over a hundred patients for two macrophage markers.

Cells in the tumor's supporting stroma, not those inside tumor nests, carried the clinical signal. Stromal counts of the M2 marker CD163 tracked with higher grade, larger size, and hormone-negative disease. Stromal counts of the general marker CD68 independently predicted worse breast-cancer survival. Location, the authors conclude, is the message: studies must score where macrophages sit, not just whether they appear.
europmc-pmc3434182:
Chassaing and colleagues validated a stool test in 2012 for tracking gut inflammation in mice without harming the animal. Classic measures need tissue samples, so the same mouse cannot be followed over time. Their candidate was lipocalin 2, a protein shed into feces, read by a standard lab assay.

In chemically induced colitis, fecal lipocalin rose in step with dose, from very mild irritation to full-blown inflammation, matching tissue signs and inflammatory gene readings. It flagged inflammation a day after exposure began, long before other markers moved. In mice bred to develop colitis on their own, it mirrored disease severity faithfully. The test is cheap, stable, and repeatable, making it a practical stand-in for gut inflammation checks.
europmc-pmc3446382:
Liu and colleagues counted killer T cells inside breast tumors in 2012 to test whether they forecast survival, and in which tumor subtypes. Immune cells infiltrating tumors may signal the body fighting back, but their meaning in breast cancer was contested. The team stained tissue samples from nearly four thousand patients with early-stage disease.

T cells touching tumor cells directly appeared in about a third of cases, and stromal T cells in well over half. In the whole group, the direct-contact pattern tracked with better breast-cancer survival. Sharper analysis narrowed the benefit to one subtype, basal-like cancers, where the cells independently predicted longer life. Triple-negative tumors lacking basal markers got no such advantage. Immunity, they conclude, must be read subtype by subtype.
europmc-pmc3463482:
Li and co-authors presented a software suite built around DelPhi in BMC Biophysics in 2012. DelPhi solves a key equation used to model electric charge around large biological molecules in water. Such modeling helps explain how proteins fold and bind, but new users often struggle to set the program up.

The suite gathers the program files, source code, manuals, and parameter files in one place. Worked examples show how to run DelPhi and check its output against known answers. Li's team also linked outside tools that build on DelPhi and opened a forum for users. Academic users could download the whole package free of charge.

europmc-pmc8508982: This 2021 review paper covers endometriosis: epidemiology (how diseases spread in populations), classification (sorting into groups), pathogenesis (how the disease develops), treatment and genetics. Endometriosis is a "mysterious" disease and its exact cause has not yet been established. Solid numbers like these help health officials aim prevention money and effort where they count most.
europmc-pmc8611382: Published in 2021, this review paper takes on a systematic review (a review of every study) of racial/ethnic and socioeconomic disparities. The authors gathered every relevant study they could find and weighed the results together. Having the evidence weighed in one place saves busy doctors from sifting through dozens of papers alone.
europmc-pmc8714082: Doctors and scientists took on multivariable link discovery in people-scale meta-omics studies in this 2021 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. A tested new tool like this gives doctors a steadier way to measure what they see in patients.
europmc-pmc8913782: Published in 2022, this research paper takes on fully-automated and ultra-fast cell-type identification using specific marker combinations from single-cell (one cell at a time) transcriptomic (gene-activity) data. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8940982: Doctors and scientists took on advances (new steps forward) in COVID-19 mrna vaccine growth in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc8969382: Doctors and scientists took on CAR race to cancer immunotherapy (treatment that boosts the immune system): from CAR t, CAR NK to CAR macrophage (immune cleanup cell) in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc9057982: Yamasoba and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on virological traits of the SARS-CoV-2 omicron ba-2 spike. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9157382: Published in 2022, this research paper takes on global, local, and national incidence (new cases) and deaths of neonatal preterm birth, 1990-2019. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Solid numbers like these help health officials aim prevention money and effort where they count most.
europmc-pmc9270782: A fresh look at the global prevalence (how common a condition is) of autism spectrum illness: a thorough systematic review (a review of every study) arrived with this 2022 research paper. Autism spectrum illness is one of the serious developmental illnesses that is usually diagnosed below the age of three years. With firm counts in hand, planners can size the problem and track whether it grows or shrinks.
europmc-pmc9274782: Doctors and scientists took on mental health during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic: a review and recommendations for moving forward in this 2022 review paper. It walks through what the field currently knows, study by study. Having the evidence weighed in one place saves busy doctors from sifting through dozens of papers alone.
europmc-pmc9547882: Lei and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on signaling (cell-to-cell messaging) pathways and treatment treatments in stomach cancer. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
europmc-pmc9725182: This 2022 research paper covers infertility prevalence (how common a condition is) and the methods of estimation from 1990 to 2021: a systematic review. Study question what is the contemporary prevalence (how common a condition is) of infertility in world groups and how do. Solid numbers like these help health officials aim prevention money and effort where they count most.
europmc-pmc9726982: This 2022 research paper covers gut microbiome (microbes living in the body)-wide link study of depressive symptoms. Depression is one of the most poorly understood diseases due to its elusive pathogenesis (how the disease develops). Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
fludd-schutzschrift-rosenkreuzer-1782:
Robert Fludd, the English physician and philosopher, answered the Rosicrucian manifestos with a defense of the fraternity in 1617. His Tractatus Apologeticus argued that the brethren's aims were godly and their critics unjust. This German translation of 1782 carried the English apology back to German readers, late but still valued.

Fludd never met a Rosicrucian, yet he staked his name on their defense. His reply became the pivotal English answer to the manifestos. The 1782 printing shows the old quarrel still alive in the century of the Illuminati. Fludd's elaborate cosmology stands behind the apology. England's most learned occultist speaks here for the invisible college, in the tongue of the manifestos themselves.
fontane-irrungen-wirrungen-1882:
Theodor Fontane's Berlin novel Irrungen, Wirrungen appeared in German in 1888 from an 1882 serial start, and Katharine Royce Englished it in 1917. Her version, Trials and Tribulations, ran in the Harvard Classics Shelf of Fiction. Lene, a seamstress, loves Botho, a young baron and officer, across the class line of Berlin.

Both know the match cannot last, and both accept its end with quiet grace. Fontane tells the parting without villains, blame, or melodrama. Talk, walks, and small social signs carry the whole weight of feeling. The novel is often called the finest German story of love across class. Its restraint is the source of its lasting power.
frus-1861-d182:
Carl Schurz wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 17 October 1861. The dispatch is document 182 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two Schurz reports in eight days close the autumn run from Madrid. His eye for character made his letters lively reading then and now. The second report rounds out a file that mixes court news with a young envoy's growth. Lively letters from Madrid were read in Washington with more pleasure than most. Pleasure in reading a post's letters was a sign the post was doing its work.
frus-1861-d282:
Seward wrote again on 25 July 1861, this time to Mr. Haldeman. It was printed as Document 282 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d82:
From his London post on 14 September 1861, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 82 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams wrote as the leaves turned in London and the war ground on. His reports tracked the slow drift of British thought on the blockade and the South. Each one gave Washington a fresh reading of the power that could still break the Union's hopes. The slow drift he tracked was the real battle for Britain in 1861. The drift he tracked was slow, but its end point was the fate of the Union.
frus-1862-d182:
On 4 November 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a dispatch to Charles Francis Adams in London, printed as Document 182 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was one of three Seward letters to Adams under that date.

Election day in the North fell on 4 November that year, and foreign governments watched the results for signs of war weariness. Seward wrote through the political noise, keeping his envoy supplied. The cluster of letters that day shows a department working at full pace while the British cabinet neared its answer on joint action with France. Southern agents worked London's clubs and press hard, and the legation tracked their moves.
frus-1862-d282:
William L. Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 June 1862, in a report printed as Document 282 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The report opened the June run of the Paris file.

June began with the armies locked around Richmond and Corinth fallen to the Union in the West. In Paris, Napoleon III was weighing a bigger army for Mexico and keeping his Confederate options open. Dayton's reports in this season are valued for a rare thing. They show the court thinking aloud, as much as a court ever does, through hints his letters preserve.
frus-1862-d382:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Cassius Clay, the American minister in Russia, on 4 February 1862. The dispatch is printed as Document 382 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Seward's letter reached St. Petersburg weeks after it was written, at the end of the longest mail route in this file. Clay was preparing to hand the post to Simon Cameron. A February dispatch to Russia shows the Department tending its friendliest channel with the same care it gave the dangerous ones. A habit that kept Russian goodwill in good repair. Russian goodwill gave Washington one capital where it need not argue its right to exist.
frus-1862-d482:
On 4 October 1862 James E. Harvey sent a further report from Lisbon to Secretary of State William H. Seward, one day after his last. It is Document 482 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Back-to-back reports from a quiet post usually mark a case in motion: a ship in question, a ruling awaited, a complaint to answer. In the autumn of 1862 such cases in Portuguese waters grew out of the cruiser war. In that war, hours in port could decide whether a raider got coal. Harvey's paired October letters belong to that grind. They remind the reader that the Union's diplomacy was mostly this: steady attention, quickly reported, from dozens of small posts.
frus-1862-d582:
Thomas Corwin, the American minister in Mexico City, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 February 1862. It is Document 582 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, opening the Mexican file.

Corwin, a former senator and treasury secretary, served the Union in the most sensitive capital in the hemisphere that year. British, French, and Spanish troops had landed in Mexico to collect debts, and Washington feared a European foothold next door. Corwin backed the Juárez government and reported the allied moves at close range. His February letter begins a file that runs beside the Spanish papers in this same volume, the two halves of one crisis.
frus-1862-d682:
William Sydney Thayer wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 November 1861. Thayer was the American consul general in Egypt, based at Alexandria. His letter is document 682 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, opening the Egypt file.

Consuls in the Mediterranean ports watched trade, shipping, and the safety of Americans far from home. From Egypt, Thayer reported on the rule of the viceroy and on the cotton trade that the war had made dear. His letters gave Washington a steady view of a land that sat on the road to India. That land grew more key to the war's trade each month.
frus-1862-d82:
In a report dated 20 June 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 82 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d182:
One of the Secretary's regular instructions to London, this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, is dated 4 May 1863. It appears as document 182 of the 1863 papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d282:
On 5 September 1863, orders left Washington for London: Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The paper is document 282 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

For readers today, these instructions reveal the thinking inside the State Department as clearly as any memoir. They show choices being made in real time, with poor information and high stakes. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d382:
One entry in the running Washington exchange, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, is dated 5 February 1863. It stands as document 382 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Washington believed Confederate agents used British ports, ships, and soil too freely. Seward pressed Lyons to have his government tighten its watch. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d482:
On 28 April 1863 a formal note passed from W. Hunter, chief clerk of the State Department to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d582:
Under the date 1 July 1863, the record holds a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d682:
