Written on 5 December 1863, this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward went to Charles Francis Adams in London. It stands as document 682 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863. It is the third Seward note to Adams dated that same day in this run of records.

Three letters in a day shows how much business ran through the London desk. Adams spoke for the United States in the capital of the world's top sea power. What Seward sent him shaped talks on the war, on trade, and on ships built in British yards. The dispatch rewards slow reading. Its plain form hides high stakes.
frus-1863p1-d82:
William H. Seward wrote this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 14 February 1862, a full year before the letters around it in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 82 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

An older letter set among newer ones is a quirk of the printed file, where stray sheets were placed as they came to hand. Its date puts it in the war's first winter, when the Trent affair's wounds were still fresh. Seward's early letters to London set the claims the Union would press for years. This one, read on its own date, shows that brief in its young form.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d182: Secretary Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on November 1, 1943, as the Moscow protocols were signed. His letter is Document 182 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Hull's mission had ended in the strongest show of allied unity of the war to that date, and his reports home carried that news. The record gives the date and the two men. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series, near the volume's Moscow close.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d282:
General Stilwell, chief of staff to Chiang Kai-shek, issued paper C.C.S. 405 at Cairo on 22 November 1943 under the title Role of China in Defeat of Japan. It answers a direct question: what operations mounted from China would most affect the course of the Pacific war.

His ladder of operations starts with helping in north Burma and building the land route to China. It runs through very-long-range bombing of Japan in early 1944. Then come the recapture of Canton and Hong Kong in the winter of 1944 and 1945. An attack on Formosa follows if needed by May 1945. Stilwell claims the plan is cheap, clashes with no other theater, and could cut a year or two off the Quebec timetable for Japan's defeat. It asks for three American divisions earmarked for China.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d382: Mike Reilly, supervising agent of the Secret Service, telegraphed the White House from Tehran on 27 November 1943, reporting to Chief Wilson and Agent Lowery. The President arrived that day and is well, and the protective party feels confident it has done everything possible to insure his protection. Stalin and Churchill are also in the city, their security officers working closely with the Americans. Return plans are indefinite, but the party will go back to Cairo when the conference ends, and Reilly is pressing for a route by Khartoum, Kano, and Dakar.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d482:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff addressed General Dwight D. Eisenhower, commanding Allied forces in North Africa, on December 5, 1943, during the Second Cairo Conference. The catalog heading misspells the general's name as “Eisenhotoer.” The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Eisenhower's headquarters in Algiers ran the war in the Mediterranean, the theater most directly touched by Cairo's choices. A message from the combined chiefs at this moment carried the conference's authority straight to the commander who had to act on it. For readers, the record connects the summit table to the field headquarters, one day before the conference closed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d82: Hull wrote to Roosevelt on October 31, 1943, after the close of his Moscow mission. The letter is Document 82 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The secretary's standing rose with Moscow's success, and his end-of-month reports helped set the terms for Tehran. The record gives the date and the two men and no topic. The letter appears in the Foreign Relations series with the rest of the Moscow closing papers.
frus-1944-quebec-d182:
Harry Dexter White recorded the meeting of September 14, 1944, between Morgenthau and Lord Cherwell, the session Roosevelt had arranged. Cherwell took lend-lease first, outlining British needs for the period between Germany's defeat and Japan's. A cut of 27 percent in American aid, he suggested, would appear reasonable to the British.

Morgenthau rejected fixing aid by percentages; the question, he said, was how much munitions Britain needed for her Pacific role. Both men liked a joint committee, and White and MacDougall were set to drafting its directive. On Germany, Cherwell doubted American labor would approve so drastic a program. Morgenthau framed the choice bluntly: a strong Germany and weak England, or the reverse. He chose the reverse.
frus-1944-quebec-d282: A secretaries' note dated September 19, 1944, records the final approval of the Japan planning date. Roosevelt and Churchill approved the Combined Chiefs' recommendation. For planning production and allocating manpower, the war against Japan would be assumed to end eighteen months after Germany's defeat. The date would be adjusted periodically to conform to the course of the war. Approval came through their endorsement of the final report, C.C.S. 680/2.
frus-1944-quebec-d82:
America's Joint Chiefs of Staff wrote to the Secretary of State on September 4, 1944. The letter appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume. It came eight days before the Quebec Conference opened. The chiefs directed American military strategy during the war.

Military chiefs rarely wrote as a body to the diplomats. Such a letter signals questions where war plans met foreign policy. In September 1944, those questions centered on Germany's defeat. They also touched the campaign against Japan. For readers, the message shows the armed services stating a joint view. The State Department received it while summit briefings were being finished.
frus-1945-50-intel-d182:
A memorandum dated 13 January 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Chief of the Interdepartmental Coordinating and Planning Staff, Central Intelligence Group (Edgar). The reader was the Assistant Director for Reports and Estimates (Huddle). It stands as document 182 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d282:
A memorandum dated 2 June 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was George H. Butler of the Policy Planning Staff. The reader was the Under Secretary of State (Lovett) and Secretary of State Marshall. It stands as document 282 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The Cold War was turning harder that year, and the new Council and CIA were being tested by it week by week.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d382:
On 20 April 1949, staff wrote up the discussion at the 38th Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. The State Department prints it as document 382 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Reform talk filled the files that year, as the government weighed the Dulles team's harsh grades for the CIA.

Staff trusted these notes because they were made at once, and files across Washington cite them as the record of a talk. For a reader, the gain is scene and voice, rare goods in a file of stiff forms. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d82:
Russell wrote to Byrnes again on 29 December 1945, near the end of the intelligence office's first season. Eight weeks had passed since his November paper to the secretary. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A year-end paper from the administration chief often carries the hard arithmetic: what an office costs, what it returns, and what must give. Russell's December memorandum belongs to the season when the State Department began to reckon with keeping a large analysis service it had not sought. Readers approaching the volume's account of the office's transfer and shrinking in 1946 will find the turn prepared in papers like this one.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d182:
The State Department stated its rule for Italy in public on 5 December 1944. This press release, answering reporters' questions on the Italian cabinet crisis, is reprinted in the Malta and Yalta volume. It draws a hard line against outside meddling.

The make-up of the Italian government, the statement says, is purely an Italian affair. The sole exception is an appointment where weighty military factors come in. Washington has in no way hinted at any bar to Count Sforza. Since Italy is an area of shared allied charge, both London and Rome have been told the American expectation. Italians are to settle their government questions on democratic lines, free of pressure from abroad. The rule holds still more strongly, it adds, for allied governments in freed lands.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d282:
The American chiefs drew up the table of subjects for the next three-power staff conference on 17 January 1945. Their memorandum, C. C. S. 765/1, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It looks past Malta to a full military meeting with the Soviet staff.

For the war against Germany, the first subject is the enemy: his dispositions, capabilities, and intentions, in a frank exchange of information. Next comes coordination of the offensives. Those in the west and in Italy must be matched with those in the east, down to the timing of attacks and liaison between field commanders. Bomblines and air liaison parties are named. Shuttle bombing follows, with the staging of Fifteenth Air Force units in the Vienna-Budapest area. Last come the military aspects of the occupation zones in Germany and Austria, Berlin and Vienna included.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d382:
Eden chaired the foreign ministers on February 8, 1945. Page's minutes list five subjects: the world security body, Yugoslav frontiers, control commissions in Bulgaria and Hungary, reparations, and Iran. On the world body, two points had been sent down from the leaders. Membership came first, including seats for two or three Soviet republics.

The time and place of the founding conference came second. Stettinius added a third: exactly which nations should be invited to the first conference. He said he wished to start at the bottom, and the record breaks off as his argument begins. Page shows the United Nations being assembled question by question.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d482: Stephen Early wrote home to Jonathan Daniels from Yalta on February 7, 1945, in this brief telegram. A pouch with a letter and a press conference transcript had arrived. Early regretted the troubles Daniels faced in Washington. He could honestly assure him that the headaches at Yalta were no less severe. The situation there was much too involved to explain by wire; all they could do was carry on as best they could. The message survives in the Roosevelt Papers, a tired press secretary's aside amid the summit's paper flood.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d82:
Washington answered Harriman the same day, in a secret cable sent on 19 December 1944. Secretary of State Stettinius says the embassy's reading of the disputed passage is right, but only part of the story. The cable is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

The passage, he explains, covers local disputes settled in a peaceful way by groups of nearby states. It also lets the Security Council keep watch on such groups. The Council checks that they stay true to the aims of the new world body. The Council may even use them, when it sees fit, to settle a dispute without force.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d182:
The Combined Policy Committee recorded British consent to use the atomic weapon in minutes dated July 4, 1945. The extract is document 182 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The committee, which oversaw the joint Anglo-American atomic project, met at the Pentagon that morning.

The printed passage is brief. Field Marshal Wilson stated that the British government concurred in the use of the weapon, called here the T.A. weapon, against Japan. He added that the Prime Minister might wish to discuss the matter with the President at the Berlin meeting. A note adds that Secretary Stimson also raised whether Truman might speak to Stalin about the new weapon. The consent recorded here was the formal British agreement required under the wartime atomic partnership.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d282:
The four powers' agreement on control machinery for Austria is printed as document 282 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The text was concluded in the European Advisory Commission in London in July 1945. It sets how Austria would be governed until a freely elected Austrian government could be recognized.

Article 1 creates the machinery: an Allied Council, an Executive Committee, and appointed staffs, the whole to be known as the Allied Commission for Austria. Article 2 provides that the council consists of four military commissioners, one from each government, each also in supreme command of his own occupation forces. Supreme authority on matters touching Austria as a whole rests with the commissioners jointly, acting on their governments' instructions. The agreement's preamble recalls the Moscow Declaration of 1943, which promised a free and independent Austria.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d382:
Winant reported from London on June 28, 1945, on British thinking about Germany's external assets, the Safehaven problem. His embassy had talked with the Ministry of Economic Warfare and the Foreign Office about recent cables from Washington, Madrid, and Paris. The British showed him a draft telegram to Monckton in Moscow, cleared by all interested agencies.

That telegram answered Monckton's reports that Pauley had suggested the Reparations Commission or the Control Council claim German external assets at once. London's points, Winant learned, looked toward joint trusteeship over German official assets, and joint notes to neutral governments about private German property. The cable maps a careful British approach to Safehaven.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d482:
Personnel for Italy's Allied Commission is the subject of a Washington message from Reber to Matthews dated July 13, 1945. Field Marshal Alexander, Reber understands, has proposed that Stone be retained as chief commissioner for three to four months. A civilian chief commissioner would be hard to install while military government still runs in the north of Italy.

During the interim, Douglas would go to Italy as vice president of the economic section, replacing Stone when the period expired. The British chiefs, judging that probably unacceptable, propose instead that Douglas be appointed temporarily as deputy chief commissioner. Neither Douglas nor the War Department, Reber notes, has yet been informed of the plan.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d582:
Tokyo's foreign minister Togo cabled Ambassador Sato in Moscow on July 12, 1945, with word from the Emperor. The secret urgent cable, in translation, is document 582 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It was to reach the Soviets before the three-power conference opened.

Togo relays the Emperor's deep concern at the rising toll of the war on all peoples. The Emperor longs for a swift end to the fighting. Yet while America and England demand unconditional surrender, Japan sees no path but to fight on for its survival and honor. Japan will send Prince Konoye to Moscow as a special envoy, bearing the Emperor's own letter. Sato must win Soviet leave for the trip and ask for a plane to fetch the envoy's party.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d682:
A top secret briefing paper on United States policy toward Turkey was dated June 29, 1945. It is document 682 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It was written as Soviet pressure on Turkey over the Straits was mounting fast.

The paper says U.S. ties with Turkey have been friendly and profitable since Admiral Bristol's time. Washington has no special aims in Turkey beyond the normal gains of peaceful dealings. Its stance is summed up as live and let live, within set principles. Those principles include the right of peoples to choose their own political and social systems without outside meddling. They also include equal chances in trade and transit, and free access for the press. Freedom for U.S. charitable and school work in Turkey is named as well.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d82:
General Deane reported Moscow's reasoning to Eisenhower on June 20, 1945, in an urgent telegram that is document 82 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. Harriman had pressed Vyshinsky the night before on letting General Parks's survey party into Berlin at once. Vyshinsky answered that the trip would be pointless before Zhukov returned.

No Soviet officers left in Berlin could act with authority, Vyshinsky said, but once Zhukov was back, intensive preparations would start, and there was no need for worry. The British had the same answer, Deane notes, and Montgomery was writing to Zhukov himself. Deane also floats a plan for Harriman and Vyshinsky to visit Berlin together, and offers to carry a message from Eisenhower to Zhukov through Antonov.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1082:
The Acting Secretary of State cabled the American chargé in Belgrade on July 28, 1945. He is to answer Yugoslavia's notes of July 18 and 19, which charged Greece with abuses in Greek Macedonia. Washington welcomes Belgrade's hint that the matter should be settled in a friendly way, under the principles of international law.

America offers to recommend a commission of military and political officers, drawn from the Allied missions in Belgrade and Athens. It would test the charges against the Atlantic Charter and the United Nations Charter, then propose terms for both governments to accept. London and Moscow are being asked to join. Meanwhile, neither Yugoslavia nor Greece should act alone to worsen the dispute.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1182:
Winston Churchill wrote to President Truman on 24 July 1945. He was in the last days of his time as prime minister. The British vote had been cast weeks before; the count, due on 26 July, would sweep him from office and from the summit.

A letter written under that shadow carries a double weight. It is state business, and it is also the war leader's near-farewell to his American partner. The two men had steered the Western alliance through the war's hardest years. This message belongs to the close of that partnership. Within days, another Briton sat in Churchill's chair at Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1282:
President Truman wrote to Generalissimo Stalin on 31 July 1945, two days before the conference closed. It was the pair's second exchange in the volume. By then the final terms were nearly fixed, and the leaders' own channel carried the last weight.

A late note between the two men could confirm a bargain, smooth a last dispute, or set the tone for parting. Truman and Stalin would not meet again. This message belongs to their final dealings. It closes the leader thread of the volume, as each man turned toward the new world the summit had made.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1382:
The proclamation printed as document 1382 is the Potsdam Declaration, issued on 26 July 1945 by the United States, Britain, and China. It called on Japan to surrender at once or face utter destruction. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

The declaration listed the terms Japan could expect: loss of its conquests, occupation of its islands, and a new order built on freedom and peace. It warned that the alternative was prompt and total ruin, words written weeks before the atomic bombs fell. Few papers in the volume match its fame. Readers meet here the last public offer made to Japan before the war's end took its final, terrible turn.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-82: Printed without a number after document 710, this short piece is a note by the volume's editors. It stands in the second Potsdam volume of the Foreign Relations series. Editorial notes in the series add context the raw papers lack. They point readers to linked files, name sources, and flag gaps in the record. Readers meet the note as a guide placed beside the formal papers of July 1945.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d782:
Headquarters of United States Forces in Austria wrote to the Joint Chiefs of Staff on July 27, 1945. Document 782 is a military channel paper in the Potsdam record. American forces in Austria reported up the chain to Washington's chiefs. The message entered the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

Army headquarters wrote in a terse, factual style. Their reports covered troops, zones, and the friction of occupation. Readers see the soldier's Austria, distinct from the diplomats' version. The document ties the conference to the men holding ground it argued over. It shows how summit choices rested on reports like this one for their facts.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d882:
American drafters compiled this working paper as the text of the proposed agreement on Germany sent to the foreign secretaries. It holds the economic principles for the first control period. The copy is undated, and the volume files it with the papers of July 27, 1945.

The clauses shown cover restitution, German assets abroad, and foreign-owned property in Germany. Looted goods, from heavy machines to works of art, would be returned when they could be identified. The Control Council would take charge of German external assets. Property owned by citizens of Allied or neutral nations gets its own rules, with payment promised where goods are removed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d982:
The Acting Secretary of State cabled George Kennan, the American chargé in Moscow, on July 17, 1945. Britain has agreed to a joint proposal on German assets abroad, and the Spanish situation is urgent. Kennan must tell the Soviets that Washington assumes their consent. Reports from Ankara and Stockholm say Soviet officials already warned Turks and Swedes in like terms.

The cable stresses two ideas for all talks on the subject. Action must be coordinated among the occupying powers. A trusteeship principle must hold, so no single power can dispose of German external assets for its own gain. Two live cases are named: German legation property in Stockholm, and German shares in Rumanian oil companies.
frus-1950v07-d82: A 1950 intelligence estimate on Korea from the FRUS volume. Analysts assessed the peninsula's war. This entry holds that estimate. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
gao-gaoreports-b-295882: Firetech Automatic Sprinkler took its May 2005 contract fight to GAO, and the ruling lands the verdict. The sprinkler maker said the award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Even sprinkler contracts get the full fair hearing. Even sprinkler contracts get the full fair hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297282: M&M Ret. Enterprises took its December 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298082: Paramount Group took its June 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298282: Intercon Associates doubled its August 2006 protest — two case numbers, one tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-298682: Global Solutions Network took its November 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Global names get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-299382: C. Martin Company took its April 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the call. The firm challenged the award; the ruling tests the claims against bid law. Family-named firms get the same formal hearing as the corporate giants.
gao-gaoreports-b-307382: Homeland Security's management money got a fiscal ruling in this 2006 GAO call, which tests using directorate funds for component costs. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the dollars could legally move. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-309982: A Government Accountability Office bid-protest decision dated October 25, 2007, filed by the Pacific Lock Company. The lock manufacturer challenged a federal contract award, and the ruling applies procurement law to its claims. Published decisions like this one preserve the reasoning GAO uses to judge competitions — guidance for every company bidding on government padlocks, hardware, and beyond.
gao-gaoreports-b-310582: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by IMLCORP LLC; Wattre Corporation. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-182: Pentagon weapons program reporting needed polish in 2005, and GAO's report says the information for Congress could be more complete, timely, and accurate. The review demands the better briefings. The lawmakers deserved the straight data. The reporting had to improve. The lawmakers deserved the straight data.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-482: The IRS's data locks were failing in 2005, and GAO's report says the agency had to remedy serious weaknesses over taxpayer and bank secrecy data. The review sounds the alarm. The filers' secrets deserved the guard. The weaknesses had to be remedied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-782: IRS taxpayer assistance training needed better planning in 2005, and GAO's report says strategic planning and evaluation were required. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the helpers deserved good training. The planning had to be better. The helpers deserved good training.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-882: War on terrorism cost data needed reliability in 2005, and GAO's report says the Pentagon had to improve the figures and guidance. The findings demand the accuracy. The report warns that the war dollars deserved honest counting. The reliability had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1082: Tax-exempt bond rules got a GAO explainer in 2006, and the report details selected capital facilities and the governmental function test. The findings parse the policy. The report shows the tax break's boundaries needed mapping. The test had to be clear.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-282: Infant formula marketing could discourage breastfeeding in 2006, and GAO's report says some marketing strategies might deter nursing, urging better state contracts. The findings sound the concern. The report warns that the babies' best food deserved defending. The contracts had to be better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-682: The Congressional Award Foundation's books got audited for 2005 and 2004, and GAO's 2006 report delivers the financial opinion. The findings grade the statements. The report shows the youth charity's money got counted. The audit kept the books honest. The youth charity's books stayed open.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-82: Workforce investment data was improving but incomplete in 2005, and GAO's report says Labor and states acted, though more steps were needed. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the job-training numbers deserved trust. The steps had to be taken.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-982: The transport worker ID card needed work before launch in 2006, and GAO's report says Homeland Security should address key challenges first. The findings demand the fixes. The report warns that the credential for millions should not launch half-baked. The card had to be ready.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-282: Locking down the world's loose radioactive material needed focus in 2007, and GAO's report says the Energy Department's threat-reduction program should aim its future efforts better. The findings set the priorities. The report argues for guarding the worst stuff first. The glow could not wait.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-82: The YouthBuild program needed proof in 2007, and GAO's report says analyzing outcome data was the only way to judge its long-term benefits. The findings demand the evidence. The report asks whether the second chances were really changing lives. The program had to prove its worth.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-182: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at bilingual Voting Assistance: Selected Jurisdictions' Strategies for Identifying Needs and Providing Assistance. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-282: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on immigration Benefits: Internal Controls for Adjudicating Humanitarian Parole Cases Are Generally Effective, but Some Can Be Strengthened. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-482: GAO published its findings on aboveground Oil Storage Tanks: More Complete Facility Data Could Improve Implementation of EPA's Spill Prevention Program in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-582: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on centers for Disease Control and Prevention: Human Capital Planning Has Improved, but Strategic View of Contractor Workforce Is Needed. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gautier-cleopatras-nights-hearn-1882:
Théophile Gautier wrote tales of ghosts, vampires, and living mummies for French readers in the mid-1800s. Lafcadio Hearn translated six of them into lush English in 1882. The lead tale, One of Cleopatra's Nights, imagines a poor Egyptian youth granted one night with the queen, at the price of his life.

Other tales give Clarimonde, a courtesan who returns from the dead, and Arria Marcella, a spirit met among the ruins of Pompeii. The Mummy's Foot turns a comic purchase into a dream of ancient Egypt. Gautier mixes beauty with dread in rich, exact prose. These stories helped found the French literature of the fantastic.
genji-suematsu-1882:
Kencho Suematsu carried The Tale of Genji into English in 1882, the first rendering of Murasaki Shikibu's masterpiece. His version gives chapters one to seventeen, abridged, of the long tale of Prince Genji and the Heian court. Suematsu, a Japanese scholar-diplomat, presented his country's classic to a West that knew nothing of it.

Genji's loves, exiles, and refinements unfold in a world of poetry contests and scented letters. Many call the Genji the world's first novel, and its portrait of court life has no early rival. Suematsu's landmark effort opened that world, however partially, to English readers.
gita-telang-sbe8-1882: The Bhagavadgita with the Sanatsugatiya and the Anugita, translated by Kashinath Telang in Sacred Books of the East volume 8. Krishna's dialogue with Arjuna on duty and devotion. This edition preserves those Hindu scriptures. It waits for future eyes.
guldenes-kleinod-oder-schatzkastlein-178: Güldenes Kleinod, oder Schatzkästlein, 1782. The golden jewel. This book preserves that work. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol6-1882:
In 1882 the sixth volume of Hering's Guiding Symptoms joined the growing row on prescribers' shelves. The work stands as the great American materia medica of its school. Its plan does not change here: remedies in order, symptoms grouped by the part of the body they touch.

Editors working from Hering's own papers shaped the entries with care. They kept his signs for confirmed and characteristic symptoms, the marks a busy reader scans for first. A lifetime of provings stands behind the terse lines, each one earned in tests on healthy volunteers. Doctors treated the whole set as a final court when brief handbooks gave too little.
hierocles-golden-verses-pythagoras-1682:
An anonymous English translation of Hierocles on the Golden Verses appeared in 1682. Hierocles of Alexandria, a Neoplatonic teacher, commented on the Pythagorean Golden Verses. Those verses are brief maxims on how to live a pure life.

Hierocles turns each verse into a lesson on cleansing the soul. Prayer, self-examination, and rising toward the divine structure his commentary. He treats moral discipline as the first step toward mystical union. Early modern seekers treasured the book as both ethics manual and spiritual guide. The 1682 translation carried Greek Neoplatonism into Restoration England. Its counsel stays practical even where its theology feels remote.
hobbes-behemoth-1682:
Behemoth: or, The Long Parliament is Thomas Hobbes's history of the English Civil War, written in dialogue and published in 1682. Four parts carry an old man's account of how England fell into rebellion between 1640 and 1660. Hobbes, who had fled to Paris when the war began, watched his country's ruin from exile and thought hard about its causes.

The dialogue blames seditious preaching, ambitious parliament men, and universities that taught men to love dispute. Against the chaos stands Hobbes's remedy: one sovereign power, feared and obeyed. Behemoth is Leviathan turned historian, applying its doctrine to fresh wounds. Hobbes's king had kept the work back; its 1682 printing let England judge the old man's verdict.
huntingtower-pg3782: John Buchan's Huntingtower is a rollicking Scots adventure. A retired Glasgow grocer and the Gorbals Die-Hards foil a desperate Russian plot. The 1922 thriller never pauses for breath or rest. Buchan at his most delightful and high-spirited.
i-ching-legge-1882:
James Legge translated the Yi King, the I Ching or Classic of Changes, into English in 1882. His complete version appeared as volume sixteen of the Sacred Books of the East. The Chinese classic builds its counsel from sixty-four hexagrams, figures of six broken and unbroken lines used in divination.

Legge gives each hexagram with its ancient judgments, the Tuan and Hsiang comments, and the appendices called the Ten Wings. King Wen and the Duke of Chou stand behind the oldest layers, by tradition. The book served China as oracle, philosophy, and mirror of change for two thousand years. Legge's laborious version long anchored English study of it. His notes map the text with Victorian thoroughness.
jane-kent-old-bailey-1682:
London's Old Bailey heard the case of Jane Kent in June 1682, and a sessions paper tells it in full. A Full and True Account of the Proceedings at the Old Bailey prints the court's work for that term. Kent's witchcraft charge sat among the usual run of thefts and killings.

The report gives her charge, the proof laid against her, and the court's verdict in plain order. That a London court still tried witches so late surprises many readers. Yet the record shows the charge alive in the capital decades past the panic's height. The paper is a plain, rare look at a city trial.
jevons-state-relation-labour-1882:
The State in Relation to Labour appeared in 1882, the last year of Jevons's life. It lays out his liberal program for the labor question, the burning issue of Victorian politics. Jevons steered between two camps he distrusted: those who would leave workers wholly unprotected, and those who would hand industry to the state.

He supports factory laws and limits on child labor where the case is proved, and defends unions' right to exist. At the same time he warns that each new state power must clear a high bar of evidence before it is granted. The tests he proposes, case by case and fact by fact, are the book's real subject. Plainly spoken and carefully argued, the little volume reads as Victorian liberalism's economic testament on the question of labor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-luliani-ben-tab:
Luliani ben Tabrin, a Palestinian scholar of the early fourth century, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His name is the same as Julianus ben Tiberianus, though it appears in corrupted forms in some texts. He is known chiefly as a transmitter of teachings from his master, Isaac Nappaha. He appears often in the Midrash and in pre-Talmudic literature.

The article gives one saying of his own. When small people heed the great, he taught, the great must lighten their burden or answer to God. It also notes a legal question he put to his teacher Isaac. His son Hiyya is mentioned often in the Jerusalem Talmud and was said to have brought rain in a drought. The brief entry preserves what little survives of a scholar who mostly passed on the words of others.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magyar-zsido-sz:
Magyar Zsido Szemle, a Hungarian Jewish review, is described in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. It was founded in 1884 by Josef Simon with professors Wilhelm Bacher and Josef Banoczi of the Budapest rabbinical seminary. Its aim was twofold. It would advance the scientific study of Judaism and report on the social and legal condition of the Jews.

The article tracks the journal's changes of hand and form. Banoczi and Bacher edited it until 1890, when L. Blau and F. Mezey took over. After a Hungarian Jewish literary society was founded, the monthly became a quarterly under Blau alone. The entry claims it as the first Jewish scientific periodical in Hungarian. It drew contributors from America as well as Europe, especially among the younger generation. For readers, the piece fixes the birth of Hungarian-language Jewish scholarship in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manuel-eugene-1:
Eugene Manuel, a French educator and poet, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Paris on July 13, 1823, he was the grandson of the Paris cantor Lovy. He stayed attached to his ancestors' faith through a brilliant career. He died at Paris on June 1, 1901.

The article follows his rise in French education. At the Ecole Normale his classmates included Pasteur and other future luminaries. He taught rhetoric at several colleges, then served the minister of public instruction after the Franco-Prussian war. In 1876 he became inspector-general of secondary instruction. His poems made his literary name, above all the patriotic Poemes Populaires of 1871. Two of his dramatic poems played at the Theatre Francais with Sarah Bernhardt. He also taught Greek and Latin literature at Paris's Jewish seminary for twenty years. He was one of the six founders of the Alliance Israelite Universelle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mattathias-macc:
Mattathias, the priest whose defiance began the Maccabean rebellion, is introduced in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss. Instead of rushing to the revolt, the article opens as source criticism. The First Book of Maccabees, called the most authentic source, makes him son of John and grandson of Simeon, a priest of the line of Joiarib from Jerusalem who settled at Modin.

Josephus adds one more name, Asamoneus, and the article argues he should be read as a distant ancestor of the whole Hasmonean house, not as Mattathias's great-grandfather. Rabbinic sources tangle matters further, sometimes making Hasmonai his father and sometimes a separate hero of the same age. The entry then compares how the sources name his sons, never all together in the rabbinic telling, but listed in full by Maccabees and Josephus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ben-samuel:
Meir ben Samuel, known by his initials as RaM, stands near the head of the French tosafists in his Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906, by Richard Gottheil and Max Schloessinger. Born about 1060 at Ramerupt, he studied in Lorraine and married Jochebed, Rashi's second daughter. Their three sons, Samuel ben Meir, Isaac ben Meir, and Jacob, the famous Rabbenu Tam, all became leading scholars, making Meir the root of a dynasty of commentary. He lived to a great age and was still alive after 1135.

The entry credits him with helping to found the tosafist school of northern France, whose glosses quote his ritual decisions. He also changed the wording of the Kol Nidre formula. A gentler note survives beside the learning: when his son Isaac died young, grief left the old man unable, for a time, to answer a legal question from a friend.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mengs-ismael-is:
Ismael Israel Mengs was a Danish portrait-painter in miniature and enamel. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer notice him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Copenhagen in 1690, he learned his art at Lübeck and spent a lifetime traveling through Germany, Italy, and Austria. He earned, the entry says plainly, a scant livelihood. Fortune arrived only in 1764, a year before his death. He was made professor at the Dresden Academy of Art. He was made court painter to King Augustus III too, with an annuity.

He died at Dresden on December 26, 1765. The brief notice rests on two Danish biographical dictionaries. It contrasts with the long entry for his son Anton Rafael. This traveling miniaturist drilled his son toward a European fame he never reached himself. Here the father's obscurity and the son's celebrity stand side by side. They stand together in the alphabet.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michael-isaac-1:
Isaac Michael, a German laryngologist born at Hamburg on November 16, 1848, is the subject of a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman, published in 1906. He studied medicine at Heidelberg, Leipsic, Berlin, and Würzburg, taking his degree in 1873. Vienna gave him his specialty, in its throat and ear dispensaries.

In 1876 Michael returned to Hamburg and practiced there until his death in 1897. His books match his clinic: a study of singing and the formation of the vocal registers in 1887, and a translation of Mackenzie's Hygiene of the Vocal Organs two years later. He also wrote a history of the Hamburg medical association, published in 1896.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-missouri-10882:
Missouri's Jewish history is mostly St. Louis's. Cyrus Adler and Isaac Schwab present it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews were in the territory before statehood in 1821. The Bloch family was earliest of all. Settlement in the city began shortly after 1830. By the article's time it supported six permanent congregations and several temporary ones.

The four Reform congregations counted about eight hundred families between them. They were Shaare Emeth, Temple Israel, B'nai El, and United Hebrew. The Orthodox bodies worshipped on the north side. Tifereth Israel alone ran a Talmud Torah for two hundred children. The United Hebrew was founded in 1838 and first met in a private house. It built synagogues in 1858 and again in 1881.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morbidity-10982:
Morbidity — the tendency to disease, as distinct from the death rate — is measured for the Jews in a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Joseph Jacobs and Maurice Fishberg, published in 1906. The writers concede the sickness ratio had not yet been satisfactorily studied, though Jewish mortality had been investigated in several countries. Their argument starts from the conditions of Jewish life that shape health either way.

On one side stand the dietary laws and sanitary regulations of the religion itself; on the other, ghetto crowding in eastern Europe, town dwelling, mercantile work, sobriety, and devotion to family. The article works through Glatter's Hungarian figures from the county of Pest and the comparative statistics of the day — an early attempt at a Jewish epidemiology.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahman-b-simhah:
Nahman ben Simhah of Bratzlav founded the Bratzlaver Hasidim, and Herman Rosenthal with A. S. Waldstein wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia life. Born at Medzhibozh in 1770, he was a great-grandson of the Baal Shem Tov. In youth he practiced harsh asceticism, even rolling naked in the snow. In 1798 he visited Palestine and was received with honor.

Nahman taught that the zaddik stands between man and God, almost a father confessor. He stressed fasting and self-castigation for repentance, and held the evil inclination necessary to man's perfection. Other zaddikim, charging him with secret Frankism, persecuted his followers into exile at Uman. His disciple Nathan published his teachings and tales after his death in 1811.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nations-and-lan:
The seventy nations idea comes from the table in Genesis. Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broydé wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Genesis chapter ten lists seventy grandsons of Noah. Each one became, in tradition, the founder of a nation. The count shaped old views of mankind's spread.

Some counts differ, since the Septuagint lists seventy-two grandsons. The Book of Jubilees splits the earth among three sons. Shem, Ham, and Japheth each took a share. Rabbis matched Bible names to lands they knew. Gomer, for one, was tied to Carthagena or Gothia. Each nation had its angel, but Israel had God Himself. Seventy Tabernacles offerings, one per nation, close the picture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neustatter-loui:
Louis Neustätter was a German painter of portraits and scenes. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Munich on Sept. 5, 1829. He died at Tutzing on May 24, 1899. He trained first under engraver Peter Latz.

He entered the Munich Academy in 1847. Paris work with Cogniet followed in 1852. Rome and Naples shaped his eye after that. Vienna held him a decade painting many portraits. Genre work began in 1860 with The Orphans. The Widow, too, was copied for eager buyers. At Tutzing he helped make a plain town a resort. The town voted him its freedom for that work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nomism-11582:
Nomism is rule of life by law alone. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee, Jacob Zallel Lauterbach, and Kaufmann Kohler for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In a bad sense it means bare formalism. Keeping the letter then passes for the highest ideal. Judaism, the entry insists, never owned that sense.

Jews fought mere formalism whenever it showed itself. In its sound sense, nomism is Judaism's own trait. Life in all its ties is molded by the Law. The Psalms picture the pious meditating on it always. Yet delight and a willing heart belong to it. The hope was a covenant written on hearts. Later ages called the Sabbath a gift of God. The commandments, they taught, purify and sanctify mankind. Their reasons were sought, not blindly obeyed without thought.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orshanski-isaac:
Isaac Orshanski was a Russian doctor from Yekaterinoslav. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born there about the year 1851. His early lessons were in the Bible and Talmud. His parents were poor folk with small means.

As a boy, Isaac had to help his father make butter. His elder brother Ilya led him to books in time. At fifteen and at sixteen he tried for the town school. Both tries failed to gain him a place there. He moved to Odessa and read in figures and sums. In 1869 he signed up for the course in cures there. A love of the mind's lore drew more and more of his time. He took his degree in the year 1875.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pan-taube-11882: Taube Pan was a Jewish German author of Prague. Isidore Singer and Alexander Kisch wrote her short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She lived in the Prague ghetto in the sixteen hundreds. Her father was Rabbi Moses Löb Pizker of that town. Her husband was Rabbi Jacob Pan, a man of Prague. She wrote works of faith and right conduct for Jews. In 1609 she put out a poem of six pages, it seems.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pedro-iii-11982:
Pedro the Third ruled Aragon from 1276 to 1285. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He shielded Jews from attacks by the clergy. The article is clear that money, not mercy, drove him.

Pedro leaned on Jewish taxes to fund his wars. His wars touched Africa, Sicily, and France. In 1283 he made Jews pay half the cost of new towers. A year later he demanded a huge tax at short notice. He even taxed Jews to fill his daughter's dowry. When he needed no money, his favor cooled fast.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pfersee-12082:
Pfersee is a small place near Augsburg in Bavaria. Gotthard Deutsch and Moses Löb Bamberger wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived there from an early date. Augsburg had expelled its own Jews in 1440. Its scholars won a wide name.

An archduke shielded the Pfersee Jews in 1559. The village became the chief Swabian Jewish center. Its district rabbi served the towns around it. Famous scholars taught there across the centuries. In the 1800s families drifted back to Augsburg. By 1904 no Jews remained in Pfersee. A fine Talmud manuscript from Pfersee survives at Munich.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pirbright-henry:
Henry de Worms, Lord Pirbright, was an English statesman. Joseph Jacobs and Victor Rousseau Emanuel wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in London in 1840. He died at Guildford in 1903, a peer. His father was an Austrian baron of Jewish birth.

Pirbright trained as a barrister, then entered Parliament in 1880. He served at the Board of Trade and the colonies. In 1888 he chaired the sugar bounties conference. His treaty there abolished the sugar bounties. He led the Anglo-Jewish Association for years. He spoke up for Jews oppressed in Rumania.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-b-mari-1:
Rabbah bar Mari was a Babylonian teacher of the fourth set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived for a time in Palestine in his youth. Then he went back to his home in Babylonia. There he passed on sayings of the Palestinian masters. Johanan and Joshua ben Levi are named most.

Rabbah gave talks on the tales of the Bible as well. Some of his words were known even in Palestine. Yet his name stands in no Palestinian book of note. It is not in their Talmud or their midrash. The entry traces how his words crossed the lands. It lists the tractates where his name still stands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raschpitz-rasch: Hayyim Raschpitz was a scholar of the seventeenth century. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He was martyred, probably at Prague. He wrote the prayer Iyyun Tefillah. It deals with the persecutions and martyrdoms of Prague. The prayer went through many editions. Later ones appeared at Amsterdam, Dessau, and Frankfort. One edition added a German translation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rephidim-12682:
Rephidim was a camp site on the edge of the desert of Sin. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Israel camped there after crossing that desert. The people suffered from a lack of water.

The article retells the Exodus account of the place. The people complained, and Moses struck water from the rock. Moses named the spot Massah and Meribah. A parallel account in Numbers places the event at Kadesh. At Rephidim Amalek attacked Israel from behind. Modern scholars place the site in Wadi Firan. Robinson instead put it in a narrow gorge nearby. The entry weighs Bible story against desert geography.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rizpah-12782:
Rizpah was a daughter of Aiah and a concubine of Saul. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. After Saul died she stayed with his son Ish-bosheth. General Abner then took possession of her.

The article explains that act signaled a claim to the throne. It caused Abner's breach with Ish-bosheth as well. Later David gave her two sons to the Gibeonites. They were killed and left unburied as revenge for Saul. Rizpah spread sackcloth on a rock beside the bodies. She kept watch, driving birds and beasts away. David was moved by her maternal love. He had the remains buried in the family tomb. The entry turns a small figure into a study of devotion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenzweig-gers:
Gerson Rosenzweig was a Russian-American editor, author, and poet born at Byelostok in April 1861. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He ran a Hebrew school at Suwalki before emigrating in 1888.

Settled in New York, Rosenzweig helped edit three Jewish papers for years. He also ran his own weekly, Ha-Ibri, and a monthly called Kadimah. His Masseket Amerika, from 1891, is a satire written in Talmud style. The entry calls it a masterpiece of satire and humor, still popular then. He wrote poems and 1,005 short Hebrew epigrams as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sackheim-abraha:
Abraham ben Joseph Sackheim was a Lithuanian scholar and Talmudist who died at Wilna in 1872. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His learning in rabbinics shows in his one book.

That book, Yad ha-Hazakah, comments closely on the Passover Haggadah. Printed at Wilna in 1835, it bears the editor's name, not Sackheim's own. He also knew several European languages well enough to interpret for guests. When Montefiore was entertained at Wilna in 1846, Abraham interpreted the English. His letters appeared later in other men's published works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schlettstadt-13:
Isidore Singer and Marc Levi wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Schlettstadt. The Alsatian town lies some twenty-seven miles south of Strasburg. In 1349 its Jews suffered in the general persecution across Germany. They were expelled, then returned, then persecuted again. In 1387 Emperor Charles placed the town under a ban for two years.

From the mid-fourteenth century to the early nineteenth, no Jew could spend the night in town. Business visitors had to leave before dark. A bell rang out the hour of departure. The bell and its tower still stand. The old synagogue also survives, long used as an arsenal. The burial ground dates to the thirteenth century. Many of its stones were stolen for building. In 1806 Solomon Moise first won leave to settle. About 230 Jews live there in 1905.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seelig-abi-ezri:
M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Seelig ben Isaac Margolioth, called Abi 'Ezri. He was a Polish Talmudist of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Seelig was born at Polock. He died probably in Palestine. He preached at Prague and at Kalisz. After Israel Darshan died, he moved to Yaroslav.

From 1701 to 1711 Seelig lived on support from Bärmann Levi's study house at Halberstadt. His patron finally sent him to Palestine. His Kesef Nibḥar, printed at Amsterdam in 1712, comments on the Pentateuch in sermon form. His Ḥibbure Liḳḳuṭim followed at Amsterdam in 1715. That book gathers Talmudic readings and responsa. Auerbach's history of the Halberstadt community records his years there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shadchan-heb-sh:
Shadchan is the Hebrew word for a marriage broker, one who brings two families together. Cyrus Adler and Peter Wiernik wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the role. Talmudic texts use a related verb for parents arranging children's marriages. The broker's title itself appears only in the thirteenth century.

By then the trade was old and well established. Legal writers debated the broker's status and his right to pay. Austrian Jews paid him only after a wedding took place. Jews in the Rhineland paid once the parties agreed. The entry traces how matchmaking grew from family talks into a paid, lawful profession with its own customs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shinar-13582:
Shinar is the Old Testament name for Babylonia, used eight times in all. Emil G. Hirsch and George A. Barton wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the name. Genesis places Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh in Shinar. Those cities formed the start of Nimrod's kingdom there.

Shinar is also the site of the tower of Babel. Amraphel, now matched with Hammurabi, came from Shinar. Daniel sets Nebuchadnezzar's home in the land of Shinar. The other mentions add no fresh facts, the entry notes. Critics agree Shinar covered both north and south Babylonia. That breadth makes the name's origin hard to fix. One view links it to Sumir, an old name for the south.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-abba-1:
Simeon ben Abba was a Palestinian amora of the third generation of teachers. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He learned from Hanina ben Hama, who esteemed him highly. Johanan also taught him and wished to ordain him.

His family came originally from Babylonia to Palestine. Simeon lived in such deep poverty in the land. Johanan applied Ecclesiastes to him: bread is not to the wise. On Hanina's advice he married Mar Samuel's daughters in turn. Both brides died soon after their weddings, the entry relates. When Simeon planned travel abroad, Hanina talked him out of it. A letter of praise would shame his father's house, Hanina warned. The entry mixes learning, poverty, and loss.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sinzheim-joseph:
Joseph David Sinzheim was the first rabbi of Strasburg, born in 1745. Isidore Singer and Eduard Neumann wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was the son of Isaac Sinzheim of Treves. Napoleon called an Assembly of Notables in 1806. Sinzheim was its most learned and prominent member by far.

The task of answering Napoleon's questions fell to Sinzheim. He did the work to the emperor's own satisfaction. In 1807 he chaired the Great Sanhedrin as its nasi. He later led the Central Consistory of French Jews. He was seen as the top French Talmudist of his time. His Yad Dawid appeared in print only in part.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-mos: Solomon ben Moses ben Joseph was an Italian liturgist of the thirteenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Some identify him with Jehiel ben Jekuthiel Anaw. Others identify him with Solomon ben Jedidiah instead. He likely descended from Zedekiah ben Benjamin Anaw. An exhortation by him, called Widdui or Tokahah, survives in a Roman manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stade-bernhard-:
Bernhard Stade was a German Protestant Hebraist and historian of Israel. Crawford Howell Toy and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Arnstadt on May 11, 1848. He became a lecturer at the University of Leipsic in 1873. In 1875 he became professor of theology at Giessen.

His early work dealt with Isaiah's oracles on Ethiopia. He wrote a textbook of Hebrew grammar in 1879. His History of the People of Israel followed Graf and Wellhausen. It offered a critical rebuilding of Israel's past in two volumes. With Siegfried he issued a Hebrew dictionary in 1893. Since 1881 he has edited a journal of Old Testament study.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stricker-salomo:
Salomon Stricker was an Austrian pathologist born in Hungary in 1834. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Waag-Neustadt that year. He studied law first at Vienna, then medicine. He died at Vienna on April 2, 1898.

Stricker took his medical degree in 1858 at Vienna. He joined the communal hospital staff a year later. In 1868 he gained a new institute for experimental pathology. He directed it while teaching at the university. In 1872 he became professor of general and experimental pathology. He held that chair until his death. His 1869 studies attacked Cohnheim's theory of pus formation. About 140 journal papers carry his findings. The entry honors a tireless laboratory teacher.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tedesco-ignaz-a:
Ignaz Amadeus Tedesco was an Austrian pianist born at Prague in 1817. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied under Triebensee and Tomaschek at Prague. He died at Odessa on November 13, 1882. Tours and teaching filled his working life.

Tedesco toured widely and won special success in southern Russia. He settled at Odessa as his home base. Hamburg and London hosted him for shorter stays. His fine technique earned a striking nickname from critics. They called him the Hannibal of octaves. The Grand Duke of Oldenburg named him his pianist. His salon music includes a piano concerto. Caprices, mazurkas, nocturnes, and waltzes fill his catalogue. The entry sketches a touring virtuoso of the salons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-thunder-14382:
Thunder in the Bible is far more than weather, this article shows. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. Hebrew often calls thunder simply the voice of God. It marks God's presence and serves as His weapon. Prayer even includes a blessing for hearing it.

Thunder rolled at the Red Sea crossing. It came with hail in Egypt's seventh plague. Sinai shook with thunder when the Law was given. A storm won Samuel's battle against the Philistines. Another storm awed Israel when they demanded a king. Psalm 29 gives the most poetic storm picture. Job uses thunder as a figure for God's power. Battle noise, too, is likened to thunder.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-unger-joseph-14:
Joseph Unger was an Austrian jurist and statesman of the Liberal party. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Vienna in 1828, he studied law there. He became professor of jurisprudence at Vienna in 1857. Ill health cut short his first parliament terms.

The emperor made him a life member of the House of Lords. He soon served as whip of the Liberal Party. In 1871 he joined Prince Auersperg's cabinet as minister. He resigned when the cabinet fell in 1879. Two years later he presided over the Reichsgericht. His System of Austrian private law became a standard work. An anonymous 1861 book urged a dual monarchy. Unger was a convert to Christianity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-verse-division-:
Verse division is the system that splits the Bible text into verses. Crawford Howell Toy and Max L. Margolis wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Chapter division and verse division have different roots. Chapters came first in the Latin Vulgate. Jewish scholars later adopted them for reference.

Verse division is far older in Jewish practice. It rests on the Masoretic tradition of the Hebrew text. A double point marks the end of each verse. Numbered verses in print came much later. Latin Bibles used margin figures from 1528 onward. The Athias Bible of 1659 was the first Jews could use with verse numbers. The entry sorts out this shared history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wars-of-the-lor:
The Book of the Wars of the Lord is a lost ancient work. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Bible names it once, in Numbers chapter twenty one. The verse links it to the geography of Arnon. Its title suggests songs of Israel's victories.

Scholars think parts of Numbers quote the book directly. Verses on the well and on Arnon may be extracts. Some cited events came long after Moses. That fact pushes its date to later centuries. Some place it under David and Solomon. Others set it in the ninth century B.C. The entry weighs these views on a vanished book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weyl-max-14882:
Max Weyl was an American painter of landscapes. Cyrus Adler and Florence N. Levy wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Mühlen, in Württemberg, in 1840. At fifteen he came to the United States. He later returned to Europe to study art. His home is now Washington, D.C.

Weyl belongs to the Society of Washington Artists. He also joins the Washington Water Color Club. His specialty is landscape, felt with nature's moods. In 1891 he won first prize from Washington's artists. He has shown at New York's National Academy. The Corcoran Gallery holds his landscape Approaching Night.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolf-simon-1498:
Simon Wolf (born 1836) was an American lawyer, writer, and friend to the poor. Joseph Jacobs and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Bavaria, he came to the United States in 1848. He worked in trade in Ohio and then read law.

He joined the bar in 1861 and soon moved to Washington. There he served as recorder of the district for nine years. A president made him a city judge, but he left that post in 1881. He then went to Egypt as consul-general for one year. For years he led the board that guards Jewish civil rights. In that role he brought hard cases to the federal chiefs. He was also a top voice in B'nai B'rith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zayin-15182: Zayin is the seventh sign of the Hebrew letter set. Crawford Howell Toy and Isaac Broyde wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The sense of the name is not sure to men now. Its sound is that of the English letter z. It trades place at times with the soft s sound. It stands as a root sign and never as a form sign. In late use it holds the count worth of seven.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zoref-samuel-ha:
Samuel ha-Levi Zoref was a rabbi at Posen who died between 1710 and 1716. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He is known for one book, Mazref la-Kesef, printed at Frankfort-on-the-Oder in 1681. That work gathers extracts from Isaiah Horowitz's Shene Luhot ha-Berit and adds an index to it.

Two appendixes complete the volume. One, Kur la-Zahab, draws extracts from Gabirol's Mibhar ha-Peninim, a book of moral sayings. The other, Teshubot Shib'im Zekenim, gathers maxims of seventy elders. The Kur la-Zahab was later printed on its own at Offenbach in 1710. In 1716 it appeared again together with the maxims.
joan-buts-tryal-examination-1682:
Late in England's witchcraft era, a court set Joan Buts free. An Account of the Tryal and Examination of Joan Buts, printed as a broadside in 1682, tells how. Most trial prints end at the gallows, so an acquittal on the page is rare.

The sheet records the charge against her, the proof brought in, and the way the court weighed it. By 1682 judges and juries were growing harder to sway with tales of spells and spirits. More of the accused were walking free, and this case shows why. The broadside marks the slow turn of the tide against the panic.
kojiki-chamberlain-1882:
Japan's oldest chronicle, the Kojiki, was set down in the year 712. Basil Hall Chamberlain made the first English version in 1882. The work tells how the gods made the islands and ruled the sky and sea. It then traces the line of early emperors.

Myths crowd the first part, with the storm god, the sun goddess, and tricks and fights among the gods. Songs sit inside the prose, some of them very old. Later parts turn to court tales, births, deaths, and wars. The Kojiki stands at the root of Shinto myth and of Japanese letters as a whole.
machiavelli-discourses-thomson-1882:
Ninian Hill Thomson translated Machiavelli's Discourses on Livy in 1882. The full title names the first decade, or ten books, of Titus Livius. Machiavelli builds his lessons on the early history of ancient Rome.

Longer and deeper than The Prince, the Discourses favor republics over princes. Free states stay free, he argues, through citizen armies and open debate. Even public conflict can keep a republic healthy if laws channel it well. Religion, too, must serve the public good rather than private power. Modern republican thought starts in these pages, and the real Machiavelli proves far subtler than his dark legend suggests.
machiavelli-writings-detmold-vol-1-1882:
Christian E Detmold's translation of Niccolò Machiavelli's writings, issued from 1882 to 1891 in four volumes, opens here with volume one. Machiavelli, the Florentine secretary of the early 1500s, changed how the world thinks about power. Detmold gathered his historical, political, and diplomatic writings into one English set, and this volume begins it.

Across the full set stand the Discourses, the Florentine Histories, The Art of War, comedies, letters, and state papers. Machiavelli writes about republics, princes, armies, and fortune with cold clarity. His name became a byword, yet the full range of his work is wider and wiser than the legend. Volume one starts the complete English Machiavelli of the Victorian age.
machiavelli-writings-detmold-vol-2-1882:
Volume two continues Detmold's English Machiavelli, the four-volume set of 1882 to 1891. Niccolò Machiavelli wrote in the thick of Italy's wars and invasions, serving Florence as envoy and militia planner. His Historical, Political, and Diplomatic Writings, as Detmold titled the set, hold nearly everything he left.

The works gathered across these volumes run from the Discourses on Rome to the Florentine Histories and The Art of War. Letters and diplomatic reports show the thinker at work, reading courts and captains. Machiavelli founded modern political thought by describing power as it is, not as preachers wished it. This second volume keeps that full portrait building, in Detmold's sturdy English.
machiavelli-writings-detmold-vol-3-1882:
Detmold's Machiavelli reaches volume three of four, in the English set issued from 1882 to 1891. Niccolò Machiavelli, Florence's sharp-eyed secretary, had been dead three centuries, yet his writings still started arguments in every capital. The set presents his historical, political, and diplomatic works whole, rather than the single famous book, The Prince, alone.

Plays and letters stand in the set beside the Discourses, the histories, and the writings on war. That mix matters: Machiavelli the comic playwright and the fond letter writer round out Machiavelli the analyst of power. Volume three carries the reader deeper into that complete figure. Few political writers reward a full reading more, or punish a partial one less fairly.
machiavelli-writings-detmold-vol-4-1882:
Volume four completes Christian E Detmold's translation of Machiavelli's Historical, Political, and Diplomatic Writings. The set ran from 1882 to 1891. With this volume, English readers gained the whole Machiavelli in four books: Discourses, Florentine Histories, and The Art of War. Comedies, letters, and papers of state stand beside them.

Niccolò Machiavelli watched republics rise and princes fall, and wrote down the rules he saw beneath the chaos. His clear, hard teaching on power made him the founder of modern political thought. The closing volume finishes the fullest English Machiavelli of its century. Readers who end here hold the complete case, from statecraft to stage comedy, in one author's hand.
mccrindle-ancient-india-ctesias-1882:
McCrindle translated the fragments of Ktesias the Knidian's Indika in 1882. Ktesias was a Greek doctor at the Persian court around 400 BCE. His Indika became the foundational Greek account of India's marvels.

Dog-headed men, giant worms, and a fabulous unicorn-like ass populate his India. Ktesias claimed information from Persian officials and traveling merchants. Later Greeks doubted many tales, yet copied them for two thousand years. His wonders stocked the Western imagination of India through the Middle Ages. McCrindle's translation revived the fragments with notes for Victorian readers. Tall tales that made history is a fair summary of the Indika's career.
medical-essays-1842-1882:
Oliver Wendell Holmes gathered his Medical Essays, written from 1842 to 1882. Two prefaces and a third for the new edition open the book. The contents mix sharp critique with warm tales of teachers.

Homoeopathy and Its Kindred Delusions leads the list of essays. The Contagiousness of Puerperal Fever, his famed claim, comes second. Later pieces treat bedside teaching and the state of the trade in Massachusetts. The Young Practitioner and Medical Libraries speak to new doctors in training. Some of My Early Teachers gives the set a warm close. Holmes turns from feuds to the men who formed his own craft.
muallaqat-jones-1782:
William Jones published The Moallakat in 1782, the first English rendering of the Mu'allaqat, the seven suspended odes of pre-Islamic Arabia. The odes, by poets such as Imru al-Qais, Tarafa, and Zuhayr, were said to have hung in the Kaaba at Mecca for their excellence. Jones adds a preliminary discourse on Arabian poetry and full philological notes.

Each ode moves from a halted campsite's ruins to love, boast, desert travel, and tribal war. Camels, storms, and night journeys carry some of the finest early Arabic verse. Jones learned Arabic and Persian in India and reshaped British knowledge of Eastern tongues. This translation began his fame as an Orientalist. The odes still open every history of Arabic poetry.
newbrough-oahspe-new-bible-1882:
John Ballou Newbrough said spirits drove his hands on a new type craft. Oahspe came out in 1882 as a new Bible for a new age. Newbrough was a New York dentist and a man of the spirit creed. The book calls its age the Kosmon era, a time of light.

Vast tales tell of gods, heavens, and the rise and fall of lands now sunk. A Book of Cosmogony lays out the make of the sky and of man. Old lands such as Atlantis take a large share of the tale. The book is the great said text of the spirit line in the States.
nordenskiold-voyage-vega-vol1-1882:
Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld, a Finnish-Swedish geologist and sailor, took the steamer Vega along Siberia's Arctic coast in 1878. Volume One of The Voyage of the Vega, in its 1882 English form, opens the story. The Northeast Passage had beaten sailors for three centuries.

Nordenskiöld sails from Norway past the great Siberian rivers, mapping coasts and collecting fossils and plants. He meets the Chukchi people of the far northeast with respect and care. Late in the season the Vega freezes in, just short of the Bering Strait. The volume ends with a winter of science and patience among the ice.
openalex-w2045578182:
James Mallet, Margarita Beltran, Walter Neukirchen and Mauricio Linares studied cross-breeding between butterfly species. Their paper appeared in BMC Evolutionary Biology in 2007. The butterflies belong to the Heliconius group. Understanding species limits needs data on natural hybrids. The team gathered records from the wild.

Hybrids between species occur regularly in these butterflies. Roughly a quarter of species take part in hybridisation. Yet hybrids are rare among individual butterflies. In most mixed areas they form a tiny share. One contact zone held many more hybrids. Hybrid numbers fell steeply as species grew more distant genetically. The authors found no sign that human disturbance raised hybrid rates. Species borders look like a continuum, they argue.
openalex-w2055620782:
Kenneth Aamodt, Betty Abelev and colleagues in the ALICE Collaboration measured particle flow patterns in lead collisions. Their paper appeared in Physical Review Letters in 2011. Colliding lead nuclei create a hot, dense fluid. Particles fly out in patterns that reveal its properties. Fine pattern shapes had not been measured before.

The team used the ALICE detector at CERN. They measured three higher flow patterns for the first time. One pattern, triangular flow, matched the starting shape of the overlap zone. Random unevenness in that shape explained it well. In the most head-on collisions, two patterns were similar in size. A puzzling double peak in other data followed naturally. The results constrain how the hot fluid forms.
openalex-w2074687782:
Jaime Miranda, Victor Herrera, Julio Chirinos and colleagues measured heart disease risk factors in Latin America. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2013. Little was known about how common such risks were there. That gap hampers prevention planning in the region. The team compared the region with the United States.

They pooled data from studies across Latin American countries. The work came from the LASO consortium on obesity. They measured high blood pressure and diabetes rates. They also measured cholesterol, smoking and excess weight. Patterns differed between countries in the region. Some risks matched or exceeded United States levels. The authors call for prevention plans based on local data.
openalex-w2104860582:
Marco Molina-Montenegro and Daniel Naya tested a climate idea using the common dandelion. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2012. Flexible traits help species survive changing climates. They also help invaders spread widely. One hypothesis links flexibility to latitude. Places farther from the equator vary more in temperature.

The team grew dandelions from five populations. The populations spanned a broad latitude range. Plants were raised at two test temperatures. Six body and fitness traits were measured. Flexibility rose with latitude for every trait. Average trait values also rose with latitude. Warmer test conditions amplified the differences. The results support the variability hypothesis in plants.
openalex-w2113670582:
William Manzanares, Rupinder Dhaliwal, Xuran Jiang and colleagues reviewed antioxidant supplements for critically ill patients. Their paper appeared in Critical Care in 2012. Severe illness creates heavy oxidative stress in the body. That stress feeds swelling and organ failure. Extra vitamins and trace elements might restore balance.

The team searched trial databases and reference lists. They covered studies from 1980 to 2011. Twenty-one randomised trials met their rules for inclusion. Pooled results linked supplements with lower death rates. Patients also needed breathing machines for less time. Infections showed a trend toward fewer cases. No clear harm signal appeared in the trials. The authors back further large trials to confirm the gains.
