openalex-w2137064182:
Annie Pardo, Kevin Gibson, José Cisneros, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Medicine in 2005. They studied idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a lethal lung disease where scar tissue builds up for no known cause. Using gene arrays, they searched for genes that set diseased lungs apart from healthy ones.

One gene stood out: osteopontin, which was active in the air sac lining cells of diseased lungs. Levels were also high in lung wash fluid from patients. Adding osteopontin to human lung cells in the lab made them grow and move more. It also shifted genes that control scar material, favoring buildup over breakdown. The results suggest osteopontin helps drive the scarring.
openalex-w2147141582:
Marie-Anne Durand, Lewis Carpenter, Hayley Dolan, and colleagues published this review in PLoS ONE in 2014. They asked whether tools that support shared decision-making between doctors and patients widen health inequalities. Patient engagement is a policy priority, yet better-off patients might gain more from such tools than disadvantaged groups.

The team searched many databases for trials and observational studies up to mid-2012. Studies had to focus on disadvantaged groups or report their results separately. Nineteen studies qualified, and ten were pooled in a meta-analysis. The pooled results showed a moderate positive effect of shared decision-making support. The review weighs that benefit against the fear that such programs leave vulnerable patients behind.
openalex-w2236343782:
Antonella Delle Fave, Ingrid Brdar, Marié Wissing, and colleagues published this study in Frontiers in Psychology in 2016. They asked ordinary people across many nations a plain question: what is happiness? Researchers often swap happiness for life satisfaction or well-being scores, which blurs the idea and confuses results between cultures.

Earlier work hinted that lay views of happiness differ by culture, but few studies tested this directly. The authors gathered definitions from participants in many countries and compared their themes. As their title states, inner harmony and close relationships came first in people's own words. Feeling at peace with oneself and connected to others outweighed wealth or excitement, a finding that challenges purely personal or pleasure-based accounts.
openalex-w2585326482:
Sandra Frabasile, Andrea Cristine Koishi, and Diogo Kuczera, with colleagues, published this study in Scientific Reports in 2017. It tests naringenin, a compound from citrus fruit, against the dengue virus. Dengue is a major health problem across tropical and subtropical regions, with millions of cases yearly. A vaccine was recently approved in some countries, but no antiviral drug is available.

In human cell cultures, naringenin prevented infection by all four dengue virus types. Tests with partial virus genomes confirmed it blocks virus replication itself. The compound still worked when added a full day after infection began. It also curbed the virus in primary human blood cells taken from donors. The authors present naringenin as a suitable candidate molecule for drug development. Plant compounds like it may offer starting points for future dengue treatments.
openalex-w2806742282:
Tali Lang, Jacinta P. W. Lee, and Kirstin Elgass, with colleagues, reported an inflammasome finding in Nature Communications in 2018. Their subject is MIF, a versatile immune protein stored ready for quick release by many cells. MIF already had known roles against infections and in autoimmune diseases. How it controls the inflammatory molecule IL-1β, though, was not understood.

The paper's title gives the answer: MIF is required for activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome. The inflammasome is the cell machinery that matures and releases IL-1β. Without MIF, that activation fails, the experiments show. This links a fast-release immune messenger to a central inflammation switch. The result helps explain MIF's grip on diseases from sepsis to arthritis. It also marks MIF as a possible drug target for inflammasome-driven illness.
openalex-w2889867882:
Jean-Pierre Gattuso, Alexandre K. Magnan, and Laurent Bopp lead a large team proposing ocean solutions to climate change, in Frontiers in Marine Science in 2018. The metadata title reads only ORIGINAL RESEARCH; the sample supplies the real title and authors. Warming, acidification, and sea-level rise are already stressing marine ecosystems. The paper assesses what ocean-based actions could blunt those effects.

Ecosystems differ in sensitivity to each driver, the authors note. Drivers also interact: their combined effects can add up, multiply, or partly cancel. Research on such multiple-driver impacts still has big gaps, they caution. The paper evaluates candidate solutions against ecosystem responses and services people depend on. It was written as the IPCC's special report on the ocean and cryosphere took shape. For policymakers, it separates plausible ocean interventions from wishful thinking.
openalex-w2899991882:
David A. Wiss, Nicole M. Avena, and Pedro V. Rada traced sugar's grip on the modern diet in Frontiers in Psychiatry in 2018. Obesity has become one of healthcare's largest burdens since the Second World War. It feeds cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and cancer worldwide. Interventions so far have barely slowed the epidemic. The authors ask what changed so fast.

One theory blames sedentary living; another, the surge of highly palatable foods. Supermarkets added thousands of new products yearly by the late 1990s. Sugar sits at the center of their addiction argument. Drawing on evolution, they argue sweet-seeking once served survival. Industrial food supplies now exploit that circuitry without limit. The review assembles evidence for treating sugar addiction as a real clinical phenomenon. Framing it that way, they suggest, could change treatment and policy alike.
openalex-w2964143382:
Rocío Rojo, Anna Raper, Derya Ozdemir, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2019. It deletes a single gene switch, an enhancer of the Csf1r gene, and watches what happens to macrophages. Macrophages are immune cells that patrol tissues, and a receptor called CSF1R controls their growth.

Removing the whole Csf1r gene in mice wipes out most tissue macrophages and stunts growth badly. The enhancer deletion was far more selective, changing receptor levels and macrophage development only in some tissues. That contrast shows how one small control element can govern one gene in specific places. The work helps explain how macrophage populations in different organs are set up and maintained.
openalex-w2979222282:
Elsa Dent, John Morley, Alfonso Cruz-Jentoft, and colleagues published these clinical practice guidelines in The Journal of Nutrition, Health and Aging in 2019. They come from a task force of the International Conference of Frailty and Sarcopenia Research. The topic is physical frailty in older adults, a state of weakness that raises health risks.

The task force reviewed the current evidence base on frailty. From that review, the guidelines give practical advice on how to identify frailty in clinics and how to manage it once found. They are aimed at doctors and care teams who treat older patients. Clear, shared guidance matters because frailty is common, often missed, and closely tied to falls, disability, and hospital stays.
openalex-w3005469082:
Isidro Cortés-Ciriano, Jake Lee, Ruibin Xi, and colleagues published this analysis in Nature Genetics in 2020. It measures chromothripsis across more than two thousand six hundred human cancers with whole-genome sequencing. Chromothripsis is a catastrophic event in which a chromosome shatters and is stitched back in scrambled order.

Studies of single cancer types had hinted that this shattering may be far more common than once thought. Whole-genome data give a much clearer view of such rearrangements than older methods. The team set sharper rules for calling a true case, improving detection accuracy. They then counted cases across the full cancer set. The results show how often this violent form of genome damage occurs in human tumors.
openalex-w3010658582:
Qiangyi Yu, Liangzhi You, Ulrike Wood-Sichra, and colleagues published this data paper in Earth System Science Data in 2020. It introduces SPAM2010, a set of global maps showing where crops were grown and how much they produced around 2010. Farm output is usually reported only by province or district, which hides local patterns.

The maps place production on a fine grid, making spatial studies of farming and the environment possible. This release updates the base year, lengthens the crop list, and covers more subnational regions than earlier versions. It also uses the newest global cropland layer to place crops. The paper is the second of a pair describing the dataset and its methods.
openalex-w3093999282:
B. Abi, R. Acciarri, M. A. Acero, and fellow members of the DUNE team published this paper in The European Physical Journal C in 2020. It forecasts what a giant new neutrino detector, still being built, will be able to learn. The forecast rests on full computer models of both its near and far detectors.

The team counted the main sources of error, from the beam to the detector itself. They find the experiment will settle the order of neutrino masses with high confidence within about two years of running. It also has a strong chance to catch a gap in how neutrinos and their mirror partners act. That gap could help explain why the world is made of matter, not antimatter.
openalex-w3130179782:
Nikita Toropov, Gema Cabello, Mariana Serrano, and colleagues wrote this review in Light: Science and Applications in 2021. It covers biosensing with whispering-gallery mode lasers, tiny ring-shaped lasers that trap light in endless loops. Their small size and clean beams suit them to detecting biology.

These microlasers have caught single virus particles without any label, sensed electric changes at surfaces where molecules bind, and tagged living cells like barcodes for tracking. The review explains how the resonators work and how light-emitting media are built into them. It then surveys the newest devices for probing samples at micro and nano scales. The field aims to move such sensors from lab benches toward clinics.
openalex-w4285207082:
Olaf Erenstein, Moti Jaleta, Khondoker Mottaleb, and colleagues survey world wheat in a 2022 book chapter on production, consumption, and trade. Wheat was domesticated around ten thousand years ago. It now supplies a fifth of the world's food calories and protein. It is the most widely grown crop on Earth, covering more than two hundred million hectares each year.

The chapter reviews a quarter century of data on supply and demand for wheat. Feeding a growing population, and the Global South's rising taste for wheat foods, keeps pressure on yields. The authors argue for heavy research investment to raise productivity within planetary boundaries. Without it, they warn, the crop that anchors food security could fall behind demand.
openalex-w4365795982:
Bryan Wallace, Zachary Posnik, Brendan Hurley, and colleagues update the regional management units used to protect sea turtles, in Endangered Species Research in 2023. Sea turtles roam whole ocean basins, crossing many national waters. Conservation needs units bigger than single nesting beaches yet smaller than the whole species. Regional management units, first drawn in 2010, group turtle populations that share conditions and likely futures.

The update folds in new research and advice from the IUCN Marine Turtle Specialist Group. It defines forty-eight units covering six of the seven sea turtle species. Borders reflect fresh knowledge of turtle movements, habitats, and population structure. Shared units let countries judge threats consistently and plan protection for animals that ignore borders.
openalex-w4416781482:
Ryosuke Kadono simulates how muon spin relaxation behaves when ions jump inside a material. His paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2026. Muon spin relaxation is a key tool for studying ion motion in battery materials. Past experiments showed a puzzling peak in the fluctuation rate.

Kadono models the spectra with an extended relaxation function. It treats the ions' jump motion with its own correlation pattern. Analysing the simulated spectra the usual way reproduces the puzzle. The peak and a related linewidth drop appear on their own. Both trace back to a sharp rise in the ions' jump rate at a certain temperature. The result warns against reading such features as muon behaviour.
openalex-w7160514682: Malaria still kills, and new drugs are needed. This paper reports actinomycin derivatives isolated from a Streptomyces library with stronger selectivity against malaria parasites. The authors scaled up the search from a promising pilot screen. A natural-products study of soil microbes versus a global killer.
openalex-w7164811582: Ising machines make mistakes, and this paper asks how best to fix them. The authors reframe error mitigation as a design problem, comparing two architectures, penalty-spin versus other replica-coupled models, using simulated annealing as a clean testbed. They judge the structures head to head. A systems-level study of making novel computers reliable.
openalex-w7204620182: In Brazil, patients often sue the state to get medicines the public health system does not provide. This article reviews the research on that trend: how court orders protect the right to health, and how they strain public budgets and planning. The authors weigh rights against management reality. A clear-eyed look at what happens when the courtroom becomes the pharmacy.
petit-albert-1782:
Le Petit Albert, the Little Albert, is the most loved of the French grimoire chapbooks. This edition of 1782 carries the text that peddlers sold across France for generations. Its magic is homely: natural and cabalistic secrets, recipes, and charms for the needs of farm and household.

Readers learn to find treasure, win love, protect cattle, and make useful wonders. The book rides in every peddler's pack in the old accounts because buyers kept asking for it. No French grimoire circulated more widely among ordinary people. Its authority borrowed the name of Albert, the medieval scholar-saint of learning. The Petit Albert is the people's magic book, practical, hopeful, and unembarrassed.
plos-pone-0000082:
B. Nelson Chau, Chris W. Pan, and Jean Y. J. Wang dissected the retinoblastoma protein in PLOS ONE in 2006. This protein, called Rb, is a famous tumor suppressor with two broad jobs: it slows cell division and it can promote cell death. The team made targeted changes that split those jobs apart.

Mutant forms that kept one job but lost the other let the authors test each role alone. That split clarifies how Rb normally guards tissues, and which loss matters most when cancer starts. It also has a therapy angle. A drug that restores only the missing function might do, if researchers know which function a given tumor lost.
plos-pone-0000182:
Min Jiu, Xue-Ping Zhou, Lin Tong, and colleagues published this plant virus study in PLOS ONE in 2007. A whitefly that invades new regions is a major crop pest, partly because it spreads plant viruses. The authors report a mutualism between the insect vector and the virus it carries. That partnership speeds up the growth of the invasive whitefly population.

When a pest and its virus help each other, invasions can snowball. The authors document how the virus benefits its carrier, not just the plants it infects. That twist matters for pest control, because fighting the virus and fighting the insect may turn out to be the same fight.
plos-pone-0000282:
Romulus Breban, Raffaele Vardavas, and Sally Blower published this epidemiology methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Its title is a question: theory versus data, how to calculate R0? R0, the basic reproduction number, counts how many new cases one case causes in a fully susceptible population. It is the central number of outbreak science.

Different formulas for R0 can give different answers from the same data. The authors confront theory-based and data-based ways of calculating it. Getting R0 right decides whether an outbreak is predicted to die out or explode, so the paper speaks to every model used in epidemic planning.
plos-pone-0000382:
Marinos Kallikourdis and Alexander G. Betz asked how a mother's immune system prepares for pregnancy, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A fetus inherits half its genes from the father, making it partly foreign to the mother's body. Regulatory T cells, immune cells that calm other immune responses, may help the body accept that foreign tissue.

The authors describe these cells building up in the uterus in cycles. It is as if the tissue were preparing in advance for a fertilized egg to implant. That advance preparation suggests the immune system treats pregnancy as an expected event, not a surprise. Understanding this truce could inform care for infertility and pregnancy loss.
plos-pone-0000482:
Moisés Selman and colleagues described a fast-moving form of a scarring lung disease, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis gradually scars the lungs for no known cause, and most patients decline over years. The team characterized an accelerated variant, describing its clinical behavior and its gene expression pattern.

An accelerated form breaks the usual slow course, overwhelming patients in months. Comparing its gene activity with the typical disease may reveal what drives the scarring engine at full speed. For a disease with few treatments, understanding its worst variant could expose the processes that any therapy must stop.
plos-pone-0000582:
Shonna M. McBride and colleagues surveyed how much one hospital germ varies, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Enterococcus faecalis lives in the gut without harm for most people. In hospitals, though, it can infect wounds and the blood, and it shrugs off many drugs. The team measured the genetic spread among its strains.

Spread data answer a key question. Do hospital cases come from many sources, or from a few strains that have adapted to wards? A few strains would mean a target that control teams can aim at. Surveys like this also track how drug resistance moves through the germ's ranks, an early warning for drug policy.
plos-pone-0000682:
Orna Man, David C. Willhite, Chiquito J. Crasto and colleagues built a framework for comparing smell receptors, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Olfactory receptors form the largest gene family in mammalian genomes. Nearly all of them are orphan receptors, meaning their matching odor molecules are unknown. Judging whether two receptors work alike usually rests on comparing their sequences.

The team based their framework on alignments of the entire coding regions of these genes. A better yardstick for functional differences helps predict which odors a receptor detects. It also orders a huge, mostly uncharted family. For a sense as chemical as smell, such a map is a starting grid for experiments.
plos-pone-0000782:
Sandra Pankow and Casimir Bamberger found a cancer-guard protein at work in a sea anemone, reported in PLOS ONE in 2007. They identify the p53 tumor suppressor-like protein nvp63 in the starlet sea anemone Nematostella vectensis, and describe its molecular function. Until then, p53-like proteins had been found in bilaterians only, animals with left-right symmetry. The anemone is a non-bilaterian, from an older branch.

Their title states that nvp63 mediates selective germ cell death in the anemone. A p53 relative culling germ cells pushes the family's origin deep into animal history. It also suggests quality control of reproductive cells is an ancient job, older than cancer suppression.
plos-pone-0000882:
Jian Liang, Mingui Fu, Ester Ciociola and colleagues examined what the protein ENPP1 does as fat cells mature, in PLOS ONE in 2007. How well fat tissue can grow to store extra energy shapes a person's risk for blood sugar and fat problems. ENPP1, also called PC-1, was already known to play a part in that wider picture.

The team focused on adipocyte maturation, the process by which young cells become full fat storing cells. They asked where ENPP1 helps or hinders along the way. The work connects a single protein to the way the body handles stored energy. That link is one piece of the larger story behind obesity and diabetes risk.
plos-pone-0000982:
James Knight, Bin Qian, David Baker and colleagues worked on modeling the active forms of protein kinases, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Kinases are enzymes that tag other proteins with phosphate, switching them on or off. The human set is huge, and kinases sit at the heart of cell behavior.

To understand signaling networks, researchers need good models of kinases in their active shape. The team use conservation and variability, what stays fixed across kinases and what changes, to guide that modeling. Better kinase models feed directly into drug design, since many cancer drugs target these enzymes. Accuracy here is worth real effort.
plos-pone-0001082:
Daniel Beniac, Shauna deVarennes, Anton Andonov and colleagues imaged how the SARS virus spike changes after binding, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The SARS coronavirus spike is the largest known viral spike. It works like other class one fusion proteins. It must refold to merge the virus with a cell.

Earlier structural work used static fragments in crystals. This team examine the whole spike's conformational reorganization after receptor binding. Watching the change, not just the start and end shapes, explains how fusion is triggered. That trigger is a drug target: stop the refold and the virus stays outside. The work came from the post SARS push to understand this virus.
plos-pone-0001182:
Chromatin, the packaged form of DNA inside the cell nucleus, is usually described as DNA plus proteins. Antonio Rodríguez-Campos and Fernando Azorín argue that RNA belongs in that picture too, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Chromatin structure responds to many influences, from acidity and temperature to chemical marks on its proteins.

The authors present RNA as an integral component of chromatin that contributes to its structural organization. RNA was already known to regulate chromatin activity; treating it as part of the structure itself is a stronger claim. Their work invites a fresh look at how the genome is physically held together.
plos-pone-0001282:
Under the microscope, diseased human tissues sometimes show striking geometric order. Jairo Díaz, Natalia Jaramillo, and Mauricio Murillo document one such pattern in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They describe self-assembly of geometric triangular chiral hexagon crystal-like complexes in diseased human tissues.

The authors report finding this architecture at both large and small scales, mainly in cancerous tissues. They present it as a form of biological collision order in abnormal tissue. The paper is descriptive, presenting an unusual claimed pattern for other pathologists to confirm or refute. The authors offer the pattern as a finding for others to test in their own samples.
plos-pone-0001382:
David Serre and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a hidden trap in gene studies of disease. Most single gene effects on common ills are small. Studies thus need huge groups to spot real links. But if the group mixes roots in uneven ways, false links can appear. This mix effect is called population stratification.

The authors offer a way to fix this bias in large studies with many ethnic groups. Their method aims to keep true signals while cutting false ones. Clean methods matter, since a false gene link can waste years of follow up work. The paper gives study teams a more sound base for their claims.
plos-pone-0001482:
Reeta Rintamäki and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study linking seasonal mood shifts to metabolic syndrome. That syndrome is a cluster of traits that raise heart disease risk. Faults in the body clock had been tied to the syndrome in past work. The team drew on a national health survey of 8,028 adults.

They compared seasonal swings in mood and acts with the traits of the syndrome. Links there would tie the body clock to both mind and metabolism. Such links urge care that treats sleep, light, and mood as part of heart health. The large survey gives the claim a broad base in the general public.
plos-pone-0001582:
Anne Rowley and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on Kawasaki disease, a childhood ill that harms the heart. Its cause is unknown, but a common germ that most children shake off is the prime suspect. The team searched lung airway cells of past patients for marks of that past infection. They found them months to years later.

The marks are blobs inside the cells that hold RNA. Their long stay hints the agent, or its traces, linger long past the acute ill. Lingering traces could help name the agent at last. They also give a tissue mark to test in future cases.
plos-pone-0001682:
Karen E. James, Harald Schneider, Stephen W. Ansell, and their co-authors applied a DNA array method to species that lack genome resources, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Diversity Arrays Technology, or DArT, reads thousands of DNA markers across a genome at once. High-throughput tools like microarrays had sped up work on model organisms, but most species have no such platform.

DArT works without prior sequence knowledge, which makes it suited to pan-genomic studies of non-model organisms. The full text gives the method, the species tested, and the evolutionary patterns the markers revealed. For field biologists tracking how wild populations split and adapt, the tool opens new studies. Genome-poor organisms had been shut out of such work.
plos-pone-0001782:
Takashi Nakakuki, Noriko Yumoto, Takashi Naka, and their co-authors modeled the wiring of a cancer-linked signaling cascade in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. ErbB receptors sit on cell surfaces. When ligands bind, they pair up in various combinations and trigger different outcomes, even though they recruit similar effector proteins. Earlier work showed cells expressing both EGFR and other ErbB members behave in complex ways.

The team ran a topological analysis of the MAPK cascade for kinetic ErbB signaling: how the network's structure shapes signal flow over time. The full text gives the model and the simulations. Predicting how receptor pairings steer signals could help choose among the many ErbB-targeted cancer drugs.
plos-pone-0001882:
Maria Figueroa and colleagues built a joint method to study how genes get switched on or off in cancer, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Acute blood cancers vary a great deal from case to case, and that spread blocks both insight and new targeted drugs. Faulty gene control is a mark of cancer and helps set how a tumor acts.

The team paired two kinds of data. One was the gene sequence itself, and the other was the chemical marks laid on it, which can mute a gene without changing its code. Used together, the two views sort real control faults from noise. The aim is a clearer map of what drives each tumor, a step toward care matched to the patient.
plos-pone-0001982:
Bobo Mok and co-authors studied how the malaria parasite hides a key surface protein, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The parasite Plasmodium falciparum survives by varying the proteins it shows to the immune system. Its main variable surface protein, PfEMP1, sits on infected red blood cells and helps them stick to vessel walls.

One gene for this protein, var2csa, is special: it is tied to malaria in pregnancy. The team examined the default path by which this gene is switched and how its message is repressed before translation. Knowing the switch rules may reveal a weak point in the parasite's disguise system.
plos-pone-0002082:
Stephanie Stotz and co-authors studied how nerve cells sense citral, the lemon scent compound, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. A family of channels called TRP channels mediates key parts of taste, smell, pain, and temperature sensation. More lab tools that switch these channels are needed to map what each one does.

Citral is a bioactive part of lemongrass oil. The team tested it on dorsal root ganglion neurons, the nerve cells that carry sensation from the body. Finding which TRP channels answer to a plant compound adds a tool for pain and sensation research, and may explain some effects of scent oils.
plos-pone-0002182:
Sandra Meidute Abaraviciene, Ingmar Lundquist, Juris Galvanovskis, and co-authors studied how a fatty acid harms insulin-making cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Type 2 diabetes often comes with high blood fat levels. The team examined palmitate, a common saturated fatty acid, and its effects on the pancreatic islets that release insulin.

They traced the harm through a fat sensor called GPR40 and through nitric oxide made in the islet. A diabetes drug, rosiglitazone, reversed much of the palmitate effect by blocking those steps. The work helps explain how high fat levels wear down insulin release, a core failure in type 2 diabetes.
plos-pone-0002282:
Andrea Camperio Ciani, Paolo Cermelli, and Giovanni Zanzotto modeled a puzzle about the genetics of male homosexuality, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Several lines of evidence point to genetic factors behind male homosexuality and bisexuality. Yet a trait that lowers direct reproduction stays present in all human populations at a stable, low rate, an apparent Darwinian paradox.

The authors explore sexually antagonistic selection as the answer. Genes that reduce fitness in males may raise it in females, for example through higher fertility in mothers and aunts. A trait can then persist because the same genes pay off in the other sex. Their model tests whether the balance can hold the trait steady.
plos-pone-0002382:
In 2008, Liu and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Wendy W. Liu, Joseph Goodhouse, Noo Li Jeon, and others. Its subject is a Microfluidic Chamber for Analysis of Neuron-to-Cell Spread and Axonal Transport of an Alpha-Herpesvirus. Alpha-herpesviruses, including herpes simplex virus and pseudorabies virus (PRV), infect the peripheral nervous system (PNS) of their hosts.

Here, we describe an in vitro method for studying neuron-to-cell spread of infection as well as viral transport in axons. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002482:
A research team led by Du reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Likun Du, Deborah K. Dunn-Walters, Krystyna H. Chrzanowska, and others. Its subject is a Regulatory Role for NBS1 in Strand-Specific Mutagenesis during Somatic Hypermutation. Activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) is believed to initiate somatic hypermutation (SHM) by deamination of deoxycytidines to deoxyuridines within the immunoglobulin variable regions genes.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002582:
Work from Balraj and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Premanand Balraj, Khalid El Karkouri, Guy Vestris, and others. Its subject is rickA Expression Is Not Sufficient to Promote Actin-Based Motility of Rickettsia raoultii. Rickettsia raoultii is a novel Rickettsia species recently isolated from Dermacentor ticks and classified within the spotted fever group (SFG).

The inability of R. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002682:
Ranji Singh led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was a novel strategy involved Anti-Oxidative defense: the conversion of NADH into NADPH by a metabolic network. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Ranji Singh, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) is pivotal to the cellular anti-oxidative defence strategies in most organisms. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002782:
Cornelle W. Noorlander led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was modulation of serotonin transporter function during fetal development causes dilated heart cardiomyopathy and lifelong behavioral abnormalities. The catalog record names Cornelle W. Noorlander first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Women are at great risk for mood and anxiety disorders during their childbearing years and may become pregnant while taking antidepressant drugs. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002882:
Laura E. Fuhrman, Kevin V. Shianna and Alejandro Aballay offered a faster way in 2008 to find worm mutants that fail against infection. Their host was C. elegans, a tiny roundworm widely used in labs. Mutants that let pathogens build up inside them show what a normal defense needs.

Published in PLOS ONE, the method pairs high-throughput isolation with mapping, so many mutants can be found and placed on the genome quickly. The authors show that worms with an enhanced pathogen buildup trait can be picked out fast. Geneticists studying basic immunity gain a practical screen they can run at scale.
plos-pone-0002982:
Jianjun Guo, Qingning Zeng, Mohammad Emami and co-authors tested whether the GCR2 gene family is needed for ABA control in Arabidopsis in 2008. Abscisic acid, or ABA, is a plant hormone governing seed germination and early seedling growth, among many jobs. GCR2 had been proposed as its receptor, but that claim was disputed.

The title gives a clear verdict: the family is not required for ABA control of germination and early development. Published in PLOS ONE, the negative result matters because it closes a wrong lead and pushes the search for the true ABA receptor elsewhere.
plos-pone-0003082:
Karin Hägni, Kynan Eng, Marie-Claude Hepp-Reymond and co-authors extended the rubber hand illusion in 2008. Multimodal stimulation can induce the brain to incorporate external objects into the body image, as when a fake hand feels like one's own. Such setups usually need touch matched to sight.

Here audio-visual stimulation plus mental imagery elicited the effect more rapidly, and watching virtual arms one imagines as one's own raised the skin response to a sudden threat. Published in PLOS ONE, imagery alone strengthening body ownership matters for prosthetics and virtual reality design. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003182:
Olaf Müller, Manuela De Allegri, Heiko Becher and colleagues compare ways to distribute treated bed nets in rural Burkina Faso in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Insecticide-treated nets are a highly effective tool against malaria in endemic parts of sub-Saharan Africa. Opinions differ, though, on the role of social marketing versus free distribution in rolling out net programmes.

Their cluster-randomized controlled trial tests distribution systems for malaria control in a real rural setting. Readers get trial evidence on a policy choice that affects coverage and cost. For malaria programmes, how nets reach homes can matter as much as the nets themselves.
plos-pone-0003282:
Shahin Nasr, Ali Moeeny and Hossein Esteky study filtering in visual working memory in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In a dynamic environment, what a stimulus is for can change over time. It is not always possible to separate relevant and irrelevant objects at first sight. In such conditions, subjects need to retain maximum possible information at first.

The authors seek a neural correlate of filtering irrelevant information out of visual working memory. Readers learn how the brain may drop what it first had to keep. Filtering is central to attention, since memory space is too small for every scene detail.
plos-pone-0003382:
Vanila F. Palmeira and co-authors tested HIV drugs against a fungus in this 2008 study. The fungus Fonsecaea pedrosoi causes chromoblastomycosis, a long-lasting skin disease. Current drugs for it are harsh, and the fungus often resists them. The team tried drugs that block HIV peptidase enzymes on the fungus instead.

In lab tests, those drugs slowed key steps in the life of the fungus. They also cut traits the fungus needs to cause disease. Using proven HIV drugs this way could speed up treatment options. The paper offers a fresh lead for a neglected tropical disease.
plos-pone-0003482:
Kerstin Schneider, Ursula Meyer-Koenig, and Frank T. Hufert studied a virus that dulls immune alarms in this 2008 paper. Human cytomegalovirus infects most people and hides for life. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells are the body's main source of type I interferon. Most of those cells sit in lymphoid organs.

The team showed the virus impairs those cells inside such organs. A weaker interferon alarm gives the virus room to persist. Muting the sentinels is a classic pathogen survival move. The finding clarifies one way this virus evades its host. This virus infects most adults for life, usually without causing clear illness.
plos-pone-0003582:
Caio Maximino examined a brain structure's evolution in fish and kin in this 2008 paper. The tectum sits in the roof of the vertebrate midbrain. It is often taken as highly conserved across evolution. Maximino assessed three hypotheses about its layered structure in nontetrapods.

He used a cladistic approach, grouping animals by shared traits. Changes in lamination and cell architecture were traced across lineages. Complexity in the tectum did change over time. The result complicates the story of a structure long assumed frozen. Fish vision is a strong test case for how brains change with habitat.
plos-pone-0003682:
Åsa Andersson, Magnus Isaksson, Judit Wefer, and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. A DNA vaccine encoding a piece of myelin protein can suppress a rat disease that models multiple sclerosis. The authors studied how that vaccine changes the immune attack behind the disease.

They found the vaccine impairs responses of T helper 17 cells, a type that drives the attack on the nervous system. Weaker Th17 responses went with weaker disease in the model. The result shows DNA vaccination can retune a misfiring immune response rather than just block it.
plos-pone-0003782:
Pablo Blinder, Joshua Cove, Maytal Foox, and colleagues published this brain development study in PLOS ONE in 2008. How axons spread their connections along dendrites is a basic open question in neuroscience. The team found signs, in dishes and in living animals, that dendrites help set the density and strength of their own inputs.

They report convergence among dendritic branches that are not sisters of one another. Activity itself controls this coming together, strengthening network connectivity along used paths. The finding shows developing circuits reinforcing the routes they actually use as they wire up.
plos-pone-0003882:
Arjen E. Van't Hof, František Marec, Ilik J. Saccheri, and co-authors mapped the chromosomes of a butterfly in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns Bicyclus anynana, a species widely used in lab studies. For all its use, its chromosomes had drawn little study before this work. The team set out to describe them in full.

They combined direct chromosome study with genetic linkage mapping using AFLP markers. The map covers all 28 chromosomes known from cell counts. A full map helps other labs tie traits to genes in this butterfly. It strengthens a model species used to study wing patterns and evolution.
plos-pone-0003982:
Stuart Jackson, Fred Cummins, and Nuala Brady timed flips in a reversible moving figure in 2008. Some images can be seen two ways, and perception swaps between them. A biological motion figure, like a walking person, is one such case. The authors studied how fast those swaps happen.

Their PLOS ONE article compares biological motion with other moving figures. Timing patterns reveal how the brain settles and unsettles a percept. A walking figure may flip at its own characteristic pace. The work adds to models of how perception stays stable, then changes. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004082:
John Paul Eichorst, Shaoying Lu, Jing Xu, and co-authors measured a cell movement switch in 2008. RhoA is a molecular switch that helps cells crawl and change shape. Biosensors using FRET light transfer can watch RhoA in live cells. Large image sets from those sensors need automated analysis.

Their PLOS ONE article compares RhoA dynamics in moving and still cells. Automated image analysis made the comparison consistent across many cells. Migratory cells showed different RhoA patterns from stationary ones. The method lets labs quantify movement signals without hand scoring. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004182:
Lingyun Zhu and colleagues published this vascular study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Atherosclerosis, the hardening and narrowing of arteries, grows partly through the rapid multiplication of vascular smooth muscle cells in vessel walls. Diabetes raises the risk, since high blood sugar drives these muscle cells to grow and move.

The team focused on PGC-1α, a regulator of cell energy use. They report that it is a key controller of the growth and movement that glucose triggers in these cells. The finding ties a metabolic regulator to the vessel damage that makes diabetes so dangerous for the heart.
plos-pone-0004282:
Hoau-Yan Wang and Lindsay Burns published this pain pharmacology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chronic morphine makes the mu opioid receptor switch its coupling from Gi/o to Gs proteins, producing excitatory signalling linked to tolerance and dependence. Ultra-low-dose naloxone prevents that switch and softens tolerance, but how was unclear.

The authors traced naloxone's protective effect to a pentapeptide binding site on filamin A, a scaffolding protein. Binding there blocks the receptor's switch and the CREB activation that follows acute morphine. The site offers a precise target for keeping opioids effective.
plos-pone-0004382:
Rhodopsin is the light-sensing protein in the eye's rod cells. It belongs to the large G protein coupled receptor family. Peter Hildebrand, Patrick Scheerer, Jung Hee Park, and co-authors studied its close relative opsin. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper maps a route through the protein. The route is a channel for the light-sensitive molecule retinal.

Inside rhodopsin, retinal sits in a pocket among seven coiled segments. Light flips retinal from one shape to another, starting vision. The authors describe how a ligand channel could let retinal move through the protein. That path helps explain how the sensor resets after firing. Receptor channels also interest drug designers who target this protein family.
plos-pone-0004482:
A silenced gene that brakes cell growth can be switched back on in a rare childhood tumor, report Elizabeth Algar, Andrea Muscat, Vinod Dagar, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The tumor is rhabdoid tumor, an aggressive cancer of the kidney and brain in young children. It is defined by the loss of a gene called SMARCB1, which helps control how DNA is packaged.

The missing gene seems to let other controls be silenced, including CDKN1C, a tumor suppressor imprinted from one parent. Restoring SMARCB1, or using drugs that block histone deacetylases, turned CDKN1C back on in the team's tests. That reawakening suggests a treatment angle for a tumor that now has few. It also shows how one lost gene can mute a whole safety system.
plos-pone-0004582:
Genes inside a famous autism-linked stretch of chromosome 16 are tested one by one by Ravinesh Kumar, Christian Marshall, Judith Badner, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Autism is a complex childhood neurodevelopmental disorder with a strong genetic basis. A deletion or duplication on chromosome 16p11.2, spanning about two dozen genes, is the second most frequent chromosomal disorder associated with autism.

Which of those genes actually drive the risk was unknown. The team ran association and mutation analyses on sixteen candidate genes from the region, on their account. Narrowing a whole region down to specific genes is slow, essential work. It points genetic counseling and brain research at the few genes that matter most.
plos-pone-0004682:
Xian Qi and colleagues described H5N1 bird flu viruses taken from raccoon dogs in China, for PLOS ONE in 2009. The H5N1 virus is a strong bird flu strain that can infect many kinds of animals. It poses a steady threat to farm stock and to human health as well.

Many forms of the virus occur in chickens, but few are linked to infection in mammals. The team read the genes of viruses from raccoon dogs to place them among known forms. Placing mammal cases in the family tree helps track spread. It also helps warn which forms may pose more risk to people.
plos-pone-0004782:
Cinzia Scambi and colleagues reported early evidence that folate, and Vitamin B12 may improve cell membranes in children with cystic fibrosis, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cystic fibrosis is a common fatal inherited disorder in Caucasian populations. It stems from mutations in a gene for a channel that moves salts and water across cell surfaces in the lungs and gut.

New strategies propose dietary supplements to support membrane health. The single arm trial gave 5-MTHF and B12 to affected children. Early signs pointed to membrane improvement. Larger controlled trials would be needed to confirm benefit. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend.
plos-pone-0004882:
Katarzyna Bozek led a team that mapped how the body clock controls genes in mammals for PLOS ONE in 2009. The clock turns thousands of genes on and off in a daily rhythm. Each tissue keeps its own rhythm, and the same gene can peak at a distinct hour in the liver than in the brain. Many control steps must work at once to make that pattern so exact.

The team read the start regions of clock driven genes on a large scale. They looked for shared codes that predict when and where a gene is switched on. Those codes help explain how one clock drives so many rhythms. They may also guide the best hours to give drugs.
plos-pone-0004982:
Klebsiella pneumoniae is a germ that often lives in soil and in the gut without causing harm. It can also cause serious hospital infections of the urine, lungs and blood. Sylvain Brisse and colleagues hunted its most dangerous clones. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They studied the clones' genes and traits together.

The team picked out the deadly clones from the wider group. They then sketched how these killers evolved. The family tree shows which lines turned dangerous. Hospitals gain a way to spot the worst strains early. The work also shows how a quiet gut germ can become a feared cause of disease.
plos-pone-0005082:
Tracking MRSA outbreaks needs fast, sharp strain fingerprinting. Current techniques are either resource-intensive or too blunt. Leo Schouls and colleagues tested a newer method in PLOS ONE in 2009. It is called MLVA. It counts variable repeats at several DNA loci. They compared it with two workhorses: pulsed-field gel electrophoresis and spa-typing.

The comparison shows where MLVA wins on speed and detail. It also shows where the older methods still hold up. Hospitals gain a practical tool for tracing staph spread. Rapid typing can catch transmission routes early. Stopping spread early saves lives and money. The study gives infection-control teams an evidence-based choice.
plos-pone-0005182:
Hedgehog signals guide how embryos build their bodies, and a protein called Smoothened carries those signals onward. In mammals, Smoothened moves to a tiny cell antenna, the primary cilium, when the signal arrives. Wilson and colleagues examined the shapes Smoothened can take in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team found that Smoothened can rest in several active and inactive shapes. All of those shapes can still travel to the cilium. That flexibility helps explain how the signal can be tuned up or down. It also matters for drugs that target Smoothened in cancer, since shape decides drug response.
plos-pone-0005282:
Cell division runs on a strict timetable in which key proteins must appear and then be destroyed. Van Leuken and colleagues traced one such timed destruction in PLOS ONE in 2009. It involves Aurora A, a kinase that helps organize division.

Polo-like kinase-1 is switched on before division by Aurora A itself. The team showed Plk1 is also required for Aurora A's timely destruction, by activating the APC/C-Cdh1 disposal machinery. A protein helping to destroy its own activator is a neat timing loop for orderly division. Cell division fails if these parts linger too long, so the loop that builds and then clears them is one of the checks that keeps each new cell sound.
plos-pone-0005382:
RNA interference uses small RNA pairs to switch off chosen genes, a workhorse research tool. Which strand of the pair guides the silencing was thought to be settled: one guides, the other is discarded. Wei and colleagues challenged that picture in mammalian cells in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Using small RNAs aimed at complementary targets, they showed both strands can guide posttranscriptional gene silencing. Strand selection in the silencing complex is therefore less one-sided than assumed. Designers of RNA interference experiments must account for activity from the strand they meant to ignore.
plos-pone-0005482:
Dong-Young Choi and colleagues studied brain inflammation and Parkinson-like illness in rats, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Parkinson's disease slowly kills nerve cells, and its cause in most cases is unknown. Signs found after death hint that inflammation in the brain may help drive the damage.

The team triggered inflammation in a movement area of the rat brain. The rats went on to show Parkinson-like signs and nerve cell loss. That supports the idea that inflammation is not just a side effect. It is part of how the disease harms the brain, and a possible target for treatment.
plos-pone-0005582:
Allister Crow and co-authors solved the structures of a bacterial weapon protein in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Many harmful bacteria shoot proteins straight into the cells they infect. One such protein family, called Cif, helps the bacteria take over host cells.

The team worked out the shapes of Cif proteins from two different pathogens. Comparing the shapes shows what the family shares and where it differs. A clear shape helps workers guess how the protein acts and how it might be blocked. Shapes from two species side by side also reveal which parts of the protein a drug would need to fit.
plos-pone-0005682:
Stephanie Watts and colleagues reported in 2009 that serotonin can attach itself to proteins in blood vessel walls. Serotonin is best known for mood, but it was first named for its power to tighten blood vessels. Most work has focused on serotonin latching onto receptors on the cell surface.

The team shows a second route: serotonin is bonded onto vessel proteins in a process called serotonylation. Those proteins help drive contraction of the vessel wall. This route may change how scientists think about blood pressure and vessel tone. It also opens a new place to look for drugs that relax vessels.
plos-pone-0005782:
Takao Fukui and co-authors described in 2009 a strange illusion from their lab: a moving phantom limb sensation. Sometimes a well-understood action fails even with full skill and a clear plan. One exception they probed involves a phantom that seems to move on its own.

The odd feeling appears to trigger a subconscious motor program, a set routine the body runs without orders. Studying such slips reveals how much of movement is automatic. The work speaks to rehab after amputation and to the design of prosthetics the brain will accept. Small illusions can expose big control systems.
plos-pone-0005882:
Fiona Pryde and co-authors tied a chemical mark on histones in 2009 to the schedule of DNA copying. Different stretches of DNA copy at different times in S-phase, set by their neighborhood. A protein called Cdc45 must load onto origins to start copying.

Methylation of histone H3 at one spot helped determine when Cdc45 associates with origins, the team found. That links a chromatin mark directly to replication timing. Timing faults can destabilize the genome, a cancer hallmark. The study names one timer among several, giving the replication field a firmer parts list.
plos-pone-0005982:
Dodder is a parasitic plant that steals food from its hosts and barely needs its own green tissue. Joel McNeal, Jennifer Kuehl, Jeffrey Boore and colleagues traced how its chloroplast genome has shrunk in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper follows one intron, a spacer inside a gene, and the helper enzyme, called a maturase, that cuts it out.

The intron and its helper were lost side by side across the dodder genus, a pattern the title calls parallel loss. A parasite that drops photosynthesis can afford to drop the tools that served it. The twin loss makes a clean case of genome streamlining, useful for reading how other parasites trim their genes.
plos-pone-0006082:
Stem cells from a human embryo and from a mouse's early lining look different, yet may obey the same rules. Ludovic Vallier, Thomas Touboul, Zhenzhi Chng and colleagues tested that in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper compares early cell fate decisions in human embryonic stem cells and mouse epiblast stem cells, the choices that start the making of body tissues.

The same signaling pathways control those first choices in both, the title reports. Shared rules mean mouse findings can guide human stem cell work with more confidence. That matters for regenerative medicine, where steering stem cells into the right tissue is the whole craft, and where human cells are costly to test directly.
plos-pone-0006182:
Parts of the genome are packed shut and kept silent in a form called heterochromatin. Elena Gracheva, Monica Dus, and Sarah Elgin studied two related proteins in the fruit fly Drosophila in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The proteins, VIG and Vig2, belong to the RISC complex, which is best known for silencing genes with small RNAs.

Their results support a role for both proteins in building the silent packed regions. That links the RNA silencing machinery to the wider packaging of the genome. Keeping the right regions shut protects gene control and genome stability. The fly work offers clues that may apply to many animals, since these systems are widely shared.
plos-pone-0006282:
Viruses and their hosts shape each other over evolutionary time, leaving matching marks in their genomes. Francisco Lobo and colleagues compared short nucleotide patterns in flaviviruses and their hosts in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The flavivirus family holds fast-changing RNA viruses infecting mammals, birds, ticks, and mosquitoes.

Common patterns of motif usage appear across the viruses and the animals they infect. Shared usage hints at long co-evolution between virus and host. Such fingerprints can reveal which hosts a virus is adapted to. They also help predict how readily a virus might jump species.
plos-pone-0006382:
Cells pull on the jelly around them, and the jelly's answer can carry information. Jessamine Winer, Shaina Oake, and Paul Janmey studied non-linear elasticity of extracellular matrices in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. On soft linear substrates, sparse tissue cells stay small and round; they spread as stiffness rises, up to a limit.

Because matrices stiffen as they are pulled, one cell's tug can be felt at a distance. Contractile cells can thus communicate local position and orientation through the material. That mechanical signalling complements chemical messages. It matters for wound healing and tissue engineering.
plos-pone-0006482:
Matteo Garofalo, Thierry Nieus, Paolo Massobrio, and colleagues compared methods for mapping brain cell networks in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied neuronal networks grown in vitro, recorded with micro-electrode arrays. Different statistical algorithms can estimate functional connectivity, the pattern of which cells influence which. The team first evaluated how these methods perform.

They applied information theory-based methods and cross-correlation to the same array data. Knowing which estimator to trust matters, since wrong maps mislead experiments. Their comparison guides neuroscientists who infer networks from spike recordings. It also shows where each method breaks down.
plos-pone-0006582:
Andrea Serino, Laura Annella, and Alessio Avenanti studied the space right around the body in PLOS ONE in 2009. An object moving toward the body needs fast work by the brain and a quick motor response. In monkeys, networks at the front of the brain merge senses to map this near space. The team asked how this peripersonal space works in humans, with a focus on its motor side.

Near space is the zone where we reach, grab, and defend. Its motor traits show the zone is mapped for action, not just for seeing. Knowing how it works informs robot design and rehab after brain injury. The study brings monkey brain findings into human terms.
plos-pone-0006682:
Zul Premji and co-authors ran a large malaria drug trial in Africa for PLOS ONE in 2009. The trial compared two combination treatments for uncomplicated falciparum malaria. One treatment joined chlorproguanil, dapsone, and artesunate in a fixed dose. It was designed to be affordable and simple for use in Africa. The other was the established pairing of artemether and lumefantrine.

Children and adolescents with malaria took part in the study. The trial was randomized, double-blind, and run as a phase three study. That design is the standard final test before wider use. Comparing a cheaper, simpler option against a proven one matters for clinics with tight budgets. The results inform which combination doctors in Africa can rely on.
plos-pone-0006782:
Eduardo J. M. Nascimento and his team linked one arm of the immune shield to bad dengue in PLOS ONE in 2009. The shield is the complement system. It can fire in three ways: the classic way, the lectin way, and the other way. Dengue can be mild, or it can turn grave. What tips a case toward grave is in part the immune reply itself.

The team checked complement parts in blood from dengue patients. The other pathway ran off track in step with how sick patients were. Off-track readings rose as the illness grew worse. Such checks might flag grave cases early. They also hint that calming this arm could help the sickest patients.
plos-pone-0006882:
Antonio Salas and colleagues read mitochondrial DNA to trace El Salvador's first settlers in PLOS ONE in 2009. The Mesoamerican isthmus channeled movement across the Americas. It shaped variability from Paleo-Indian times to recent history. Genetic information from Central America was scarce. El Salvador's population history was especially thin.

Mitochondrial DNA passes from mothers to children, preserving lineage history. The authors found echoes of first settlement in modern samples. They also found evidence of genetic continuity across time. Continuity means later upheavals did not erase the founding lineages. The results anchor El Salvador in the peopling story of the Americas.
plos-pone-0006982:
Robbert van der Most, Andrew Currie, Amanda Cleaver, and colleagues combined chemotherapy with immune attack in PLOS ONE in 2009. A cancer drug can both drain immune cells and stir them up. Earlier work showed chemotherapy can team well with immunotherapy. The question was how to turn that pairing into tumor control.

Using cyclophosphamide, the team made tumor cells more open to immune killing. The attack depended on a death signal called TRAIL and on CD8 T cells. Tumor growth was then suppressed. The result supports schedules that use chemo first to soften tumors for the immune system.
plos-pone-0007082:
Katiuska Molina-Luna, Ana Pekanovic, Sebastian Röhrich, and others studied dopamine and skill learning in rats in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dopamine by mouth seemed to help people learn motor skills. It also seemed to aid recovery of movement after stroke. How it did so was not known.

The team showed that dopamine in the motor cortex is needed for skill learning. They tied it to the strengthening of links between nerve cells. Rats without that signal did not improve as they should. The work helps explain a drug effect doctors had only seen from outside. It may guide stroke care that pairs practice with dopamine support.
plos-pone-0007182:
Anita A. Kumar, Emmanuel Bhaskar, Ghanshyam Palamaner Subash Shantha, and colleagues reported a 2009 PLOS ONE study of muscle breakdown during severe infection. The condition is rhabdomyolysis, where damaged muscle releases its contents into the blood. It often appears alongside sepsis, a life-threatening response to infection.

The authors review cases of community-acquired bacterial sepsis in a South Indian cohort. They record which bacterial pathogens were involved and what factors were linked to muscle breakdown. Clinicians can use the pattern they describe when they watch sepsis patients closely for this serious complication.
plos-pone-0007282:
Adrien Ducret, Etienne Maisonneuve, Philippe Notareschi, and colleagues built a microscope system for watching bacteria live in 2009. Most time-lapse studies of bacterial growth and movement use thin nutrient agar pads. That setup limits researchers, because conditions cannot be changed dynamically during an experiment without disturbing the cells.

The authors present an automated fluidic system for microscopy. Fluids can be swapped while bacteria are observed in real time. Their PLOS ONE tool opens studies of growth, cell cycle progression, and motility under changing conditions. Microbiologists gain cleaner tests of how bacteria respond to sudden shifts.
plos-pone-0007382:
Sreya Chattopadhyay, Sankar Bhattacharyya, Baisakhi Saha, and colleagues studied how tumors weaken helper T cells in 2009. Many tumors show decreased cellular immunity and high levels of prostaglandin E2. That compound, called PGE2, is a known inhibitor of CD4 T cell activation and biases immune responses in tumors.

Its role in T helper cell survival remained unclear. The authors show tumor-shed PGE2 impairs a receptor signaling pathway needed for CD4 T cell survival. They also study regulation by theaflavins, compounds from tea. Their work links a tumor product to immune cell death.
plos-pone-0007482:
Eugénie Ansseau and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy, a common inherited muscle-wasting disease. The condition is linked to a shrinking repeat array in the DNA of chromosome 4. Inside each repeat sits a gene called DUX4, normally silent in adult muscle. The team studied a related variant, DUX4c, and its behavior in patients' cells.

They found DUX4c is switched on in muscle from FSHD patients. Once active, it raises production of MYF5, a protein that guides muscle development. It also pushes muscle precursor cells to multiply. Those effects place DUX4c on the list of concrete players in the disease. A named molecular culprit is easier to target than a silent repeat. The work gives therapy research a specific gene to aim at.
plos-pone-0007582:
Julien Pothlichet and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on RIG-I, a sensor that detects invading viruses inside cells. RIG-I is pivotal: it spots many RNA and DNA viruses and raises the alarm. A defective sensor could strongly impair antiviral immunity. Yet little was known about natural human variants of the gene and their effects. The team scanned its single-letter polymorphisms for functional impact.

Two variants stood out with opposite effects. One strengthened the antiviral immune response, the other weakened it. The same virus can therefore meet different defenses in different people. Knowing which version a person carries may help explain uneven outcomes in infection. It also flags variants worth checking in patients with unusual viral illness. The study turns genetic trivia into working immunology.
plos-pone-0007682:
Bryan Moyer, Peter Hevezi, Na Gao and their co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on taste buds in primates. The team had earlier built a large list of genes active in taste buds, drawn from two tongue sites. That list held more than two thousand genes linked to taste.

Here they narrowed in on genes that make proteins spanning the cell membrane many times. Such proteins often act as receptors, the cell's sensors for the outside world. Mapping which ones sit in which taste cells helps explain flavor detection. It also shows what sets one taste cell apart from another.
plos-pone-0007782:
Shevin Jacob and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It reports how severe sepsis is treated in two Ugandan hospitals, and how patients fare. Sepsis, a runaway response to infection, likely drives much illness and death in low-income countries. Data from sub-Saharan Africa were very limited.

The study followed patients prospectively, watching care as it happened. Most of the patients were also infected with HIV-1. The team recorded treatments given and outcomes achieved. First-hand numbers like these show where simple improvements could save lives. They give hospitals and ministries a baseline to build on.
plos-pone-0007882:
Isabelle Ote and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It maps the jobs of one protein from the chickenpox virus, varicella-zoster virus. The protein, IE4, regulates how viral and cell genes are expressed. Its effects seem to act after genes are copied into RNA.

The exact mechanisms behind IE4 were not fully known. The authors show IE4 interacts with SR proteins, which help process RNA messages. IE4 also exports those messages through the TAP/NXF1 pathway. Tracing that export route explains how the virus gets its proteins made. It may reveal points where antiviral drugs could intervene.
plos-pone-0007982:
Jianhui Guo and colleagues hunted for faults in a growth-signal brake in colon tumors, for PLOS ONE in 2009. The brake gene is NKD1, the human kin of a fly gene found in wing studies. The signal it brakes, called Wnt, runs wild in most colon cancers.

Tumor samples held changed forms of NKD1, and tests showed those changes warp the Wnt signal chain. A faulty brake fits the picture of a signal left on too long. The work adds a new name to the list of gene faults behind a very common cancer.
plos-pone-0008082:
Lisa Meeks and colleagues charted a gene family that finishes plant messages in PLOS ONE in 2009. The enzymes, poly(A) polymerases, add the tail that most messenger RNAs need to work. Plants carry small families of these genes rather than one.

Comparing the genes across several plants showed signs of past copying, with the copies taking on split duties. One copy may serve seeds, another leaves, and so on. That division of labor helps explain how plants fine-tune their messages for each tissue and stage of life. More copies mean more chances to tune that tuning.
plos-pone-0008182:
Motoko Mukai and colleagues studied song sparrows in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Male song sparrows defend territory all year long. Yet their hormone response to a fake rival differs by season. In spring, a staged intrusion raises luteinizing hormone. In autumn, the response looks quite different.

The team compared gene activity in the hypothalamus, a brain region that helps control hormones. They sampled birds in breeding and non-breeding seasons. The profiles show which genes shift as aggression changes with the season. That helps explain how the same behavior can run on different brain settings across the year.
plos-pone-0008282:
Andrew B. Nesterovitch and colleagues reported a mutation with striking effects in PLOS ONE in 2009. Angiotensin-converting enzyme, or ACE, breaks down many peptides in the body. It plays a key role in blood pressure control and vessel remodeling. Raised ACE levels may increase risk of heart, vessel, and lung diseases, including asthma. The mutation studied is named Trp1197Stop.

Carriers showed a dramatic increase in blood ACE levels. A single gene change thus has a large effect on this enzyme. Knowing such mutations helps explain why ACE varies between people. It may also refine risk estimates for related diseases.
plos-pone-0008382:
Ken Tsumiyama, Yumi Miyazaki, and Shunichi Shiozawa proposed a theory of autoimmunity in PLOS ONE in 2009. The cause of autoimmune disease remains unknown. The authors investigated it from a different angle, looking at defects in the immune system itself. In mice not prone to autoimmunity, repeated immunization caused systemic autoimmune disease. That paradox is the starting point for their theory.

They frame autoimmunity through self-organized criticality, a concept from physics. A system at criticality can tip into large responses from small triggers. This view could explain why autoimmunity erupts suddenly. It offers a fresh framework for research.
plos-pone-0008482:
James Dillon and co-authors present software called AutoEPG in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Their tool analyzes electrical signals from a tiny worm, Caenorhabditis elegans. The worm's throat circuit is a model for studying nerve networks. A method called the electropharyngeogram records its electrical activity. Those records have shown how the feeding circuit works. But reading them by hand is slow and uneven.

AutoEPG processes the records in an automated, consistent way. It finds spikes and patterns that mark circuit states. Faster analysis lets labs run larger drug and gene screens. The tool serves work on feeding behavior and nerve control more broadly.
plos-pone-0008582:
Davida Smyth and co-authors map a resistant staph group in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The group is ST239-MRSA-III, a methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus lineage. It is notable for its hybrid origin, mixing two parent strains. It has caused sustained hospital epidemics worldwide since the late nineteen seventies. The team study the population structure of this clonal group. They sample isolates from many places and times.

Their analysis shows how the hybrid lineage is structured and spread. Distinct subpopulations track with geography and hospital outbreaks. Knowing that structure helps track and control MRSA spread. It also shows how hybrid germs can become global hospital threats.
plos-pone-0008682:
Janina Hellmann, Sylvia Münter, Michael Wink, and coworkers tested two plant chemicals against malaria parasites. Their report came out in PLOS ONE in 2010. One chemical, EGCG, comes from green tea. The other, digitonin, comes from foxglove plants. They studied sporozoites, the form of the parasite that a mosquito injects.

Plant medicines often mix many active parts, and parts can help each other. The team measured survival and movement of sporozoites under each chemical alone. They then tried both together and looked for effects beyond simple adding up. Strong combined action would hint that plant mixtures deserve a closer look as drug leads.
plos-pone-0008782:
Marshall Hampton, Wayne Xu, Brian Kram, and colleagues read the gene tags active in flower nectar glands. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Nectaries make the nectar that lures pollinators to flowers. Despite their key role, the molecular recipe for nectar stayed murky. Brassica rapa, a mustard relative, offered a workable study plant. Expressed sequence tags give a snapshot of active genes.

Sequencing those tags from nectaries revealed which genes were switched on. Candidates for sugar making and secretion stood out. The list gives pollination biology a molecular starting point. Breeders may someday tune nectar to support bees better.
plos-pone-0008882:
Silvia Cainarca, Simone Fenu, Cinzia Ferri, and colleagues built a glowing calcium meter into mouse stem cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Drug screening usually forces test genes into altered cell lines at unnatural doses. Such forcing can distort the results badly. Embryonic stem cells offer a cleaner, more natural platform. A photoprotein that glows when calcium rises serves as the meter.

The sensor reported calcium movements in living cells on demand. It also worked inside living animals, not just dishes. Screening in a natural cell setting should cut false drug leads. The platform suits targets that altered cell lines handle poorly.
plos-pone-0008982:
Jonathan Touboul and Alain Destexhe asked whether a fashionable brain pattern could be a statistical mirage, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Brain researchers often report neuronal avalanches, bursts of activity of many sizes. The sizes follow a power law, which some take as proof the brain sits at a critical point. Criticality is said to keep the brain poised between order and chaos.

The pair showed that plain random dynamics can also produce power-law patterns. A straight line on a log plot, they argue, does not prove true criticality. Random noise, measured the usual way, can wear the same disguise. The paper urges more careful tests before claiming the brain is self-organised critical.
plos-pone-0009082:
Jonas Waldenström and co-authors dosed wild birds with the food-poisoning germ Campylobacter jejuni, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Campylobacter is a common cause of bacterial stomach illness in most of the world. It infects many kinds of animals without making them sick at all. Birds are suspected of spreading it into water and food supplies.

The team built a controlled infection experiment using captive wild birds. They tracked how long the birds shed the bacterium in their droppings. Shedding came in changing patterns rather than one steady stream. Knowing those patterns sharpens estimates of birds' true role in human infections.
plos-pone-0009182:
Junjie Luo and colleagues published this systems biology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Its subject is chemotaxis, the way bacteria swim toward food and away from poisons. Bacteria sense chemicals around them and steer by switching between runs and tumbles. If scientists understood that steering circuit fully, they could reprogram it.

The authors reverse engineered the pathway using frequency domain analysis, a math tool borrowed from engineering. They fed the bacteria chemical signals that rose and fell at set rates. Watching how the cells responded at each rate revealed how the circuit is wired. The design rules they extracted could guide efforts to steer bacteria for useful tasks.
plos-pone-0009282:
Chiara Azzari and co-authors published this diagnostics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pneumococcal disease in children is usually typed by the Quellung reaction, the classic gold standard. That test needs living bacteria grown in culture. Many sick children's samples grow nothing, leaving doctors without a type.

The team compared two DNA-based tests on such culture-negative samples. Real-time PCR proved more sensitive than multiplex PCR for finding and typing the bacteria. A more sensitive test means more cases get a firm diagnosis. It also improves tracking of which pneumococcal types vaccines must cover.
plos-pone-0009382:
Takako Shima-Sano and co-authors published this HIV testing study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Testing pregnant women for HIV is essential to stop the virus reaching their babies. Screening tests, though, often return false positives in pregnancy. A frightened mother then waits for a confirmatory result that clears her.

The team designed a screening algorithm meant to cut that false alarm rate in Japan. Their stepwise approach sorts true infections from test noise faster. Fewer false positives mean less needless stress for expectant mothers. The work shows screening programs must be tuned to the population they serve.
plos-pone-0009482:
Song Liu examined how genes start their messages in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many genes have more than one start site, called a promoter. Using a different start can change when and where a gene is active. Unusual start choices have been tied to disease. Liu asked whether genes with more start sites behave in a distinct way.

Across the data, genes with richer sets of start sites varied more in activity between tissues. They were also more often linked to disease risk. That means start site choice is not a minor detail. It helps shape how flexible a gene is, and how prone it is to go wrong.
plos-pone-0009582:
Juan Wang and co-authors pinned down how a malaria drug works in PLOS ONE in 2010. Artemisinin is the most potent drug against malaria. For years, experts argued about how it kills the parasite. The team had built a yeast model that pointed to mitochondria, the cell's power units. Now they tested that claim directly on the malaria parasite.

The drug acted on the parasite's mitochondria and was switched on inside them. That local activation explains its killing power. Knowing the true target matters as drug resistant parasites spread. It helps chemists protect the drug's action and design successors if resistance wins.
plos-pone-0009682:
The left and right halves of the human brain do not split every job evenly. Gjurgjica Badzakova-Trajkov and colleagues studied that uneven split in PLOS ONE in 2010. They asked whether the two sides work as partners on shared tasks or run as separate, independent systems.

The team compared performance on tasks that lean on one side more than the other. Their results pointed to both patterns at once, with some processes backing each other up. Other processes ran on their own without help from the opposite side. The work helps explain how a two-sided brain organizes thought.
plos-pone-0009882:
Cooperation is fragile: cheats can wreck it, yet groups somehow keep it alive. Bo-Yu Zhang, Ross Cressman, and Yi Tao modeled one way groups hold cooperation steady. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The puzzle sits at the heart of game theory.

The mechanism is periodic impulses, regular jolts applied at set times. Pulses like these can push a wavering system back toward cooperation. Stability through impulses is a known control idea borrowed from engineering. The model asks whether the same trick works in social and biological groups.
plos-pone-0009982:
Embryonic cells move toward chemical signals as the body takes shape. Thomas Southgate and colleagues studied a protein that tunes that movement in mouse embryonic cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Chemotaxis is movement directed by a chemical trail. CXCR4 is the receptor that reads one such trail. Cell movement sculpts tissues long before birth. The team showed that 5T4, an oncofetal glycoprotein, tunes how CXCR4 drives that movement. Oncofetal means the protein appears in embryos and again in some cancers. Tuning movement matters in development and in cancer spread. The cells came from mouse embryos.
plos-pone-0010082:
