Igor Kuznetsov, Marc Herant, and Micah Dembo analyzed moving cell machinery in a 2010 paper. Their subject was actin, the protein that forms a moving scaffold inside cells. They used a rat fibroblast line that moves fast. A method called FLAP let them tag actin and follow it after light bleaching.

Tagged actin traveled from mid-cell to the leading edge surprisingly fast in their recordings. The PLOS ONE study worked through what those transit times mean for the leading lamella, the cell's front sheet. Fast actin flow helps explain how crawling cells push forward.
plos-pone-0010182:
Lucília Miranda, Allen Collins, and Antonio Marques used DNA to untangle a jellyfish relative's life in 2010. Cnidarians, the group that includes jellyfish, have life cycles that vary widely and are hard to document. The newest proposed class, Staurozoa, was especially poorly known. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE that year.

Genetic data tied together two forms once thought to be separate animals. A tiny form called Microhydrula limopsicola proved to be an early life stage of an Antarctic stalked jellyfish. Matching stages by DNA can rewrite life histories that observation alone could not settle.
plos-pone-0010282:
The authors were Noa Madar-Balakirski, Catherine Tempel-Brami, Vyacheslav Kalchenko, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study attacked solid tumors in mice through their blood vessels. Vessel-targeting therapies delay tumor growth, yet none had shown long-term cures. The team used vascular targeted photodynamic therapy with a drug called Tookad, activated by light at the tumor site.

A single treatment, they report, permanently closed both feeding arteries and draining veins of tumors. Starved and unable to drain, such tumors may die outright. The result suggests vessel shutdown can be complete, not just a delay.
plos-pone-0010382:
Chia-Feng Liu, Keith Parker and Humphrey Yao studied how female germ cells survive in the mouse ovary for PLOS ONE in 2010. Egg precursor cells are essential: without them, no follicles form and the ovary fails. Two related signals, Wnt4 and beta-catenin, had been shown to protect these cells. Turning either off in the fetal ovary caused losses. The team traced how the protection works.

The pathway guards the cells by holding down another signal, activin beta B. Too much of that signal appears harmful to young germ cells. Balance between the two signals decides survival. Understanding that balance may inform research on infertility and ovary development. It also shows development often runs on brakes as much as accelerators.
plos-pone-0010482:
Andreas Hinz and colleagues solved the structure of a llama antibody that blocks HIV for PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV enters cells by latching its surface protein, gp120, onto CD4 and then a second receptor. Antibodies covering the CD4 site can stop entry cold. Llamas make unusual small antibodies; one, called D7, neutralizes HIV. The team crystallized D7 and worked out its shape.

They also mapped how D7 grips gp120 at the entry site. A tiny antibody that reaches a guarded spot is valuable for vaccine design. Vaccines try to teach our bodies to make such blockers. Seeing exactly how D7 fits shows what a vaccine should aim for. Small llama antibodies may also become drugs themselves.
plos-pone-0010582:
Cristina Becchio, Morena Mari, and Umberto Castiello studied visual perception in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their volunteers were children with autism spectrum disorders. The task involved judging pictures where shadows fell across a scene.

Shadows can mislead anyone, since a dark patch can be mistaken for a hole in the ground. The children handled shadow information in a way that differed from typical patterns. They seemed less likely to discount a shadow when judging what they saw. Small differences like these can reveal how autistic perception weighs parts of a scene, and they may inform better tests of visual processing.
plos-pone-0010682:
Nidhi Gupta and colleagues tested a drug that silences a cholesterol gene, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene makes PCSK9, a protein that removes cholesterol-clearing receptors from liver cells. With fewer receptors, harmful LDL cholesterol stays in the blood, raising heart risk.

Their drug was a locked nucleic acid, a tough synthetic strand that binds the gene's message. In cells and in mice it cut PCSK9 and raised receptor numbers. Blood cholesterol fell as a result. Work like this paved the way for a whole class of gene-silencing heart drugs that followed in later years.
plos-pone-0010782:
Jeff Shrager simulated scientific publishing under different review rules, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Peer review before publication is science's main quality gate. The internet made looser and tighter gates both possible, and debate about them runs hot. Real journals cannot be experimented on lightly, so a simulation offers a safer test bed.

Virtual scientists in the model made discoveries, wrote them up, and passed review gates of varying strictness. Very loose gates flooded the record with errors. Very strict gates slowed true findings and wasted reviewer effort. Middle settings performed best overall. The model cannot settle the debate, but it gives reformers numbers instead of slogans.
plos-pone-0010882:
Andreas Oberbach, Nadine Schlichting, Matthias Blüher and co-authors published this bladder study in PLOS ONE in 2010. People with type 2 diabetes get urinary tract infections more often, for reasons that are not fully explained. The authors suspected that high levels of free fatty acids, common in obesity, might stir inflammatory signals in the bladder wall itself.

They grew human bladder smooth muscle cells taken from surgical biopsies and exposed them to palmitate, a common fatty acid, or to a bacterial toxin. Both triggers raised production and release of IL-6 and MCP-1, two chemical messengers that draw immune cells and drive inflammation. Oberbach and colleagues thus link a diabetes-related fat signal to an inflamed bladder lining. That connection may help explain why infections take hold so readily in diabetic patients.
plos-pone-0010982:
Pika Miklavc, Manfred Frick, Oliver Wittekindt and co-authors published this lung cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Calcium is essential for the moment a secretory vesicle fuses with the cell surface and releases its cargo. What calcium does after fusion was undescribed, so the team watched single vesicles in rat lung cells that secrete surfactant, the substance that keeps air sacs open.

They combined light-scattering and dye signals that mark pore opening with calcium-sensitive imaging. Most fusion events, they found, trigger local calcium entry right at the fusion site. This happens during the slow release phase. Miklavc and colleagues call this a postfusion active zone of elevated calcium. Discovering a signal after the main event rewrites the timetable of secretion, and may matter for surfactant release in newborn and adult lung disease.
plos-pone-0011082:
Dickson, Wahl, Fernandes and colleagues addressed a methods problem in PLOS ONE in 2010. Scientists line up protein sequences to compare them, but those line ups can contain silent errors. Worse, there was no check that did not depend on the same ideas used to build the line up.

The team used paired changes inside a single protein as an independent test. When two spots in a protein tend to change together, that pattern can reveal where a line up has gone wrong. Their approach offers a fresh quality check for a basic tool in biology. Stronger checks mean more trust in results built on sequence data.
plos-pone-0011182:
Roa, Li, Peled and colleagues examined antibody making cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. To build better antibodies, certain immune cells mutate their own antibody genes on purpose. An enzyme starts that process by damaging DNA, and repair proteins then decide how the damage is handled.

A repair pair studied here did two jobs at once. It fixed some damage cleanly, without error, and it promoted deliberate mutation at other sites. That dual role fine tunes the balance between safety and variety in antibodies. Understanding it deepens basic immunology and may inform work on immune disorders.
plos-pone-0011282:
Brauner, Bashamboo, Rouget and colleagues analyzed eleven young patients in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ovarian cysts before puberty are uncommon and can trigger signs of early puberty. The team carried out clinical, biological and genetic analysis of isolated cysts in eleven girls to understand their cause.

Detailed cases help doctors tell harmless cysts from those needing surgery or hormone care. Families facing a rare diagnosis need clear answers most of all. The genetic side of the study checks whether inherited factors explain why cysts arise so early. The report guides children's hormone care with evidence from careful case work.
plos-pone-0011382:
Jarod Swant and co-authors measured in 2010 how methamphetamine rewires signaling in the mouse hippocampus, a brain region central to memory. The drug is known to harm learning in users, but the exact electrical changes behind that harm needed pinning down. The team worked with thin slices of mouse brain kept alive in the lab.

In the slices, the drug weakened the strengthening of connections that underlies learning, while raising the background level of signaling between cells. Together, those changes leave the circuit noisy yet poor at recording new information. The paired result helps explain the memory problems seen in people who abuse the drug. It also gives addiction researchers defined circuit changes to target when they test whether the damage can be reversed.
plos-pone-0011482:
Rainer Stollhoff and co-authors timed in 2010 how the brain compensates in people born unable to recognize faces. Congenital prosopagnosia leaves face recognition severely impaired from birth, yet affected people manage social life by leaning on voice, hair, and gait. The team measured the earliest moments of face processing to catch the workaround as it starts.

Their measures showed an early time course of compensatory processing that differs from typical face processing from the first fractions of a second. The brain does not simply run the normal system more weakly; it reroutes early. Charting that rerouting in real time shows the brain's capacity to build an alternate path around a missing function. It may also guide training that strengthens the compensatory route on purpose, instead of drilling the broken one.
plos-pone-0011582:
Kaspar Delhey and colleagues studied how bird feather colour shifts with the seasons, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Feather colour helps birds signal quality to mates and rivals. Birds make colour in three main ways: through feather structure, through dark melanin pigments, and through carotenoids that come from food.

The authors tracked all three colour types across seasons to see which ones fade or change most after moulting. Their comparison shows the three systems do not age in the same way. That helps explain why a bird that looks bright in spring may look dull months later, even without growing new feathers.
plos-pone-0011682:
Anna Kuta and co-authors catalogued parts of the mouse cell's freight machinery, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells haul organelles, vesicles and RNA cargoes along inner tracks to keep working. The dynein complex is a key motor for that transport, and its intermediate chains help decide what gets carried and where.

The authors identified new versions of these chains produced by alternative splicing, and charted where each version appears across mouse tissues. The fuller parts list refines the blueprint of the transport system. It also gives researchers precise targets for studying transport failures in disease.
plos-pone-0011782:
Yuji Yoshiko and co-authors watched bone cells switch sides in a rat cell culture, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bone-building cells and fat-storing cells come from kin lines, and grasping how a cell picks one fate over the other matters for growth and for disease. Shifts in that pick change bone mass and body fat alike.

The team found a subset of bone cells with high levels of the fat-driving factor PPAR gamma left their bone fate and became fat cells. The swap marks the point where a cell's path tips from bone toward fat. Moving that balance could one day matter for weak-bone disease.
plos-pone-0011882:
Sandrine Adiba, Clément Nizak, and Minus van Baalen argued in 2010 that many bacterial weapons may be accidents of a different struggle. For many disease bacteria, humans are a dead end they rarely spread from, so it is odd that they carry such harmful traits. The coincidental evolution idea holds that these traits first helped against predators that graze on bacteria.

Under that view, defenses built to survive being eaten by amoeba-like hunters later proved harmful inside human tissue. The study weighs this case for how virulence factors arise. If the weapons were honed elsewhere, then the environments bacteria live in outside the body become part of the story of human disease.
plos-pone-0011982:
Sophie Laget and co-workers reported in 2010 a surprise about two human proteins named for a domain they may not use as expected. MBD5 and MBD6 carry a methyl-binding domain, a part that in related proteins reads methylated DNA and helps silence genes. The pair were otherwise almost uncharacterized.

The team found that both proteins associate with heterochromatin, the tightly packed silent DNA, yet do not bind methylated DNA. That combination breaks the family rule and demands another explanation for what they do there. Proteins sitting on silent regions without reading the usual mark may guard those regions in a different way, an open question for gene regulation research.
plos-pone-0012082:
Dalila Martínez and co-workers built in 2010 a simple rule to sort tuberculosis patients by their risk of drug-resistant disease. Multidrug-resistant TB resists at least isoniazid and rifampin, the two best TB drugs, and confirming it takes time and lab capacity many clinics lack. A clinical prediction rule was developed and internally validated among adult patients with pulmonary TB.

The rule stratifies patients so that those likeliest to carry resistant disease get tested and treated accordingly first. In settings where drug-susceptibility testing cannot cover everyone, ranking risk is not a shortcut but a necessity. Used well, the rule speeds the right treatment to the patients whose wrong treatment would do the most harm.
plos-pone-0012282:
Diana Spitznagel, John O'Rourke, Neal Leddy, and co-authors characterized an odd motor protein in the sleeping sickness parasite, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Myosins are molecular motors that haul cargo and shape cells, and most creatures own dozens. African trypanosomes make do with only two candidate myosins, which turns the parasite into a clean test bed for what each motor does.

Their unusual class I myosin proved to work in the traffic of vesicles, the cell's shipping bubbles. Parasite plumbing that differs from ours is a potential drug target, since blocking it harms the parasite alone. Basic studies of this kind stock the list of targets that drug hunters draw on.
plos-pone-0012382:
Ömer Saraç, Volkan Atalay and Rengul Cetin-Atalay built a tool that predicts what a protein does, described in PLOS ONE in 2010. Assigning jobs to proteins is a core task in biology, and many computer methods exist, each using clues such as shape, sequence, or known motifs. No single method wins on all proteins, so the team combined several classifiers into one system called GOPred.

GOPred votes among its combined methods to assign Gene Ontology terms, the standard labels for protein jobs. Pooling methods beat single ones on their tests. The tool helps labs that sequence new proteins daily and need a fast, reliable first guess at function before bench work begins.
plos-pone-0012482:
Felix Schaller, Antonio Fernandes, Christine Hodler and colleagues compared Y chromosomes in chimpanzees and bonobos, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The male-only Y region differs dramatically even between humans and chimps, and it evolves fast. Chimps mate in multi-male groups with intense sperm competition, while bonobos follow different social rules, so the two species test whether mating systems shape the Y.

The team found Y variation that tracks those mating differences. A fast-changing Y that mirrors mating strategy supports the idea that sexual competition drives its evolution. The comparison also cautions against treating the human Y as a general primate pattern.
plos-pone-0012582:
Lu Lin, Houhui Song, Yuetong Ji and fellow researchers used sound waves to move DNA into tough bacteria, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Their targets were heat-loving, thick-walled bacteria that live without air. Such germs shrug off the usual ways of adding new genes, both the chemical baths and the electric shocks labs rely on. Without gene transfer, no one can improve these strains for making fuels or chemicals.

Brief bursts of ultrasound opened the way, and the bacteria took up the new DNA. One workable method can unlock a whole class of microbes for the biofuels field. Heat-loving strains are prized for brewing, since hot tanks resist spoilage and react fast, so the gain is more than a lab trick.
plos-pone-0012682:
Gong, Bourhis, Chiu and co-authors tested how blocking antibodies treat different Wnt signals differently. Wnt signals guide growth through a receptor pair, and a partner called LRP6 is needed to pass the message. Their 2010 study used antibodies against LRP6 to probe the system.

Some antibodies shut signalling down while others made it stronger, and the effect depended on which Wnt form was present. That split behaviour matters for drug design, since Wnt faults drive cancers and bone disease. A blocker for one signal may need to spare the rest.
plos-pone-0012782:
Maan, Maan, Nomikou and co-authors built lab tests that can name all seven types of a livestock virus. Epizootic haemorrhagic disease virus attacks wild deer and can cause a bluetongue-like illness in cattle. Their 2010 RT-PCR assays read the virus's RNA and sort each sample by serotype, the version that immune defences see.

They used the tests on strains from the Mediterranean region and North America. Fast, exact typing lets vets track which versions are moving where during an outbreak. That tracking guides vaccine choice and animal movement rules.
plos-pone-0332982:
Lidane Noronha, Brian P. Lazzaro, and Patrick M. O'Grady study a fruit fly that breeds only in rotting saguaro cactus in the Sonoran Desert. What the fly's food provides may decide how many young survive. Their 2026 study raises the flies on two lab diets, with and without cactus-derived additions, and tracks survival stage by stage.

Cactus additions often hurt survival from egg to the resting stage, yet helped survival from that stage to adult. The net effect flipped with the base diet: additions hurt on banana food but helped on cornmeal food. Feeding amounts did not explain the gaps. The work shows that judging a specialist's diet takes watching each life stage, not just the final count.
plos-pone-0337882:
Annemieke Boendermaker, Gideon Latten, Jelle Prins, Kiki Lombarts, and Paul Brand published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a cross-sectional survey of emergency physicians in the Netherlands. Four things are measured together: how engaged the doctors feel, whether they burn out, whether they plan to leave, and what the workforce guidelines say.

Emergency medicine loses experienced doctors when exhaustion outweighs engagement, the energy and pride in the work. Linking official workforce guidelines to those feelings tests whether staffing rules protect or strain doctors. Hospital leaders and physician associations in the Netherlands and beyond can use this evidence in workforce planning.
plos-pone-0337982:
Hassan M Aljohani and colleagues tackle a statistical estimation problem: pinning down the coefficient of variation, a unit-free measure of spread, for lifetime data that follows a weighted exponential distribution. Their 2026 study works under a flexible censoring scheme that lets life-testing experiments end early or adapt mid-course, saving time and test units.

They build estimators two ways, a classical maximum likelihood route with bootstrap confidence intervals and a Bayesian route using computer sampling with informative prior beliefs. A worked simulated example and a large Monte Carlo study compare the approaches, and the Bayesian estimators with good priors come out more precise. Reliability engineers use such estimates to judge whether a product's lifetime is consistent enough to trust.
plos-pone-0338282:
Helen Hynes and colleagues mapped what is known about how doctors trained abroad experience the clinical skills exams required to practise or specialise in a new country. These international graduates form a large share of many health workforces and often score lower, for reasons mixing personal, social, and institutional forces. The 2026 scoping review gathered forty-four publications covering more than seven thousand doctors from fifty-four countries.

Studies clustered in Britain, Australia, and Canada. Influences on exam experience fell into personal factors, social factors such as bias and belonging, and systemic factors in how assessments are designed. Almost nothing is known about age, time away from practice, or weaker language skills. The authors press for fairer, better-supported assessment routes.
plos-pone-0342982:
Badriyeh Karami and colleagues surveyed older adults during the COVID pandemic. Three hundred and forty one adults took part. All were over sixty years old. Forms measured social support and resilience. Forms also measured life quality tied to health. A structural model placed resilience in the middle. It carried part of the support effect.

More support linked with higher resilience scores. Support also linked with better life quality directly. About half the total gain ran through resilience. Supported elders coped better each day. Coping then lifted daily health and function. Future crisis plans should teach resilience skills. Support networks alone may not be enough.
plos-pone-0343182:
Songsen Su and Yanfang Lin study a rare illness in which blood vessels become inflamed and swollen. People with the illness often have asthma and high levels of a white blood cell type called eosinophils. In their 2026 paper, the authors look for a pattern of small chemicals in blood that could help doctors tell this illness apart from plain asthma.

Blood samples came from ten patients with the illness, ten with asthma, and ten healthy adults. Lab tests found hundreds of chemicals at changed levels, grouped in a few body pathways. A small set of these chemicals separated the illness from health well in tests. The pattern could one day support a blood test, though the group studied was very small.
plos-pone-0343482:
Sarah Griffiths led a team of five authors studying dementia care planning in primary care, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Care plans for people with dementia should be personal, built around the person's own goals. In busy primary care, appointments are short and planning talks can feel rushed. The team captured how those conversations are perceived by those involved.

Griffiths's study names three needs in its findings: time, talk, and teamwork. Planning works when staff have minutes to listen, words that fit the family, and roles that mesh. Those are cheap ingredients, but they are often the first cut under pressure. The study gives practices a concrete picture of what good planning conversations require.
plos-pone-0344082:
Song, Zhou, and Li studied cell cleanup failure in diabetic nerve damage in a 2026 paper. Using cell and animal models, they showed that long-term high blood sugar slows the cleanup system that recycles worn cell parts. Marker patterns confirmed stalled cleanup, tied to one growth signal switching on and one energy signal switching off.

Gene analysis flagged three master switches of the cleanup program as disturbed. Cleanup failure and fat handling also worsened each other in a loop, deepening nerve cell harm. Breaking that loop could offer a new treatment angle for a painful complication that current care only partly controls.
plos-pone-0345782:
Olivia Chivers and colleagues interviewed twenty-five older adults living in the community about the first, subtle signs that getting around is changing. Mobility here means everything from walking to driving and buses, and its early decline quietly shrinks daily life. Through themed analysis of the conversations, four shared threads emerged about how people notice and respond to the shift.

Everyday tasks were described as costing more energy than they used to. People spoke of watching risks more carefully, of a use-it-or-lose-it determination to keep moving, and of measuring themselves against neighbours and friends. The authors say support should arrive at this early stage, tackling expectations about ageing and keeping people engaged in activities they value. All this should happen long before a fall or a surrendered licence forces the issue.
plos-pone-0346682:
Rafayet Rahman Ridoy and co-workers study who gets a skilled attendant at childbirth in Bangladesh and why poorer families miss out. Their 2026 study layers classic statistics, an inequality breakdown, and ten machine learning models over survey data, then explains the winning model's reasoning.

Wealth, schooling, and proper pregnancy checkups from qualified providers predicted skilled attendance most strongly. Dhaka and Khulna regions and cities ran ahead of rural areas. Usage tilted heavily toward richer households, with checkups, wealth, and schooling driving most of that tilt. A neural network predicted attendance best. Closing the gap, the authors say, means funding checkups and schooling where mothers are poorest.
plos-pone-0347282:
Tengyao Niu and co-authors used computer toxicology to ask if sweeteners might harm bones, joints, discs, and muscle. Sweeteners get most study for weight and blood sugar. Their muscle and bone effects were near blank. Their 2026 study wove web analysis, docking, and motion runs across four ills, from worn discs to thin bones.

The screen met on thirty-five core protein targets, bunched in swelling, metabolism, and linked signal paths. Two plant sweeteners showed the strongest grip on the targets. Runs confirmed firm grip with three named proteins. Niu and colleagues stress the work is a computer view that yields targets for lab tests, not proof of harm at food-level doses.
plos-pone-0347582:
Linda Visser, Jan-Henning Ehm, and Janin Brandenburg used a huge study of US youth. It held near twelve thousand kids, aged nine or ten at the start. The team tracked three things over four waves: school marks, inner pain such as fear and low mood, and signs of ADHD. They asked how the three move each other with time.

Marks and inner pain were linked, but each did not drive the next wave of the other. ADHD signs tied to both marks and pain. Low mood, in a twist, came before falls in ADHD signs. The team says ADHD does not explain the marks and pain link. Spot low mood early, they urge.
plos-pone-0347682:
Abeer A. Mabrouk, Sameh H. Ismail, Ahmed G. Soliman, and Mervat M. Omran compared silver, gold, and mixed metal nanoparticles as wound treatments in rats. Metal particles are meant to deliver the healing punch of metal ions with fewer side effects. Thirty-two rats with standard cut wounds received daily treatment for three weeks with one formulation, a standard antibiotic cream, or nothing.

Both silver and gold formulations shrank wounds effectively and sped repair, boosting new blood vessel growth and collagen deposition, the scaffolding of healed skin. Tissue chemistry and microscopy backed the improvement, and computer modelling explored how the particles interact with inflammation enzymes. The authors rate the nanoformulations as genuinely effective wound healers.
plos-pone-0347782:
Inhye Seo and co-workers build a scoring system to guide how cities care for the carbon stored in parks and green spaces. Trees and soils hold carbon, but each city patch differs in how much it holds and how much more it could take up. Their 2026 paper combines fine-scale maps of plant carbon, soil carbon, and yearly uptake into one index.

A case study in Suwon, South Korea, showed sharp differences even inside a single green patch. Edge zones scored far lower than interiors, marking spots where care would help most. The method then points to fixes matched to each weak spot, such as keeping leaf litter, loosening packed soil, or planting in layers. City crews gain a map for spending effort where it counts.
plos-pone-0347882:
Quynh Nga Duong and Nguyen Thuy Khue Tran modelled how the shadow economy, all the work and trade hidden from tax and regulation, shapes growth in emerging economies. Rather than study informality alone, they let it interact with taxes, institutions, foreign investment, trade openness, government size, and population growth inside one Bayesian model that handles uncertain, limited data gracefully.

Across their panel of developing countries, a bigger shadow economy dragged down income per person. Strong institutions, healthy foreign investment, and open trade blunted the damage, while fast population growth and bloated government consumption made it worse. The authors argue that the harm of informality is not fixed: tidy institutions and sensible fiscal policy can shrink both the shadow and its cost.
plos-pone-0348182:
Vi T Le and Jennifer A Bailey led a study of parents in Washington State. Legal shops for cannabis opened there in 2014. The team asked if living near more shops shifts parents' own use and views. They surveyed four hundred seventy-one parents in 2015, 2016, and 2017. They counted shops within a short drive of each home. They also asked parents how many shops they felt were near.

Parents in shop-dense areas used cannabis more. They found parent use more okay and saw it as less habit-forming. Over time, a rise in shops near a home tracked a rise in how okay use felt. The team says shop spread may set new norms for parents.
plos-pone-0348282:
Jianchun Wei and co-workers track falling platelet counts in emergency patients with sepsis and test how well the fall predicts death within a month. Platelets help blood clot and fight infection, and their slide is a known danger sign. Their 2026 study reviews more than three hundred sixty sepsis cases at one Beijing hospital, scoring the lowest count, the size of the drop, and when it happened.

Patients who died bottomed out far lower and dropped much further than survivors. Risk rose step by step with deeper and bigger drops. Timing mattered too: drops landing in the middle or late phase carried heavy risk, while early ones did not. Watching the whole platelet path, not a single reading, sharpens judgment at the bedside.
plos-pone-0348582:
Shangjun Piao and Jiantao Guo modelled how seafood buyers should run purchasing auctions when sellers may lie about where the fish was caught. Origin fraud distorts prices and punishes honest suppliers, and penalties alone deter weakly. The authors derived the outcomes of two auction designs, one judged on price only and one scoring quality and origin claims alongside price. Then they varied how much fraud and how much buyers care about true origin.

Counter to intuition, the plain price auction often served the buyer better, and its edge grew when buyers prized origin most and when detection technology existed alongside heavy fraud. Under some conditions, knowingly buying from cheap, low-value origins even suited the buyer. The authors argue auction design itself is a fraud-fighting tool, and that scoring systems can backfire by rewarding polished lies.
plos-pone-0348682:
Bayley Levy and co-workers set out a plan to review how research teams use implementation science frameworks in children's rehabilitation. Such frameworks help proven therapies actually reach clinics, yet their use in this field has never been mapped. Their 2026 protocol describes a scoping review across nine databases, covering English studies since two thousand six.

Two reviewers will screen and extract data independently, settling clashes by discussion or a third vote. Counts will summarize where and how frameworks were used, and text analysis will sort the purposes they served. As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet. The finished map should show which frameworks suit the teamwork-heavy world of pediatric rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0348782:
Tika B Adhikari, Frank J Louws, and co-authors sequenced the genomes of fifty strains of a fungus that has lately hammered strawberry crops with leaf spots and rots. Little genomic information existed for this emerging pathogen group. Their 2026 study, sampling major strawberry regions in North Carolina, mapped the strains' family relationships, their arsenals of plant-attacking proteins, and mutations tied to fungicide resistance.

Strains split into two lineages of one species plus a third distinct group. Each genome carried hundreds of enzymes for digesting plant walls and around ninety predicted effector proteins used to manipulate hosts. Resistance mutations were widespread for two fungicide classes, including one that defeats a common spray, while two other classes showed none. The authors say the catalogue can guide resistance-aware disease control.
plos-pone-0348882:
Raymond Vera, Anamaria Berea, and William G Kennedy built a computer simulation of a crewed lunar base to explore how astronaut teamwork and psychology might decide the fate of long Moon missions. NASA's Artemis program aims at a permanent lunar presence, where social friction cannot be escaped by coming home. Their 2026 model gives each simulated astronaut cognitive skills, emotional states, and personality traits, drawing on research from Antarctic stations and past spaceflight.

Running tens of thousands of simulated missions, the model varies outside shocks and inside group dynamics to find which factors tip a base toward sustainability or catastrophe. Settings cover a lunar gateway station and a south pole surface base. The authors offer the model as a benchmark planning tool for mission designers who must plan for people, not just hardware.
plos-pone-0349282:
Fatemeh Shakeri and four colleagues tested a new way to kill staph germs on living tissue, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Staphylococcus aureus infects wounds and resists many antibiotics. Cold atmospheric plasma, a stream of energized gas that stays near room temperature, can kill germs without heat.

Shakeri's team applied the plasma to staph colonies growing on living animal tissue and measured the effect. The test asks whether plasma can clear germs while sparing the tissue beneath. If it holds up, wound care could gain a tool that works where antibiotics fail. Plasma devices are already used in some clinics, so evidence on living tissue is a key step toward wider use.
plos-pone-0349582:
Jarosław Herbert and co-authors strapped motion sensors to more than five hundred Polish children aged five and six to compare how active they are at kindergarten and at home. Parents also reported family details such as education and income. Objective measurement matters here, since adults often guess wrong about how much young children actually move through the day.

Children gathered more gentle movement at kindergarten, but their harder, health-building activity ran higher at home, and daily step counts were higher at home too. Boys out-moved girls in both settings. Surprisingly, children from less advantaged families often moved more, not less. The authors say the home environment deserves as much attention as the classroom when adults try to keep young children active.
plos-pone-0349682:
Georgios Nalbantis and co-authors asked whether star employees help an organization more as deep specialists or as versatile generalists, and what happens when a star switches roles. They built a game-theory model to generate predictions, then tested them on professional basketball data, where stars and roles are easy to track. Their 2026 study also allowed stars to move between roles over time rather than fixing them in place.

Teams with generalist stars outperformed teams with specialist stars, matching the model. Moving a generalist into a specialist role always hurt performance, while moving a specialist toward a generalist role could help. The pattern held most clearly for teams built around a single star rather than several. The authors suggest managers should think twice before narrowing a star's remit.
plos-pone-0349782:
Napat Jantaraprasit and colleagues built a forecasting chain for oil palm harvests in Surat Thani, Thailand. Good forecasts guide farm work and long term climate planning, yet coarse weather grids and crop model bias blur accuracy. Their chain sharpens weather data to fine local scale, feeds a crop simulator, then lets a learning model mop up leftover errors.

The hybrid cut forecast error by more than half versus the simulator alone. Seasonal outlooks made with sharpened data matched those made with past observed weather, giving useful forecasts up to eight months ahead. Century scale outlooks hint at steady yields early on, a modest mid century dip, and later change. Growers gain lead time to plan labour, milling, and planting.
plos-pone-0349882:
Eranga Pawani Witharana and five colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies the plastome, the DNA of the chloroplast, in the plant subfamily Aurantioideae. From plastome evidence the authors also build a classification of Citrus, the genus of oranges, lemons, and their kin.

Plastome evolution tracks how this DNA changed as the group diversified, giving a family history written in genes. Citrus classification has long been tangled by hybridization, so a DNA-based scheme offers firmer ground. Botanists and citrus breeders both use such classifications, breeders because knowing true parentage guides new variety development.
plos-pone-0350182:
Jiangxue Tian, Handong Li, and Shuran Lv built a fire risk forecasting system for Beijing's urban villages in 2026. These dense settlements mix homes and workshops with weak infrastructure, making fire both likely and deadly.

Their model pairs a long memory neural network with an improved swarm search that tunes it, plus step by step updating so it learns from fresh incidents without full retraining. Fed with real fire records from fifty-five villages, it cut forecast error sharply against a plain network. City teams could use such forecasts to aim inspections and crews at the blocks most likely to burn next.
plos-pone-0350282:
Samuel Anyaso-Samuel and Mark Ramos asked American adults how well they think they understand statistics, using a nationally representative survey. Numbers steer choices about health, money, and public policy, yet many people meet terms like p-value with a blank stare. The authors used the survey to measure confidence and to ask whether people would use statistics more if the ideas were clearer.

About six in ten adults admitted they had little or no idea what statistics means. Even so, nine in ten said they would base decisions on reported statistics at least sometimes if they understood them better. Schooling raised confidence, while older generations rated themselves lower. People who felt more literate were also more willing to act on numbers. The gap points to a teaching problem, not a lack of interest.
plos-pone-0350382:
Chengfu Zhang and co-authors studied how rocks that generate oil and gas behave under different salt conditions in China's Dongpu Depression in 2026 work. Salt levels in the ancient lakes where the rocks formed vary sharply across the basin.

Twenty rock samples were analysed chemically, and three went through sealed tube heating experiments to extract generation rates. Basin modelling then combined those rates with the area's heat history. Salty environment rocks yielded the most hydrocarbons, fresh water rocks the least. Zones passing a set generation threshold were flagged as prime exploration targets. Salt, it turns out, is a friend to oil formation here.
plos-pone-0350782:
Jutamas Shaughnessy and colleagues built a compound that turns the gonorrhea germ's own camouflage against it. Their 2026 study starts from the germ's trick. It grabs human proteins that block the immune system, and hides behind them. The team fused the grabbing part of one blocker to an antibody tail. The tail was reshaped so six copies bunch up, boosting its grip.

The bunched compound killed gonorrhea germs in the dish. It was hundreds of times stronger than its single-copy earlier version. It also helped immune cells engulf the germs. Given into the vagina daily, it cut infections short in specially bred mice. Gonorrhea now resists nearly every drug, and no vaccine exists. A smear-on immune weapon is a truly new path, still at proof-of-concept stage.
plos-pone-0350882:
Tadanao Hiroki led a team of eight authors on this 2026 treatment study for chronic neck pain from tight, tender muscle tissue. Thirteen adults received an ultrasound-guided injection of salt water into the fascia around a neck artery, meant to loosen the tissue. Pain at rest and in motion, disability, and blood flow were checked before and after.

Movement pain dropped within fifteen minutes and stayed lower a week later. The procedure proved quick and safe in this small group. With no comparison group, Hiroki labels the results an early signal that larger controlled trials should test.
plos-pone-0350982:
Yvette Neema Ufoy Mungu and colleagues screened women in Kisangani, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for viruses linked to cervical cancer. The area also carries high rates of the sickle cell trait. More than seven hundred women gave cervical samples and answered health and life history questions, with lab tests for virus types and cell change.

Just over one quarter carried a high risk virus type. Three types led the list, and gene reading turned up two new variants. Major cell changes linked with factors the team modelled from survey and lab data together. In a region where cervical cancer leads gynaecology cancers, local virus maps help target vaccines and screening where they will count most.
plos-pone-0351082:
Van Thuy Tran and Huu Loc Nguyen ran lab tests on what makes bolt tightening fall short or overshoot. When a nut is tightened, only part of the turning force becomes clamping force. That share shifts with friction, surface roughness, and how hard the metal is. Getting it wrong can loosen joints or damage parts.

A curved model captured how the three factors interact. The team then searched for settings that keep the clamping share inside a safe band with very high certainty, using random trials plus an evolution style search. Their reliability based search beat plain best fit methods. Touchy factor checks showed which inputs matter most, giving builders a firmer way to set torque.
plos-pone-0351782:
Mark G Anderson led a team of five authors designing a freshwater refuge network, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. As the climate shifts, fish and other freshwater species must move to cooler or wetter refuges, but dams and dry reaches block them. The team mapped a network of waters that could stay livable and stay connected.

Anderson's blueprint shows conservation staff which streams and lakes to link and protect so species can shift as conditions change. Planning connections now is cheaper than rescue later. Freshwater life is declining faster than life on land or in the sea, yet it gets less attention. A ready map of resilient, connected waters gives funders and agencies a place to start.
plos-pone-0351882:
Emily Jakob and colleagues present a protocol for a scoping review on getting people with multiple sclerosis to move more. Exercise programs do help this group on average, but their effects swing widely from study to study. The reviewers suspect the missing piece is moderation: a program feature may help one subgroup and do little for another, depending on symptoms, setting, or support.

The planned review will search eight databases plus reference lists and citing papers, screening studies that report physical activity in people with the disease. Charts will lay out which populations and methods dominate, and a tree display will gather every reported moderation finding. As a protocol it contains no results. Its aim is practical: future programs should be matched to the people they actually help.
plos-pone-0352182:
Nicole Cranston and four colleagues present a research protocol, published in 2026, for a planned review of how young horses are weaned. Separating a foal from its mother is among the most stressful events in a young horse's life. Yet breeders still lack clear guidance on which methods cause the least harm.

The team plans to search six databases plus grey literature, screen studies with two independent reviewers, and compare weaning methods through pairwise and network analysis. Outcomes will cover body changes and behaviour, graded for bias and confidence. Because no results exist yet, the value lies in the careful plan itself, which aims to give horse owners evidence-based advice for gentler weaning.
plos-pone-0352282:
Shenzhen Ding and six colleagues coach platoons of connected vehicles through traffic lights. Their 2026 simulation study addresses jammed urban intersections. It assumes vehicles that talk to each other and to the lights. Groups of them, platoons, are recognised first. Six passage scenarios follow from whether a platoon will be blocked at the signal. Three guidance styles answer them: speed up, slow down, or split the platoon. A commercial traffic simulator staged the test junction.

Against unguided traffic, guidance cut everything that wastes time and fuel. Fuel consumption fell sharply. Delays shrank from over nine seconds to under four. Stops nearly vanished. Benefits grew clearer as the share of connected vehicles approached seventy percent. Below that share, mixed traffic dilutes the choreography. City engineers weighing smart-intersection investment gain a concrete threshold story: platoon guidance pays, but only once enough communicating cars fill the road.
plos-pone-0352382:
Kyoung Ae Kong studied where South Korean adults actually get their physical activity. National survey data covered thirty-two thousand adults. Activity was split into three domains: leisure, transport, and work. Each person's main domain was then tied to how healthy they rated themselves. South Korea reports some of the lowest activity levels in the world, so the pattern matters.

Under half the adults met the activity guidelines. About a third were nearly inactive. Among the active, transport was the main source for most people. Walking and cycling to get places carried the load. That pattern was strongest in women, older adults, and the barely active. Leisure exercise was a minority pursuit. Protecting everyday walking may matter more than preaching workouts.
plos-pone-0352582:
Zhu and colleagues tested walking with tight leg cuffs in inactive college students in a 2026 trial. Cuffs partly limit blood flow during easy exercise, a method meant to bring bigger training gains from gentle work. Sixty students each tried five-minute walks at four cuff pressure levels, in random order.

Only the middle-high pressure raised heart rate clearly more than no cuff, and the change stayed modest and safe for healthy young adults. Higher pressure felt harder and more uncomfortable, and students took fewer steps. The authors favor low to middle pressure as the sensible range, while noting that lasting health effects still need study.
plos-pone-0352682:
Adi Shuchami leads a team of six asking whether emergency departments repeat blood tests that community doctors just ran, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Children often arrive at the pediatric emergency department hours after a clinic blood draw, and the tests are frequently ordered again. Using records from a nationwide Israeli health organization, the team judged each repeat against preset criteria for whether it could change care, covering blood counts, electrolytes, and an inflammation marker.

Useful repeats were rare: roughly thirteen, sixteen, and nineteen percent for the three test families respectively. The rest consumed money, time, and children's comfort without guiding decisions. A standard gradient boosting model then learned to predict, from the community results and the child's background, whether a repeat was actually necessary. The authors propose decision support at the ordering screen, sparing most children a second needle while flagging the minority whose numbers genuinely need rechecking.
plos-pone-0352782:
Gao and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, improve how fleets of warehouse robots share work and plan routes. In warehouses with movable storage pods, robots often drive empty, respond slowly to new tasks, and crowd onto the same paths. Their approach joins task scheduling with live map planning instead of treating them apart.

Long trips are split into two stages: a haul across the warehouse, then a precise placement step, with different robot types suited to each stage. A pre-allocation trick lets a robot claim its next job before finishing the current one, cutting empty driving. Routes update on the fly, with a traffic control step for busy spots and a fast method for patching local paths. In a simulated multi-zone warehouse, the combined approach lowered empty running, eased congestion, and improved overall performance against standard practice. The authors present it as a template for busier automated warehouses.
plos-pone-0352882:
Osama Abdelrahman and five colleagues classify mental workload from brainwaves in this 2026 study. Knowing when an operator is overloaded matters in cockpits and operating theatres. Brainwave systems promise that knowledge, but noise and individual differences defeat many models. Their hybrid framework attacks all three weaknesses at once. An autoencoder cleans and compresses the signals. An attention module then spotlights the most informative channels and places. A memory network reads how the patterns unfold over time.

Tested with each person held out in turn, the system averaged about eighty-four percent accuracy. It sorted four workload levels and beat the baseline models overall. Removing any single component hurt performance, confirming each part earns its place. Tuning settled on ten-second windows as the sweet spot. Because the attention module can show what it focused on, the system explains itself better than most black boxes, a real virtue in safety-critical monitoring.
plos-pone-0352982:
Nila Kusumawati and five colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One survey of what rural Indonesian teenagers know, believe, and do about type 2 diabetes. The disease is rising among young people as lifestyles change, but rural adolescents have rarely been studied. The team questioned more than fifteen hundred high school seniors in Riau Province's Kampar Regency, during late 2024 and early 2025.

Students knew little about diabetes risk factors, symptoms, and complications, and their daily habits, especially physical activity, lagged behind their generally positive attitudes. Girls, students near towns, and those previously exposed to diabetes information scored higher. Knowledge alone was only weakly tied to healthy practice, so the authors favor school programs that pair information with peer support and routines that build habits.
plos-pone-0353182:
Zhong and colleagues tested frog-skin peptides against a deadly brain tumor in a 2026 study. In dish tests, the two peptides slowed tumor cell growth, raised a growth-control protein, and quieted a pathway that drives spread and blood vessel growth. Cell death came mainly through a programmed route.

In mice without working immune systems, the peptides changed immune cells inside tumors but did not shrink them. In mice given human immune cells, tumors shrank clearly, with more killer immune cells entering and a key immune brake lowered. The peptides thus seem to fight both directly and by rallying immunity, a dual action worth developing.
plos-pone-0353282:
Mohammad Alyetama and five colleagues published this 2026 data paper enriching a giant citizen science collection. Volunteers on iNaturalist post millions of mammal observations, shown as photos of living animals, carcasses, tracks, or droppings, but most posts never say which. The team trained machine learning to label the evidence type for well over a million North American mammal records.

Each record now carries a category and a confidence score. Knowing the evidence type helps scientists model how observations arise, for instance whether dead animals cluster near roads. The dataset is released for ecological reuse.
plos-pone-0353382:
Michael Rubinigg and colleagues introduce the Pollinator Ontology, a formal word list for describing pollinators and their links with plants, people, and the environment. It was built for the European Union's Pollinator Hub platform. Their 2026 paper defines the classes, properties, and links involved. These let databases across countries record bees, hoverflies, and their interactions in exactly the same terms.

The word list ships inside open-source software. It is designed to keep growing under community control. Its purposes are practical. Standardize pollinator data across borders, make datasets findable and reusable under FAIR principles, and end the chaos of every project inventing its own labels. Better shared data is a precondition for tracking pollinator decline and judging which rescue policies work.
plos-pone-0353482:
Fien Hermans and colleagues studied thirty-six patients with chronic lung disease. They asked whether moving more changes the nervous system's grip on the heart. That grip is a control system that often malfunctions in this illness. Their 2026 study measured heart rate patterns during sleep and recovery after a walking test. It tracked daily steps with accelerometers. Everything was re-measured after a six-month activity coaching program.

At baseline, faster heart recovery traveled with brisker walking and longer distance. Over the program, patients who added steps showed falling resting heart rates. They also showed healthier variability patterns. The clearest links sat in those not on beta-blocker drugs. The associations are modest, not dramatic. But they suggest everyday activity, not just formal training, may retune the heart's control system.
plos-pone-0353782:
Kalafat and colleagues tested three AI chat tools on children's elbow X-rays in a 2026 study. The injury studied, a break just above the elbow, is common in children and can harm nerves and blood flow if missed. Records covered three hundred children seen at a city hospital in Turkey, half with the break and half without.

Each tool saw the same images three times on different days. Answers were fairly steady for two tools and less steady for the third. Sorting breaks by severity grade worked best for one tool, yet overall skill stayed limited. The authors warn these tools are not ready to judge such breaks alone and need training built for children's bones.
plos-pone-0353882:
Man-Fung Yuen and five colleagues model a cheaper way to watch for liver cancer in Hong Kong, in this 2026 PLOS ONE health-economics study. People with chronic hepatitis B or cirrhosis need regular checks, usually ultrasound plus a blood marker, but ultrasound slots are scarce. The alternative pairs that same marker with a second blood protein that rises when vitamin K is absent — a combination needing no scan appointment.

In their simulation the blood-only strategy caught more cancers at an early, treatable stage and produced fewer false alarms. It also gained a sliver of healthy life per person while saving money. The benefit was clearest for hepatitis B patients without cirrhosis, who often wait longest for scans.
plos-pone-0354082:
Tang and colleagues set out a pilot plan in 2026 to add hearing checks to a meal delivery service in Australia. Many older adults live with hearing loss that no one has found or treated. Under the plan, trained meal volunteers and hearing students will visit clients at home with a small ear scope and a tablet hearing test.

Visitors will also teach basic ear care and refer people who need fuller testing. The pilot will judge how well the visits work in practice, how clients respond, and what the service costs to run. Using a trusted home service could reach older people who rarely visit clinics, making hearing care fairer for those with few options nearby.
plos-pone-0354382:
AK Kakkar led a team of eight authors on this 2026 global study of heart rhythm patients who go without blood thinners despite stroke risk. The GARDENIA registry enrolled just over seven hundred high-risk atrial fibrillation patients with bleeding concerns across many centers, and recorded why anticoagulants were withheld and what happened over follow-up.

Past major bleeding, doctors' fear of bleeding, and patient refusal topped the reasons. Modeling suggested treatment would have cut strokes and deaths by more than it raised bleeding. Enrollment lagged, ending the study early. Kakkar urges rethinking blanket caution.
plos-pone-0354482:
Qin Qin and co-authors investigated a nucleus-anchor protein, Nesprin-1, in drug-induced heart failure in mice. The protein ties the cell nucleus to the skeleton, and its role in failing hearts was unsettled. Their 2026 study induced failure with daily injections of a stimulating drug for over three weeks and confirmed the model with scans and tissue markers.

The team measured heart chamber sizes and pumping fractions by ultrasound. Staining and protein checks tracked the anchor protein, a gap-junction partner, DNA damage signs, and gene-silencing marks. Oxidative stress gauges and a growth signalling pathway completed the panel. Qin and colleagues frame Nesprin-1 as a candidate link between nuclear strain and the failing heart's electrical and structural decay.
plos-pone-0354682:
Firdaus Aziz led a team of seven authors on this 2026 study predicting which Malaysian patients skip their prescribed medicines. Patients with diabetes, high blood pressure, or high cholesterol answered questions about their background, treatment, and beliefs in complementary and alternative medicine. The team trained a dozen standard algorithms plus blended ensembles on the survey answers.

A stacked model that combined several algorithms performed best, and a chosen cutoff sorted patients into lower and higher risk of skipping doses. Aziz argues that adding cultural beliefs to the data sharpens prediction and helps clinics target support instead of wasting medicine.
plos-pone-0354882:
Yuxi Xie and five colleagues published this 2026 computer study of a medicinal plant, Centella asiatica, and diseases that destroy the brain. The plant is eaten and used as medicine, with hints it calms brain inflammation. The team combined network analysis, gene data, machine learning, and molecule docking to shortlist its active ingredients.

Sixteen plant compounds passed filters for drug-like behavior and reaching the brain, pointing at hundreds of possible targets. Shared targets across Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Huntington's diseases were checked against patient data. Xie is clear these are candidates for lab testing, not proven treatments.
plos-pone-0354982:
Eshetu Mekonnen and four colleagues published this 2026 study of a traditional Ethiopian medicinal plant, Ehretia cymosa. Healers use its leaves for wound infections, fever, stomach ulcers, and toothache, but proof was scarce. The team made a leaf extract with methanol, tested it on bacteria in dishes, and treated infected burns in mice.

The extract slowed common infection bacteria in the lab and helped infected burns close faster in mice, especially against staph germs. Chemical screening found flavonoids, tannins, and similar plant compounds. Mekonnen says the results back traditional use and justify isolating the active ingredients.
plos-pone-0355282:
XiaCheng Song and co-authors survey humanities undergraduates in China about working with generative AI on creative and study tasks. The question is not just whether students hand work to the tool, but what kind of handing-over helps. Borrowing a trigger-response model, the team asked several hundred students how the tools feel to use, how much control they keep, and how confident they feel about future tasks.

Features students liked were tied to healthy offloading, the kind that frees effort, and to a stronger sense of control and self-belief. Those states, in turn, tracked with richer joint creation and more confidence ahead. Reliance that felt dependent showed no such gains once the other states were counted. Song and colleagues advise teaching productive use, not mere use.
plos-pone-0355382:
Shan Yan and colleagues assessed in 2026 the quality of colored rice varieties, pairing practical grain measures with a profile of their pigments. Colored rice, with red, black, or purple grains, draws interest for its looks and for the pigments linked to nutritional value. Judging such varieties fairly means measuring eating and milling quality alongside the chemistry that gives them their color.

The team combines an integrated quality assessment with pigment profiling across the varieties studied. That pairing lets breeders and buyers see whether the most colorful grains are also the best to grow and eat. As demand for specialty rice grows, grounded comparisons like this help farmers choose varieties that command a premium without sacrificing yield or taste.
plos-pone-0355482:
Benjamin Asare and co-authors build in 2026 local formulas for estimating wood volume and above ground weight of a fast growing tree planted in Ghana's Kwahu Highlands. Crews measured trunk width, height, and crown shape on dozens of trees, then cut and weighed a smaller sample. Several formula shapes were tried against the real values.

Formulas that used trunk width, total height, and wood density together fit best for both volume and weight. Simpler formulas using only width and height were fair for volume but off for weight. Better local formulas, the authors argue, make carbon counts for such plantations more trustworthy for climate reporting.
plos-pone-0355682:
Azeze Wubie Kassa and seven colleagues evaluate black cumin varieties for Ethiopia's Amhara Region in this 2026 field study. Black cumin seed is a valued spice and medicine, yet regional yields trail the national average because improved varieties are scarce. The team grew eighteen promising genotypes plus two standard varieties at three sites over two seasons, measuring yield, quality, and how consistently each line performed when conditions changed.

Environment drove more than half of the yield differences, which is exactly why stability matters. Two genotypes stood out for combining top yields with steadiness across sites and years, beating the standard varieties by a clear margin. One of them also carried good levels of the seed's prized oil extract. That line was released for commercial production in 2024 under the name Tena, and the authors recommend it for similar growing zones.
plos-pone-0356182:
Wei Xu and coauthors published a 2026 materials study in PLOS ONE on coating aviation titanium alloy with a titanium-aluminum layer using selective laser melting. A laser fuses powder into a hard protective skin. Surface quality of titanium parts decides safety in service, yet no clear guidance existed on the best laser power for this coating. The team varied power across a narrow band and examined the coatings' structure, phases, chemistry, and hardness.

Power proved decisive. At the two lower settings, long cracks ran through the coating and bonding to the base metal was poor, risking peeling. At the middle setting the coating bonded cleanly with no obvious defects, formed new strengthening phases, and reached the highest hardness measured. One step higher, cracks returned and performance fell. The authors offer the middle setting, and the reasoning behind it, as a reference point for coating titanium parts in aerospace manufacturing.
plos-pone-0356382:
Timothy Mulvany and seven colleagues test how the way a tumor is outlined on a scan affects computerized measurements used to diagnose children's brain tumors, in this 2026 study. Radiomics extracts numbers from MRI scans that machine learning can turn into diagnoses, but humans draw tumor boundaries differently. Using scans from just over one hundred young patients, the team shrank and expanded expert-drawn outlines to imitate cautious and generous drawing, then watched what happened to the measurements.

Expanding outlines disturbed nearly all measurements, and far more than shrinking them did. Diagnosis models trained on expert outlines lost accuracy under either change, but less when training included the altered outlines and only the steadiest measurements. The authors advise that when boundaries are ambiguous, leaving doubtful tissue out beats including it, and that model builders should plan for drawing variation from the start.
plos-pone-0356482:
Lisha Zou and three colleagues build a decision aid for the earliest stage of drug discovery in this 2026 paper. Virtual screening ranks thousands of molecules against a disease target, but labs can only afford to test a shortlist, and raw ranking scores say little about how much to trust them. Their package, TASC-VS, adds test-time adaptation, statistical calibration, and uncertainty-aware ranking to turn ranked lists into fixed-budget choices.

On a curated fifteen-target benchmark, the full package beat a strong comparator on enrichment and on the quality of its top twenty picks, though some gains lost significance after strict statistical correction. A separate stress test on another benchmark favored the simpler rival. The authors are frank about the limits: the method offers calibrated shortlist support on the tested subset, and broader use needs fresh validation.
plos-pone-0356782:
Maria Hjorth and Anna Forsberg report a qualitative study, published in 2026, on setting up nurse-led follow-up care for people with liver cirrhosis. Six clinics tried the new arrangement, and the researchers interviewed nurses, doctors, and managers repeatedly over several years of rollout. Their analysis looked for what helped the change take hold and what got in its way.

They found just over twenty influencing factors, split almost evenly between barriers and supports. Staff shortages, unclear roles, and weak leadership support hindered the work. Some staff also felt a moral strain when patients who needed the extra care could not all receive it under the trial's random assignment. On the positive side, the follow-up was seen as safe and worthwhile, and managers who backed the nurses strengthened their standing in the team. Simple tasks nurses could own outright worked best.
plos-pone-0356882: Iqra and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study in pure mathematics. They prove new Newton-type inequalities, bounds named for a classic rule for estimating integrals. The work covers a class of curved functions shaped by a hyperbolic form, using fractional integrals of the Riemann-Liouville type. Number checks back up the proofs. Such bounds help scientists estimate quantities that cannot be computed exactly.
plos-pone-0357382:
Xuan Wang and coauthors published a 2026 paper in PLOS ONE on shrinking three-dimensional animation files so they stream and render smoothly on modest devices. Animation data is bulky and repeats heavily between frames, but older compressors cut it into blocks with sloppy boundaries and leave redundancy behind. Their scheme tidies scattered vertex data with an improved clustering method, carves the animation into blocks adapting to how the scene moves, and polishes the result with boundary editing and matrix reorganization.

Across four datasets, the optimized algorithm compressed files to roughly a seventh of original size, beating a leading comparison method widely while cutting reconstruction error substantially and keeping structural similarity high. On mobile devices, loading times fell by over two thirds and rendering frame rates rose by nearly half. The method is presented as practical support for virtual reality, games, and digital twins on limited hardware.
plos-pone-0357482:
Sangrak Son and colleagues trial a smart watering system that feeds liquid organic fertilizer to greenhouse lettuce only when plants seem to need it. Organic fertilizer costs a lot, so feeding on a fixed calendar wastes money. Cameras measured leaf canopy size every few days and shared data online. In the smart beds, a sensor switch ran the pump only when canopy growth lagged behind hand-fed beds by a set margin.

Lettuce weight and leaf area ended up nearly equal in both setups. The fixed schedule, however, used about four times as many feeding events and left far more unused nutrients in the growing mix. Son and colleagues say growth-guided feeding can cut fertilizer bills sharply while keeping yields, a useful result for small greenhouse growers.
plos-pone-0357782:
Elena García-López and Fabrice B. R. Parmentier published a 2026 experiment in PLOS ONE on how an unexpected sound distracts people in the middle of a task. In their setup, volunteers identified where a visual target appeared while tones played in the background, most of them standard and a few rare and deviant. The key question was whether a deviant sound affects a person differently when the correct next action repeats the previous one versus when it changes.

Deviant sounds slowed people when the response repeated, in both the two-choice and four-choice versions. That braking effect did not depend on how many choices were available. The same sounds sped up response changes, though, and that benefit shrank when the choice set grew. The split suggests distraction works through two mechanisms: one inhibiting action repetition, one helping switching, with only the second sensitive to context.
plos-pone-0358182: Feng and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on diabetic retinopathy, an eye disease that can blind people with diabetes. They hunted for new marker genes tied to two cell stresses: low oxygen and a copper-driven cell death called cuproptosis. They then probed how those markers might drive the disease. Fresh markers could lead to earlier tests for a condition often found late.
plos-pone-0358482: Mutuyimana and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how suffering is voiced in Eastern Africa. They built a new survey, a Cultural Scripts of Trauma Inventory, tuned to local ways of expressing pain after trauma. Imported surveys can miss local idioms of distress. A tool built from local scripts can help counselors hear what patients truly mean.
plos-pone-0358882:
Matthew Wassall and colleagues worked in 2026 on telling apart the activities of people who use lower limb prostheses, using motion sensors worn in everyday life. Knowing whether a prosthesis user is walking, climbing stairs, sitting, or standing matters for judging how well the device serves them. Laboratory tests capture only a slice of that life, so the team used inertial sensing, the motion tracking built into small wearable devices, under real world conditions.

The study builds classification methods that read those sensor streams and sort them into activities. Reliable real world measurement would let clinicians see how a prosthesis performs across weeks, not minutes. It could also guide better fitting and fairer comparisons between devices.
plos-pone-0359282: Özel and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE trial on easing pain after open-heart surgery. A cut through the breastbone, called a median sternotomy, leaves strong pain as it heals. The trial tested elastic therapeutic taping, sticky bands meant to support tissue and ease pain. Patients were assigned at random to taping or standard care. A cheap, drug-free aid would be welcome after such major surgery.
plos-pone-0359782:
Peter Oloche David published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It proposes the Genomic Equity Accessibility Framework, shortened to GEAF. The framework models what such therapies cost people and how fairly they are shared: genomic and regenerative treatments, built on genes and lab-grown tissues, that often carry very high prices.

The author stresses that the framework's measures are built to fit together in a disciplined way. Such a model gives policymakers a structured way to ask who can actually get these therapies and who is priced out. Health economists and access advocates are the readers for a tool built on fairness.
pmc-11223882:
Madeira, Madhusoodanan, Lee, and co-authors describe the 2024 state of the Job Dispatcher tools at EMBL-EBI. Their framework gives scientists free access to popular programs for analysing DNA, RNA, and protein sequences. Users reach the tools through a shared web service rather than installing each program alone.

Along with the tools, the service supplies the sequence datasets those programs need. That pairing lets a researcher run a standard analysis even without local computing power. Keeping such shared services current matters more each year, as sequence data grows faster than most single labs can handle.
pmc-13235882:
Lin and colleagues offer a new way to estimate how much charge an electric vehicle battery holds. That figure, the state of charge, is a core reading in any battery management system. Guessing it wrong shortens range estimates and can harm the battery, so carmakers need methods that stay accurate as conditions change.

The team pairs a temporal convolutional network, a neural model built for time series, with an Unscented Kalman Filter. The network learns patterns in the battery's recent history; the filter then steadies the output and cuts its wobble. Tested on lithium-ion batteries, the combined method aims at accuracy with smooth, trustworthy readings a driver can rely on.
pmc-13240982:
Lebrecht's team at Imperial College London gauged what sets winning human-like virtual influencers apart on Instagram. The dataset covered 157 female virtual profiles, all large accounts. Coders scored realism, identity steadiness, and whether real humans appeared alongside. Reach and like rates were weighed across images and videos.

Bigger accounts led the top content, mainly on video. Among the top clips, openly computer-made personas outnumbered realistic ones. Nearly four in five top accounts kept a stable look and consistent story. The authors conclude tidy, legibly virtual personas engage fans better than realism alone.
pmc-13241382:
Lenga and colleagues at Heidelberg asked whether one quick status question can track recovery after lumbar spine surgery. Two hundred fifty-seven patients answered mobile surveys every two to three days. Six weeks produced one thousand six hundred twenty-seven postoperative check-ins. The single Global Postoperative Status score was tested against pain and medication diaries.

Worse status scores lined up consistently with heavier pain burden. Patients reporting frequent pain peaks scored far lower than pain-free peers. Scores also dropped stepwise as painkillers escalated to combined opioid regimens. The authors stress this is exploratory validity only, pending prospective confirmation.
pmc-13241582:
Lahiri's team at the University of Florida tested whether camera trap orientation changes which animals get recorded at carrion sites. Carrion feeds both vertebrate scavengers and invertebrates, yet most designs target one group. The team deployed horizontal and vertical cameras across 17 carrion placements. The site was Panther Swamp National Wildlife Refuge in Mississippi.

Both designs tallied similar total richness, but the species lists differed sharply. Vertical cameras caught more flesh-eating invertebrates, including blow flies and carrion beetles. Horizontal cameras, with their wider view, recorded more white-tailed deer wandering past. The authors advise pairing both orientations to capture the whole carrion food web.
pmc-13242382:
Söylemez's team at Mersin profiled circular RNAs in the blood of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy patients. Forty-one patients faced 41 matched healthy controls. Five candidate circRNAs were measured by PCR after RNase treatment. The study is the first to test these rings in this epilepsy syndrome.

Two circRNAs ran sharply high in patient blood; a third ran low. Two others showed no difference between groups. The high and low markers both tracked drug resistance. Sex-split patterns emerged too, hinting at marker promise worth follow-up testing. All were blood-based tests, with blood drawn from both groups.
pmc-13242482:
Yusuf Sülek and co-authors asked whether longer spinal fusions speed up wear in the hip and knee. Their cohort study appeared in the Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery in 2026. They reviewed patients aged forty to sixty-five who had lumbar surgery between 2010 and 2021 at one center. Groups ranged from decompression without fusion to fusions spanning four or more vertebrae, and joint space was tracked on imaging.

Hip joint space narrowed fastest in the long-fusion group, then the short-fusion group, then the no-fusion group. Each added fused level raised the odds of severe hip narrowing, while knee wear showed no clear difference between groups. Back and hip function scores were recorded alongside the imaging. The authors advise closer hip monitoring for patients who receive extensive fusions, so degeneration is caught early. The pattern fits the idea that a stiffer spine shifts load onto the hips.
pmc-13243882:
An Huang, Haopeng Hong, and Yonghui Sun profiled colon cancers by the side of the bowel they grow on, layering genes, proteins, and protein switches. Their study appeared in MedComm in 2026. Left-sided and right-sided tumors arise from different embryonic tissue and already behave differently in the clinic. The team ran exome, protein, and phosphoprotein sequencing on eighty tumor-and-normal tissue pairs to find out why.

Left-sided cancers were driven mainly by chromosomal instability and grew dense in blood vessels. Right-sided cancers leaned on microsatellite instability instead, a scrambling caused by failed DNA repair. Their immune neighborhoods also split: right-sided tumors showed stronger antigen display by M1 macrophages. The share of repair-deficient tumors reaching instability differed by side too. The authors argue these differences explain why targeted and immune therapies land unevenly, and they offer the atlas for tailoring treatment by tumor side.
pmc-13244382:
Molly Milano, Alec Giakas, and Eric Tecce describe a spinal abscess that crushed the cord and then starved it of blood. Their case report appeared in Case Reports in Surgery in 2026. A man in his sixties came to the emergency department with sudden paralysis of both legs and intense lower back pain. Imaging placed the damage at the fourth thoracic level, where an epidural abscess was compressing the cord and a secondary cord infarction had followed.

Spinal cord infarction is uncommon and its outlook for recovery is generally poor, with causes that often stay murky.
