The authors walk through the hospital course to show how the two injuries compounded each other. Published guidance for such cases is thin, and their report adds one fully told case to a sparse literature. For emergency teams the lesson is speed: back pain with sudden leg paralysis is a surgical clock.
pmc-13245082:
Li and co-authors published this short correction notice in Molecular Medicine in 2026. It amends their 2025 paper on how alpha-synuclein clumps abnormally in the brain during repeated low-oxygen episodes, and how a compound called Danshensu methyl ester may protect nerve cells from that damage.

pmc-13246982:
Coniglio and co-authors mined sawmill waste for antifungal chemistry in this 2026 Bioresources and Bioprocessing study. In Uruguay, Pinus taeda plantations feed a large timber industry whose knot-rich offcuts are usually discarded, yet knots concentrate the tree's defensive compounds. The team extracted those compounds with ethanol, tuning temperature, alcohol strength, and solvent ratio to find the best recipe.

Optimized extractions recovered about a fifth of the knotwood's weight, rich in phenolic antioxidants, mainly stilbenes and terpenoids. In laboratory assays the extracts strongly slowed two wood-rotting fungi, nearly stopping one of them within a week. The authors present knotwood residue as a realistic feedstock for natural wood preservatives, turning a disposal problem into a product within a circular bioeconomy.
pmc-13247182:
Seas wrote this 2026 editorial in Open Forum Infectious Diseases. It introduces a journal supplement on managing infectious diseases where resources are scarce. Infections still claim a huge share of global disability and death, concentrated in low- and middle-income countries. The supplement gathers studies on practical responses, from antibiotic stewardship to HIV and tuberculosis care.

The previews include a stewardship program in a Botswana children's surgical unit. They also cover telehealth supporting stewardship in the rural United States, long-acting HIV prevention and shorter tuberculosis regimens in Peru, artificial intelligence reading chest X-rays for tuberculosis, and mobile clinics preventing mother-to-child HIV transmission in Mozambique. The editorial's message is that progress combines simple clinical tools, digital innovation, and community education.
pmc-13248482:
Paudyal and co-authors tested machine learning for spotting hidden udder infection in dairy cows, published in 2026. Subclinical mastitis shows no obvious signs yet lowers milk quality, and cell counts in milk are the usual clue. The team combined heat camera images of udders with milk measurements from one hundred ninety-four Holstein cows.

Sampling each quarter of the udder gave nearly eight hundred data points. A random forest model using both image and milk features reached strong accuracy, with milk lactose among the strongest signals. Heat images alone performed noticeably worse. The authors say combined data looks promising, but larger studies must confirm the approach before farm use.
pmc-13249582:
Wen and co-authors sequenced the full mitochondrial genome of a rare Chinese shrew, in a 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. Sorex cansulus lives only in China and is classed as near threatened. The team described the animal's form and its mitochondrial DNA, then compared forty-three shrew species across the five tribes of the red-toothed shrew subfamily.

Selection, not chance, had shaped most of the genome's protein-coding genes, and all ran under strong pressure to stay unchanged. Family trees backed several name changes, including splitting this shrew from a close relative as its own species. Three other species shared an odd extra transfer RNA gene, forming their own branch and raising questions about its function.
pmc-13250182:
Khachidze and co-authors chart falling birth rates in the country of Georgia and project where they lead. Their 2026 BMJ Open study uses national statistics and the national birth registry, covering well over half a million births from 2014 to 2024. The team modeled past trends and forecast the decade ahead.

Fertility fell from a little over two children per woman to well under two across the study years. The steepest drops came among teenagers and women in their early twenties, while mothers grew older on average. If recent trends hold, the models project fertility near one child per woman by 2034. The authors warn that this shift could strain Georgia's economy and its social systems in coming years.
pmc-13250382:
Amito and colleagues survey malaria parasites in northern Uganda for gene changes tied to drug resistance. Their 2026 Journal of Parasitology Research study enrolled fever patients at Gulu Regional Referral Hospital between April 2022 and January 2024. Parasite DNA was sequenced for resistance genes in the multidrug and kelch families.

Among three hundred fifty-three recruits, about three in five carried falciparum malaria, confirmed by rapid tests, microscopy, and genetic checks. Fever, chills, and headache dominated the reported symptoms. Resistance-linked variants were widespread, including changes in the kelch gene associated with artemisinin resistance in about one sixth of isolates. The authors urge ongoing monitoring of these markers to protect malaria control in the region and beyond.
pmc-13250882:
Sun and co-authors examine a long non-coding RNA that seems to protect kidneys in diabetes. Their 2026 Renal Failure study compares samples from about one hundred diabetes patients and a similar number with diabetic kidney disease. The RNA, called LINC00472, also gets tested in kidney cells stressed by high sugar.

Levels of the RNA ran low in kidney disease patients and in sugar-stressed cells, and they tracked closely with kidney function measures. Adding extra copies calmed the cells, cutting scarring genes and inflammatory signals. A small partner RNA reversed those gains when boosted, and a signaling gene downstream completed the chain. The authors propose the RNA as both a diagnostic marker and a possible treatment lever for the disease.
pmc-13262582:
Alimujiang Yusufu and colleagues show that where bone cement lands inside a crushed vertebra decides how well the repair works. Vertebroplasty injects cement through a needle to stabilize osteoporotic fractures. Their 2026 review of one hundred forty-five first-time patients sorts X-rays by cement coverage into three groups.

One year on, patients whose cement spread widest or crossed the spine's midline reported the least pain. Their vertebrae also regained more height and refractured less often. Scanty coverage lagged on every measure. Pushing beyond two-thirds coverage added nothing further, giving surgeons a clear target: cross the middle, then stop.
pmc-13313082:
This 2026 letter by Öztürk comments on a study of blood inflammation indices in thyroid nodules. The original paper compared three combined blood counts as clues to whether a nodule is cancerous. Öztürk praises the comparison but questions how the authors judged the indices' value for predicting outcomes. Simple correlation tests, he argues, cannot show independent predictive power.

He notes the study ran no receiver operating analyses and no adjusted regression models for outcomes such as spread to lymph nodes. His own study of 376 patients with thyroid cancer found one index did predict distant spread and high risk category independently. The monocyte count alone also tracked stage and spread. Öztürk concludes the indices may flag aggressive cancers rather than diagnose them, and the original null result may reflect method limits.
pmc-13342482:
Lelou and colleagues investigated in 2026 how stress hormones called catecholamines, the family that includes adrenaline, act on liver cancer cells. Nerves of the sympathetic system, the body's fight-or-flight wiring, reach into liver tumors, but their direct effect on tumor cells was unclear. The team mapped nerve fibers in ten human tumor samples and tested the hormones on liver cell lines and on primary human liver cells.

Dense, twisted sympathetic fibers crowded the non-tumor tissue at the tumor's invasion front. Mature liver-like tumor cells carried both receptor types for these hormones and broke the hormones down into known waste products. Exposure switched on inflammation, growth, and tissue-remodeling programs tied to loss of mature identity and to a shift that helps cells spread. The same program marked aggressive tumor subtypes with poor outlook. The authors suggest blocking this nerve signal as a new treatment angle.
pmc-13367082:
Ozaki and colleagues report real-world outcomes for Japanese patients taking abemaciclib after surgery for early breast cancer, in 2026 oncology research using a claims database. The drug, a cell-cycle blocker, is added to hormone therapy for two years. It goes to patients whose cancer is hormone receptor-positive and HER2-negative, types describing hormone and growth-signal response. Records covered patients starting treatment between December 2021 and November 2024 across Japan.

Of 2,042 eligible patients, 439 were followed for at least two years, with a median age of 55 years and 99.3 percent of them women. Of those with full follow-up, 70.6 percent completed the full two years of abemaciclib plus hormone therapy as planned. A further group, 21.9 percent, stopped the drug but continued hormone therapy alone, while 7.5 percent stopped both within two years. Most of the patients, 92.3 percent, started at the full 300 milligram daily dose, and 58.3 percent needed a dose reduction.
pmc-13388882:
Kibirige and colleagues argue that precision diabetes care in low-resource settings should be built from bedside observation rather than imported lab tools, in a 2026 review. Such care classifies patients into true subtypes and tailors treatment. Rich countries achieve it with genomics, biomarker panels, and AI tools. Africa faces rising diabetes, missed cases, and unusual illness patterns, yet those tools remain unavailable across the region. Miscalls between type 1, type 2, and other types lead to wrong treatment and outcomes.

Their proposal: structured clinical sorting from routinely collected traits: age at onset, body mass index, how the illness showed, family history, and other conditions. Combined carefully, these data points can separate types well enough to guide insulin decisions, drug choice, and monitoring. Kibirige presents the approach as cost-effective, avoiding overreliance on advanced tests and systems that services cannot sustain. The review maps which traits signal which type, giving clinicians an algorithm.
pmc-13392782:
Park and co-authors study, in 2026, how wide-bandgap transparent conducting oxides affect kesterite thin-film solar cells. These oxide layers must let light through while carrying electric current, a balancing act that shapes cell output. The team tested zinc oxide compounds doped with magnesium and group III elements, measuring carrier levels, mobility, and light transmission, then built solar cells with each material and recorded their output.

Every oxide film transmitted more than 80 percent of visible light on average in the measurements reported. The magnesium- and gallium-codoped zinc oxide stood out, reaching the widest bandgap, measured at 3.82 electron volts, together with strong electrical properties. Cells using it gained roughly 10 percent in quantum efficiency at short wavelengths, gathered charge better, and lost less energy at interfaces. Open-circuit voltage stayed flat across materials, while current density and fill factor followed the oxide's quality.
pmc-13394782:
Lin and team build, in 2026, tiny hydrogel beads that respond to stress inside arthritic joints to control TGF-beta1, a growth factor whose abnormal activation harms cartilage in osteoarthritis. Healthy joint tissue needs this factor, so blocking it everywhere causes harm. Their beads carry weak disulfide bonds that snap under stress. That flips the charge of attached nanoparticles from negative to positive, exactly where overload switches on the growth factor.

In tests, the stress-matched system improved repair of worn cartilage lesions by 41.96 percent compared with standard beads that release their payload evenly. Just as important, its impact on healthy tissue fell by 96.89 percent versus the standard design. Because stressed regions got stronger control while quiet regions were largely left alone, the approach worked efficiently with little side harm. The authors frame the design as a model for materials that match a tissue's diseased setting.
pmc-13396182:
Avdeeva and co-authors present, in 2026, ArchVelo, a program for charting how cells change over time from single-cell measures of gene activity and chromatin access. Snapshots cannot show motion directly, so trajectory methods infer it. ArchVelo treats chromatin access as archetypes, shared regulatory programs whose shifting weight drives transcription. That lets it split each cell's path into readable parts and name the transcription factors involved.

In benchmarks on mouse brain and blood-formation datasets, ArchVelo beat existing methods on trajectory accuracy and on aligning latent time gene by gene. Applied to CD8 T cells during viral infection, it separated paths of differentiation and growth among the immune cells. Within progenitor exhausted T cells, the cells that sustain immunity, it traced the path from Ccr6-negative to Ccr6-positive ones, a route shared between acute and chronic infections. The authors offer ArchVelo for multi-omic studies across biology.

Hagan and co-authors project, in 2026, how the coupling between soil moisture and air temperature, a feedback that intensifies droughts and heatwaves, will shift under future emissions. Hotspots were regions where at least 70 percent of models agreed the coupling strength exceeded the threshold, and the answer depended on the emissions path chosen.

Under the low-emissions SSP1-2.6 scenario, coupling expanded across all historical hotspots, broadly preserving today's pattern. Under the high-emissions SSP5-8.5 scenario, a latitudinal contrast appeared: coupling weakened and contracted at low-to-mid northern latitudes but strengthened at higher latitudes, with emerging hotspots across mid-to-high-latitude North America and northern Europe. Coupling also strengthened in the humid southern tropics, where evaporation outpaced precipitation gains. Mary Rowlandson wrote her captivity account after Native warriors seized her in a raid on Lancaster in colonial New England. The title page calls the work a display of God's rule and care, written by her own hand. It opens on February 10, 1675, with houses burning at sunrise and neighbors killed or carried away.

Rowlandson spent about eleven weeks as a prisoner before ransom freed her. Grief for her dead child runs through pages shaped by deep Puritan faith. Printed in 1682, her book was the first by an Englishwoman in America. It sold widely and set the pattern for the captivity narrative.
rubaiyat-khayyam-whinfield-1882:
E. H. Whinfield published his Quatrains of Omar Khayyam in 1882, in Trubner's Oriental Series, with the Persian text and English verse on facing terms. Where Fitzgerald had chosen and reshaped a hundred quatrains into a famous poem, Whinfield gives all five hundred. His version is the full scholarly alternative, with introduction and notes.

Wine, roses, brief life, and the turning heavens fill quatrain after quatrain. Some praise pleasure; others mock the learned and the pious alike. Readers can watch Khayyam's thought range wider than Fitzgerald's selection suggests. Whinfield, an Indian civil servant and Persian scholar, translated closely rather than freely. Students still set his completeness beside Fitzgerald's art.
saint-martin-tableau-naturel-1782:
Saint-Martin published his Tableau naturel in 1782, seven years after his first book made him the Unknown Philosopher. Its full subject is the natural relations among God, man, and the universe. The work is the mature statement of Martinist theosophy, the cornerstone of the French esoteric revival that followed him.

Man stands between God and nature in Saint-Martin's scheme, able to read both. Signs in the physical world answer to truths in the spiritual one. His tableau sets those correspondences in plain order. The book ripens the thought of Des Erreurs into a system. Generations of French occultists studied it as a master text of their tradition.
sarva-darsana-samgraha-cowell-gough-1882:
E. B. Cowell and A. E. Gough translated Madhava's Sarva-Darsana-Samgraha in 1882, a learned review of India's systems of thought. Madhavacharya, a fourteenth-century scholar and minister, surveys sixteen schools in rising order of truth as he sees it. Materialists, Buddhists, Jains, and the great Hindu systems each get a fair, careful statement of their claims and proofs.

The survey climbs toward the author's own Advaita Vedanta, which the last chapter crowns above the rest. Few books let a reader compare Indian philosophies in their own terms so compactly and so clearly. The translation remains a standard guide to the darsanas, the viewpoints that shaped India's intellectual history for centuries.
sbe-17-vinaya-texts-2-1882:
Book Seventeen of the Sacred Books of the East came out in 1882. It holds Part Two of the Vinaya Texts in the dress of Rhys Davids and Oldenberg. The Vinaya is the rule book of the monks of the Buddha. Part One gave the core rules and the first books of the Mahavagga.

Here the Mahavagga runs from Book Five to Book Ten. The Kullavagga then starts, with Books One to Three in this part. Rules deal with dress, food, the rains rest, and strife in the host. The book is a dry text with rich worth for the tale of the faith.
shufeldt-treaty-1882:
Commodore Robert Shufeldt negotiated the 1882 treaty between the United States and the Kingdom of Korea, then called Chosen. Korea had long limited contact with the outside world and was known in the West as the Hermit Kingdom. Signed in May 1882, with ratifications exchanged at Seoul a year later, it was Korea's first treaty with a Western nation.

The articles promised lasting peace and friendship, opened Korean ports to American trade, and set rules for ships and merchants. One clause said the United States would use its good offices if another power treated Korea unjustly. Within decades Japan took control of Korea anyway, but the treaty marked America's first formal step onto the peninsula.
skeat-etymological-1882:
Walter Skeat published his Etymological Dictionary of the English Language in 1882, the fruit of a life's work on word origins. Skeat, a Cambridge philologist, had edited Chaucer and founded the English Dialect Society. His dictionary traced English words back through French, Latin, Norse, and the old Germanic tongues to their roots.

Each entry gives the word's history in order, showing how its form and meaning changed on the way to modern English. Skeat worked by the new scientific rules of sound change, which let him dismiss many charming but false derivations. The book became the standard English etymology for half a century. Where our words came from is authoritatively told here, and later dictionaries, the Oxford included, built on the ground Skeat cleared.
st-osyth-true-just-recorde-1582:
A True and Just Recorde gives the full account of the witch trials at St Osyth in Essex in 1582. Fourteen people faced charges there, in the largest witch case of Queen Elizabeth's reign. The pamphlet prints the charges, the witness statements, and the confessions at length.

Because the record is so full, readers can follow how each charge was built. Neighbors tell of lost beasts, sick children, and sudden deaths blamed on hidden malice. The court sorts the claims and sends some of the accused to the gallows. No Elizabethan witch case left a richer paper trail.
stanton-history-woman-suffrage-vol-2-188:
Volume 2 of History of Woman Suffrage appeared in 1882, edited by Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B Anthony, and Matilda Joslyn Gage. The volume covers 1861 to 1876, years when the movement split and reorganized. The editors again built the history from speeches, letters, and reports.

War work by women, the fight over the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments, and the founding of rival suffrage groups fill the record. The editors' own National Woman Suffrage Association stands at the center of their telling. State campaigns and early votes, including women voting in western territories, get full documentation. The volume preserves the words of a movement arguing with itself and with the nation.
stephen-science-ethics-1882:
Leslie Stephen wrote The Science of Ethics in 1882, bringing Darwin's theory to bear on moral life. Stephen was a leading man of letters and a frank agnostic. He asked whether ethics could rest on science rather than on church command. The book was his most sustained work of philosophy.

Stephen traces moral rules to the health and survival of the social group. Feelings of right and wrong, he argues, grow as societies grow. He tests his view against rival schools, including the utilitarians he partly followed. The result is a calm, tough piece of Victorian thought. It helped set terms for later ethics.
stevenson-new-arabian-nights-1882:
Robert Louis Stevenson modeled The New Arabian Nights on the old tales of Harun al-Rashid wandering Baghdad in disguise. He published the stories in magazines, then as his first book, in 1882. The setting is not Baghdad but gaslit Victorian London.

Prince Florizel of Bohemia roams London at night hunting adventure, with his loyal colonel at his side. In The Suicide Club he infiltrates a society where tired men draw cards for death. A second cycle follows a diamond stolen and passed from hand to hand. Stevenson mixes danger with wry humor and polished style. The book launched his career as a teller of tales.
strindberg-lucky-pehr-1882:
August Strindberg wrote Lucky Pehr in 1882, an allegorical five-act fairy play, here in Velma Swanston Howard's translation. Howard's authorized translation carried Strindberg's most performed early play to English-speaking stages and readers in print. The play mixes folk tale, satire, and dream in a form all Strindberg's own at twenty-three.

Pehr, a church verger's son, finds a ring that grants wishes and rides luck up the world. He tries wealth, fame, and love, and each gift sours in his hands by the tale's logic. A cathedral tower, a talking statue, and a chorus of townsfolk frame his rise and fall in life. At last he renounces the ring and chooses honest work and love without magic's false ease and shine. The fable's charm hides a sharp moral on ambition that Strindberg never outgrew in art.
the-phrenological-magazine-volume-3-1882: The Phrenological Magazine, volume 3, 1882. The magazine volume. This book preserves that periodical. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes.
tob-4282:
Apollodorus of Athens gets credit for the Library, the ancient world's own handbook of Greek mythology. Gods, heroes, and their tangled families march in order from the first beings to the Trojan War and the heroes' returns. James George Frazer translated it for the Loeb series in 1921, with rich notes.

A student who needs to know how Heracles ties to Perseus, or which king fathered which monster-slayer, finds the answer here in plain prose. The Library lacks poetry; it offers system instead, which scholars crave. Verified from the 1919 edition record, Frazer's Apollodorus remains antiquity's one-stop reference for its own myths.
tolstoy-confession-1882: A Confession and What I Believe, Tolstoy's 1882 spiritual crisis. The count's confession. This book preserves that work. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
un-ga-res-a-69-82:
Germ and toxin arms are banned by a pact that still lacks some states, and Resolution A/69/82, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, presses for its full reach. The Convention on Bacteriological and Toxin Weapons bars the making, holding, and storing of such arms, and calls for their destruction. One hundred seventy states had joined the pact by the time of this vote, among them all five permanent members of the Security Council.

States that signed but have not yet ratified are called to do so without delay. States that have not signed are urged to join at the soonest date. A full, world-wide ban, the Assembly holds, is the only fit end for arms of this kind.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/82 of the General Assembly, adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, concerns the Convention banning bacteriological (biological) and toxin weapons. With 170 states parties, it presses for universal membership. It calls on parties to file their annual confidence-building information by 15 April. It notes the 2012-2015 round of expert and states parties meetings. It looks ahead to the Eighth Review Conference, due in Geneva by 2016.
un-sc-res-1382:
The Security Council's Resolution 1382 on Iraq's oil-for-food program was adopted on 29 November 2001. The program let Iraq sell oil to buy food and medicine for its people. Sanctions were then eleven years old. A plan for smarter sanctions would screen only goods that might serve war.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the program for 180 days from 1 December 2001. It adopts a Goods Review List to take effect on 30 May 2002. Goods on the list, like night vision gear and special electronics, need committee approval before export. Inspectors must judge whether each item could be diverted to military use. All other civilian goods would flow freely under the new plan.
un-sc-res-1482:
Two Rwanda tribunal judges needed to finish their trials past their terms in 2003. Cases before them were close to judgment when their time ran out. On 19 May 2003 the Security Council let both judges complete the work they had begun. One would finish the Cyangugu case, due by February 2004. The other would finish a second trial on the same terms. Three more cases were set to end by December 2003.

The tribunal's president had to report on progress three times. The dates were August and November 2003 and January 2004. The step bent the court's normal rotation rules. Losing a judge mid-trial would have forced costly restarts. The text keeps justice moving without wasting years of testimony.
un-sc-res-1582: Security Council Resolution 1582 is held here as a record transcription, sourced from English Wikisource. The Council's resolutions form the backbone of UN action on conflicts, sanctions, and missions. This one follows the common pattern, grounding its decisions in stated findings first. The preservation of the exact phrasing is the point of the entry.
un-sc-res-1682:
More troops and police for Côte d'Ivoire were authorized by the Security Council on 2 June 2006. The Council voiced serious concern that the crisis and the blocks on peace and reconciliation persisted from all sides. The Secretary-General had recommended reinforcements in his January and April reports. The country stayed split between the government south and the Forces nouvelles north.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council raised the strength of the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire by up to 1,500 staff until 15 December 2006. The increase allowed at most 1,025 extra military personnel and 475 civilian police. The Council said it would keep the mission's proper size under review as events unfolded in the country and the subregion. The build-up aimed to give the peacekeepers weight to protect civilians and back the road map toward elections that kept slipping.
un-sc-res-1782:
Côte d'Ivoire sanctions are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1782, adopted on 29 October 2007. The Ouagadougou peace deal had been signed that March. First steps had begun, but voter listing, disarmament, and army reform all lagged. An expert group had also reported fresh breaches of the diamond rules.

The text renews the arms embargo and related bans until 31 October 2008. The ban on rough diamond exports from the earlier sanctions round stays in force too. A review will come by 30 April 2008 at the latest, or after free elections. The expert group keeps its mandate for the same full year.
un-sc-res-182:
Apartheid's arms supply lines were widened as a target on 4 December 1963. The Secretary-General's report on states' replies lay before the Council. South Africa's foreign minister had confirmed in October that Pretoria would not comply with resolution 181 (1963). The General Assembly's October text on apartheid had won overwhelming support.

The Council appealed to all states to honor resolution 181 (1963), the first arms embargo text. South Africa was urgently asked to stop its discriminatory and repressive measures at once. Its refusal to comply was condemned. All who were jailed or restricted for opposing apartheid were to be freed. States were solemnly called to halt the sale of gear and materials for making and maintaining arms and ammunition in South Africa. A small group of recognized experts would be set up under the Secretary-General to study ways of settling the race conflict in peace.
un-sc-res-1882:
Children in war gained wider grounds for the Council's name-and-shame lists on 4 August 2009. The Council restated its line of texts from 1261 (1999) to 1612 (2005). Monitoring under 1612 had freed children and opened talks with armed groups, it noted. Yet parties still broke the law shielding children without penalty in too many places.

The Council strongly condemned every breach of the law protecting children in armed conflict. Recruiting child soldiers, killing and maiming them, and rape and other sexual violence all counted. The monitoring and reporting mechanism would run on. The Secretary-General was asked to list in his report annexes the parties guilty of killing, maiming, or sexual violence against children, not only recruiters. His working group machinery and country task forces were backed. States bore the duty to end impunity and prosecute those who commit grave crimes against children.
un-sc-res-282: Council action recorded as Resolution 282 appears in this catalog under the year 1963. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-582: United Nations record keeping gives this text the number 582, and the catalog dates it 1925. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-82:
North Korean troops crossed the 38th parallel on 25 June 1950. The Security Council met the same day in New York. It recalled that South Korea's government had been found lawful by the General Assembly. That government rested on elections watched by a United Nations commission. The Council then determined that the attack was a breach of the peace. Few findings in its history carry more weight.

Hostilities had to stop at once. North Korea's authorities had to pull their forces back to the 38th parallel. The United Nations Commission on Korea had to help apply the resolution. It also had to report on the facts. All member states were told to aid the United Nations and to give North Korea no help.
un-sc-res-982: Council action recorded as Resolution 982 appears in this catalog under the year 1995. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
The situation in the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia is the business of the Security Council's 3982nd meeting, held in February 1999 and kept in this verbatim record. The Council had before it a report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Preventive Deployment Force, a small mission posted on Macedonia's borders to deter spillover from wars nearby.

Delegates debate the force's future as its mandate nears its end. The record keeps each statement as delivered, with Canada's ambassador in the president's chair. Weeks later the Kosovo war would test the region. The file is a full primary record of the Council at work.

Iraq's oil-for-food programme is extended and its import controls redesigned in Resolution 1382, adopted on 29 November 2001. The humanitarian programme under Resolution 986 (1995) was again expiring. The Council had before it a proposed Goods Review List. The list was meant to focus controls on military and dual-use goods while speeding civilian imports.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council keeps the Resolution 986 (1995) arrangements in force for a new 180-day period beginning 1 December 2001. It adopts the proposed Goods Review List and its application procedures, subject to any refinements agreed in further consultations, for implementation from 30 May 2002. The annexed list covers dual-use categories such as advanced materials, electronics, computers, telecommunications, sensors and lasers, navigation equipment, and propulsion, plus specified items from night-vision systems to missile test equipment. States are pressed to process applications quickly so urgently needed humanitarian supplies reach Iraqis fast.

Four judges at the Rwanda war crimes court faced a time trap in 2003. Their terms were about to end. Their trials were not done. A change of bench mid-case could force a fresh start. The court's head wrote to ask for a fix in March. Resolution 1482 passed with no dissent on 19 May 2003.

Each named judge could stay to close a case. Dolenc and Ostrovsky would end the Cyangugu trial. Maqutu would end two trials, Kajelijeli and Kamuhanda. Pillay would end the famed Media case. Set end dates were named: most by the close of 2003. The Cyangugu case had to February 2004. Progress notes were due in August, then November, then January.

Georgia's observer mission, UNOMIG, is extended on 28 January 2005, and the Abkhazia parties are pressed to negotiate yet again. The pattern of earlier texts holds: Geneva meetings kept the process alive, no settlement was in sight, and the 2001 helicopter attack remained unsolved. A fresh report from the Secretary-General informed the renewal.

Both sides are urged to enter constructive talks toward a political settlement and to take concrete steps to revive the process. Calls to settle the division of powers between Tbilisi and Sukhumi on the basis of the agreed principles paper are repeated. The Abkhaz side is pressed in particular to improve law enforcement in the Gali district and to allow teaching in the Georgian language there.

Extra troops and police for a stalled peace process are authorized by Resolution 1682, adopted on 2 June 2006. Côte d'Ivoire remained split after its civil war, and the Council voiced serious concern at obstacles thrown up by all sides. Reports from the Secretary-General in January and April had recommended reinforcing the UN operation there, known as UNOCI.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorized an increase in UNOCI's strength until 15 December 2006. The reinforcement drew on the Secretary-General's recommendations, which were repeated in his April report. The decision shows how the Council used temporary surges to protect a peace process it feared was sliding backward, while keeping the extra deployment on a fixed clock.

Côte d'Ivoire's sanctions are renewed by Resolution 1782, adopted on 29 October 2007. The Ouagadougou Political Agreement was being put into effect, but voter identification, militia disarmament, and restoring state authority all lagged. An attack in Bouaké on 29 June 2007 against the Prime Minister had killed several people, and the Group of Experts reported breaches of the diamond measure.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms embargo, travel ban, asset freeze, and diamond measures from Resolutions 1572 (2004) and 1643 (2005) until 31 October 2008. It demands that the Ivorian authorities end violations at once and give the Group of Experts, UNOCI, and the French forces unhindered access. Blocking their freedom of movement counts as a threat to the peace process and can trigger targeted measures. The Group of Experts is extended to 31 October 2008, with a midterm report by 15 April 2008.

On 4 December 1963 the Security Council took up the race conflict in South Africa, created by the apartheid policies of the South African government. Members were troubled that South Africa had refused to follow Resolution 181 from earlier that year. The Council said the situation was seriously disturbing peace and security around the world.

Resolution 182 condemns South Africa for ignoring UN appeals and for keeping harsh, race-based measures in force. It again asks South Africa to free everyone jailed, held, or restricted for opposing apartheid. It calls on all states to stop selling equipment and materials used to make or maintain arms in South Africa. It also asks for a small group of experts to study peaceful ways to win full human rights for everyone in the country.

Resolution 1882, adopted on 4 August 2009, widens the net used to shame armies that harm children. The monitoring system built since 2005 had listed parties mainly for recruiting child soldiers. Progress was real in places, the Council noted, with children released and action plans agreed, but violations continued with impunity in several conflicts.

The Council expanded the listing criteria. Parties that engage in patterns of killing and maiming children, or in rape or other sexual violence aimed at children in war, could now be named in the Secretary-General's annexes as well. National governments were reminded that protecting children is their job first, and that UN task forces exist to support, not replace, that duty.

South Africa's apartheid system is the target of Resolution 282, adopted in 1970. Forty member states had brought the question of race conflict in South Africa before the Council. Earlier Council calls for an arms embargo, from 1963 and 1964, were being broken.

The Council restated its total opposition to apartheid. It condemned the violations of the arms embargo. All states were called on to strengthen the embargo by applying it fully. No conditions or reservations were to be attached, and the embargo had to be strictly obeyed. The text warned that South Africa's military build-up was a threat. It endangered the security and independence of African states that opposed South Africa's racist policies.

The war between Iran and Iraq had run for nearly six years when the Council adopted Resolution 582 on 24 February 1986. The vote was unanimous. Both countries were bound by the 1925 Geneva Protocol, which bans poison gas in war. The fighting had spread to attacks on cities, shipping, and civilian aircraft.

The Council deplored the acts that had started the conflict and the way it had grown. The bombing of purely civilian centers was named in particular. Iran and Iraq were called on to observe an immediate cease-fire. It had to cover land, sea, and air, and all forces had to pull back to the recognized international borders. A full exchange of prisoners of war was urged soon after the fighting stopped. The Red Cross would help with that exchange. Both sides were also told to put their dispute to mediation at once.

War came to Korea on a Sunday in June 1950. North Korean troops swept south at dawn on 25 June. The Council met that same day in New York. The Soviet team was away, in a boycott of the body. That gap let the West act fast. Resolution 82 passed by nine votes to none. Yugoslavia held back.

The attack was ruled a breach of the peace. Guns had to fall still at once. North troops had to pull back to the 38th parallel, the line that split the land. UN men in Korea would watch the pull-back. They would send word of what they saw with all speed. All states were told to back the UN's work. None could give aid to the North's chiefs. Two days on, the Council would urge states to fight for the South.

Bosnia's war paused under a fragile cease-fire agreed in December 1994. The Bosnian government had accepted a peace plan put forward by the Contact Group of major states. The United Nations Protection Force, UNPROFOR, was working in Bosnia and in Croatia. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 22 March 1995, set out new arrangements. Resolution 982 was adopted unanimously on 31 March 1995.

The Council extended UNPROFOR's mandate in Bosnia until 30 November 1995. It approved the arrangements in the Secretary-General's report. Most of the force's people and equipment had to leave Croatia by 30 June 1995. Those needed for the new, separate Croatia operation, called UNCRO, could stay. The force's support structures in Croatia would remain in place. The parties were reminded of one duty in particular. The safety of UNPROFOR was their responsibility.
weyer-de-lamiis-latin-1582:
Johann Weyer, the Dutch physician whose De praestigiis daemonum first pleaded for accused witches, published De lamiis in 1582. The shorter Latin book gives his focused treatise on lamiae alone, the harmful women of classical and popular fear. It is Weyer's other witch book, distinct from the famous work the library also holds.

Weyer argues that the supposed witches are mostly ill, melancholy, or deceived. Their confessions describe dreams and delusions, not deeds. Mercy follows from medicine in his careful Latin. He urges judges to send such women to doctors, not to fires. The tract distills the outlook that made Weyer the accused witch's first great defender.
yusuf-zulaikha-jami-griffith-1882:
Ralph T. H. Griffith translated Jami's Yusuf and Zulaikha into English verse in 1882, for Trubner's Oriental Series. Jami, the last great classical poet of Persia, retold the story of Joseph and Potiphar's wife in the 1400s. The Quran and Persian tradition had already made Zulaikha's love a figure of the soul's longing for God.

Griffith follows Jami through Joseph's beauty, his trials, and Zulaikha's long, refining passion. In Sufi reading, her desire is purified until it becomes devotion itself. The Victorian rendering became the classic English dress of the poem. Griffith, known for his Ramayana and Rigveda versions, brought the same care here. The romance remains the crown of Jami's seven poems.
zola-piping-hot-1882:
Vizetelly issued Piping Hot in London in 1887, rendered from the sixty-third French edition. Sixteen page engravings from designs by Georges Bellenger illustrate the book. The French title, Pot-Bouille, names a bubbling stewpot in common slang.

Behind the grand front of a Paris apartment house, Zola finds a stew of vice. Adultery, false piety, and social climbing simmer on every floor. Young Octave Mouret charms his way upward from room to room. Bourgeois morals rot from within while faces stay smooth in public. Sharp and often funny, the 1882 novel may be Zola's most savage comedy of middle-class manners.
